## Summary
This document provides essential notes on gastrointestinal pathology, focusing on conditions of the small and large intestines and the peritoneal cavity, comprising Part 2 of 2. It covers intestinal obstruction (Hirschsprung disease, hernias), vascular disorders (ischemic bowel disease, hemorrhoids), various forms of malabsorptive diarrhea (celiac disease, Crohn disease, tropical sprue, Whipple disease), and a comprehensive overview of infectious enterocolitis caused by bacteria (cholera, Shigella, E. coli, Salmonella, C. difficile), viruses (Rotavirus), and parasites (Giardiasis, Cryptosporidiosis, Amoebiasis, Hookworms, Strongyloidiasis). Additionally, it details inflammatory intestinal diseases like appendicitis and inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease, Ulcerative Colitis), and discusses neoplasms including colorectal adenomas and adenocarcinomas, and appendiceal carcinoid. The final section addresses ascites in the peritoneal cavity, outlining its pathophysiology. A high-yield exam summary provides key facts across all covered topics.

## Key Points
-   **Aphthous ulcers:** Up to 40% population; associated with coeliac, IBD, Behçet; resolve 7–10 days
-   **HSV oral:** Multinucleated polykaryons + eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions
-   **Oral candidiasis:** Scrapes off (unlike leukoplakia); pseudomembranous = most common form
-   **Leukoplakia vs erythroplakia:** Erythroplakia has MUCH higher malignant transformation risk (>50%)
-   **Oral SCC:** 95% of oral cancers; two pathways: tobacco/alcohol vs HPV-16; field cancerisation
-   **HPV oral SCC:** Tonsillar crypts/tongue base; better prognosis; overexpresses p16
-   **Xerostomia:** Medications most common cause; >20% over age 70; Sjögren hallmark
-   **Mumps:** Parotids; orchitis in adults → sterility
-   **Mucocele:** Most common salivary inflammatory lesion; lower lip; blockage/rupture of duct
-   **Oesophageal varices:** 90% of cirrhotics; 50% die from first bleed; alcoholic cirrhosis most common
-   **Mallory-Weiss vs Boerhaave:** Superficial/mucosal vs transmural + mediastinitis
-   **GERD morphology:** Eosinophils first → neutrophils; basal zone hyperplasia >20%; papillae elongation
-   **Barrett oesophagus:** Goblet cells define intestinal metaplasia; 10% of symptomatic GERD
-   **Achalasia:** Triad: incomplete LES relaxation + ↑LES tone + aperistalsis; Chagas = secondary
-   **Oesophageal SCC vs adenocarcinoma:** SCC: middle third; alcohol + tobacco; adenocarcinoma: distal third; Barrett
-   **H. pylori virulence:** Flagella, urease, adhesins, CagA toxin
-   **H. pylori vs Autoimmune gastritis:** H. pylori = antrum, ↑acid; Autoimmune = body/fundus, achlorhydria, pernicious anaemia
-   **Cushing vs Curling ulcers:** Cushing = intracranial disease, high perforation risk; Curling = burns/trauma, proximal duodenum
-   **Zollinger-Ellison:** Gastrinoma → massive acid → ulcers even in jejunum
-   **PUD pain:** 1–3 hours after meals; relieved by alkali or food
-   **GIST:** c-KIT or PDGFRA mutations; interstitial cells of Cajal; imatinib
-   **Hirschsprung:** RET mutation; aganglionosis; always involves rectum; absent ganglion cells on biopsy
-   **Ischaemic bowel:** Watershed zones: splenic flexure + rectosigmoid; surface necrosis + hyperproliferative crypts
-   **Reperfusion injury:** Greatest damage occurs at reperfusion not at initial ischaemia
-   **Coeliac disease:** HLA-DQ2/DQ8; anti-tissue transglutaminase most sensitive; dermatitis herpetiformis 10%; enteropathy-associated T cell lymphoma
-   **Cholera:** Cholera toxin → ↑cAMP → CFTR opens → Cl⁻ secretion; non-invasive; fluid replacement saves >99%
-   **Shigella:** Infective dose <100 organisms; Shiga toxin → HUS; no antidiarrhoeals
-   **Typhoid:** Rose spots; Peyer patch enlargement; typhoid nodules in liver; gallbladder chronic carrier state; sickle cell → osteomyelitis
-   **C. difficile:** Volcano pattern pseudomembranes; treat with metronidazole/vancomycin; no antidiarrhoeals
-   **Rotavirus:** 6–24 months; destroys mature enterocytes; breast milk antibodies protect first 6 months
-   **Hookworms:** Leading cause iron deficiency anaemia in developing world
-   **Giardia:** Pear-shaped trophozoites; evades immunity by variant surface protein; decreases lactase
-   **Acute appendicitis:** Diagnosis requires neutrophil infiltration of muscularis propria; McBurney's sign; faecalith 50–80%
-   **Appendix carcinoid:** Almost always benign; distal tip; pseudomyxoma peritonei from adenocarcinoma
-   **FAP vs HNPCC:** FAP: APC mutation, >100 polyps, cancer <30; HNPCC: mismatch repair genes, fewer polyps
-   **Colorectal adenocarcinoma:** Two most important prognostic factors: depth of invasion + lymph node metastases
-   **Ascites:** Cirrhosis triad: ascites, encephalopathy, bleeding varices; RAAS activation; Child-Pugh score

## Detailed Notes

## SECTION 4: SMALL AND LARGE INTESTINES

**Conditions covered:** Intestinal Obstruction · Vascular Disorders · Malabsorptive Diarrhoea · Infectious Enterocolitis · Inflammatory Intestinal Disease

## 4.1 Intestinal Obstruction

### Hirschsprung Disease (Congenital Aganglionic Megacolon)
-   Occurs in approximately **1 in 5000 live births**
-   More common in **males**; tends to be more severe in **females**
-   Siblings of affected patients have increased risk
-   **Presentation:** neonate fails to pass meconium in immediate postnatal period → obstructive constipation
-   **Life-threatening complications:** enterocolitis, fluid and electrolyte disturbances, perforation, peritonitis
-   Treatment: surgical resection of aganglionic segment + anastomosis of normal colon to rectum

**Pathogenesis:**
-   Enteric neuronal plexus develops from **neural crest cells** migrating into bowel wall during embryogenesis
-   Hirschsprung disease = disruption of normal migration of neural crest cells **from caecum to rectum**
-   Produces distal intestinal segment lacking both **Meissner submucosal plexus** and **Auerbach myenteric plexus** = **aganglionosis**
-   No coordinated peristaltic contractions → functional obstruction → **dilation proximal to affected segment**
-   **Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in RET** (receptor tyrosine kinase) → majority of familial cases and ~15% of sporadic cases

**Morphology:**
-   Always affects the **rectum**; length of additional involved segments varies
-   Most cases limited to **rectum and sigmoid colon**; severe disease can involve entire colon
-   Aganglionic region: grossly normal or contracted appearance
-   Normally innervated proximal colon: undergoes **progressive dilation** from distal obstruction
-   **Diagnosis requires demonstrating absence of ganglion cells** in affected segment

### Abdominal Hernia
-   Any weakness or defect in peritoneal cavity wall → protrusion of serosa-lined pouch = **hernia sac**
-   Acquired hernias most common anteriorly: **inguinal and femoral canals, umbilicus**, or surgical scar sites
-   **Inguinal hernias:** narrow orifices and large sacs → small bowel loops most commonly herniated; omentum or large bowel also protrude
-   Pressure at neck of pouch → impaired venous drainage → stasis and oedema → increased bulk → permanent entrapment = **incarceration**
-   Over time: arterial and venous compromise = **strangulation** → infarction

## 4.2 Vascular Disorders of Bowel

### Ischaemic Bowel Disease

**Depth of Injury — Three Levels:**
-   **Mucosal infarction** — extends no deeper than muscularis mucosa; often secondary to acute/chronic hypoperfusion
-   **Mural infarction** — mucosa and submucosa; also from hypoperfusion
-   **Transmural infarction** — all three layers; generally caused by **acute vascular obstruction**

**Causes of Acute Arterial Obstruction:**
-   Severe **atherosclerosis** (often at origin of mesenteric vessels)
-   Aortic aneurysm
-   Hypercoagulable states
-   Oral contraceptive use
-   Embolisation of cardiac vegetations or aortic atheromas

**Other Causes:**
-   Intestinal hypoperfusion: cardiac failure, shock, dehydration, vasoconstrictive drugs
-   Systemic vasculitides: polyarteritis nodosa, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, Wegener granulomatosis
-   Mesenteric venous thrombosis (uncommon): invasive neoplasms, cirrhosis, portal hypertension, trauma, compressing abdominal masses
-   CMV infection — viral tropism for endothelial cells → ischaemic GI disease (especially in immunosuppressed)

**Pathogenesis — Two Phases:**
1.  **Initial hypoxic injury** — at onset of vascular compromise; intestinal epithelial cells relatively resistant to transient hypoxia
2.  **Reperfusion injury** — initiated by restoration of blood supply; **greatest damage occurs here**; mechanisms: free radical production, neutrophil infiltration, release of inflammatory mediators (complement, cytokines); severe cases → multiorgan failure

**Two Key Anatomical Vulnerabilities:**
1.  **Watershed zones** — intestinal segments at ends of arterial supplies = most susceptible:
    -   **Splenic flexure** (where superior and inferior mesenteric arterial circulations terminate)
    -   **Sigmoid colon and rectum** (where inferior mesenteric, pudendal, and iliac circulations end)
    -    Generalised hypotension → localised injury at watershed zones; ischaemia should be considered in focal colitis of splenic flexure or rectosigmoid colon
2.  **Intestinal capillary anatomy** — capillaries run alongside glands from crypt to surface → hairpin turn at surface → surface epithelium vulnerable; crypts (containing stem cells) protected
    -    **Surface epithelial atrophy/necrosis with normal or hyperproliferative crypts = morphologic signature of ischaemic intestinal disease**

**Morphology:**
-   Mucosal and mural infarction may involve any gut level from stomach to anus; frequently segmental and patchy
-   Mucosa: **haemorrhagic and often ulcerated**; bowel wall thickened by oedema
-   Severe disease: extensive mucosal and submucosal haemorrhage and necrosis; serosal haemorrhage and serositis generally absent
-   **Coagulative necrosis of muscularis propria** within 1–4 days → purulent serositis and perforation
-   Mesenteric venous thrombosis: arterial blood continues flowing → less abrupt transition from affected to normal bowel
-   Microscopy: **atrophy or sloughing of surface epithelium; crypts may be hyperproliferative**
-   Acute ischaemia: inflammatory infiltrates initially absent; neutrophils recruited within hours of reperfusion
-   Chronic ischaemia: fibrous scarring of lamina propria; uncommonly stricture formation
-   Bacterial superinfection in acute phases → enterotoxin release → **pseudomembrane formation** (can resemble C. difficile pseudomembranous colitis)

**Clinical Features:**
-   Tends to occur in **older persons** with coexisting cardiac or vascular disease
-   Acute transmural infarction: **sudden severe abdominal pain and tenderness**; nausea, vomiting, bloody diarrhoea, melanotic stool; progresses to shock and vascular collapse within hours
-   Peristaltic sounds diminish/disappear; muscular spasm → **boardlike abdominal wall rigidity**
-   Overlaps with acute appendicitis, perforated ulcer, acute cholecystitis → diagnosis may be delayed
-   Mucosal barrier breakdown → bacteria enter circulation → **sepsis**; mortality may exceed **50%**

**Progression:**
-   Mucosal/mural infarctions: may not be fatal but can progress if vascular supply not restored
-   Chronic ischaemia: may masquerade as **IBD** — episodes of bloody diarrhoea interspersed with healing
-   **Radiation enterocolitis:** epithelial damage + radiation-induced vascular injury → ischaemia-like changes; "**radiation fibroblasts**" in stroma; acute = anorexia, cramps, malabsorptive diarrhoea; chronic = indolent inflammatory colitis
-   **Necrotising enterocolitis:** acute disorder with transmural necrosis; most common acquired GI emergency of **neonates** (especially premature/low birth weight); occurs most often when oral feeding initiated
-   **Angiodysplasia:** malformed submucosal and mucosal blood vessels; most often **caecum or right colon**; usually after **sixth decade**; prevalence <1% but accounts for **20% of major lower intestinal bleeding episodes**; pathogenesis unknown

### Haemorrhoids
-   Dilated anal and perianal collateral vessels connecting **portal and caval venous systems**
-   Affect about **5% of general population**
-   Pathogenesis similar to oesophageal varices — but more common and less serious
-   **Predisposing factors:** constipation and straining (↑intra-abdominal and venous pressure), venous stasis of pregnancy, portal hypertension

**Morphology:**
-   **External haemorrhoids** — collateral vessels within inferior haemorrhoidal plexus; **below anorectal line**
-   **Internal haemorrhoids** — dilation of superior haemorrhoidal plexus; within **distal rectum**
-   Histology: thin-walled dilated submucosal vessels projecting beneath anal/rectal mucosa
-   Subject to trauma → inflamed, thrombosed, recanalized; superficial ulceration may occur

**Clinical Features:**
-   **Pain and rectal bleeding** — bright red blood on toilet tissue
-   Rarely encountered in persons younger than **30 years** (except pregnant women)
-   Portal hypertension: haemorrhoids develop with more ominous implications
-   Treatment: sclerotherapy, rubber band ligation, infrared coagulation; severe cases → haemorrhoidectomy
-   Haemorrhoidal bleeding generally **NOT a medical emergency**

## 4.3 Malabsorptive Diarrhoea

### Classification of Diarrhoea

**Definition:** increase in stool mass, frequency, or fluidity → typically **>200 mL/day**; severe cases can exceed **14 L/day** → death without fluid resuscitation
-   **Dysentery** — painful, bloody, small-volume diarrhoea

**Four Major Categories:**

| Type          | Key Features                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| :------------ | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Secretory** | Isotonic stool; **persists during fasting**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Osmotic**   | Osmotic forces from unabsorbed luminal components; carbohydrate malabsorption is example; **abates with fasting**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Exudative** | Inflammatory disease → active inflammation with purulent, bloody stools; **persists during fasting**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Malabsorption** | Failure of nutrient absorption → bulky, greasy stools; often relieved by fasting                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

### Coeliac Disease (Gluten-Sensitive Enteropathy)
-   Immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by ingestion of **gluten-containing foods** (wheat, barley, rye)
-   Genetic predisposition (strong association with **HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8**)
-   Prevalence: **1% in Western populations**
-   **Pathogenesis:**
    -   Gliadin (alcohol-soluble fraction of gluten) deamidated by **tissue transglutaminase (tTG)**
    -   Deamidated gliadin presented by APCs to CD4+ T cells in lamina propria → T-cell activation → cytokine release → epithelial cell damage
-   **Morphology:**
    -   Most striking in **duodenum and proximal jejunum**
    -   Characterised by **villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs)**
    -   Villous atrophy: reduced surface area → malabsorption
    -   Crypt hyperplasia: compensatory increase in enterocyte production
    -   IELs: T lymphocytes between enterocytes
    -   Severity correlates with duration/intensity of gluten exposure
    -   Normalisation of mucosa after gluten withdrawal
-   **Clinical Features:**
    -   Variable: range from silent to severe
    -   Infants: abdominal distention, FTT, anorexia, muscle wasting
    -   Adults: anaemia, fatigue, chronic diarrhoea, bloating
    -   **Dermatitis herpetiformis:** pruritic vesicular skin lesions, affects **10%** of patients
    -   Diagnosis:
        -   Antibodies: **anti-tTG (most sensitive), anti-endomysial (EMA), anti-gliadin (DGP)**
        -   Biopsy: characteristic villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, IELs
        -   Clinical improvement on gluten-free diet
-   **Complications:**
    -   Increased risk of other autoimmune diseases (Type 1 diabetes, thyroiditis)
    -   **Small intestinal T-cell lymphoma (enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma - EATL)**
    -   Small risk of adenocarcinoma

### Crohn Disease (CD)
-   Chronic inflammatory condition of GI tract; typically **transmural**
-   Any part of GI tract from mouth to anus, but most commonly **terminal ileum and colon**
-   **"Skip lesions"** — normal intervening bowel
-   **Granulomas** (non-caseating) characteristic, but not always present
-   **Pathogenesis:**
    -   Complex interplay of genetic, immune, and environmental factors
    -   Genetic: NOD2 gene mutations (impaired bacterial clearance/immune response)
    -   Immune: Dysregulated T-cell response to commensal bacteria
-   **Morphology:**
    -   **Gross:**
        -   **"Cobblestoning"** of mucosa due to deep ulcerations and intervening oedematous mucosa
        -   **"Creeping fat"** — mesenteric fat wraps around bowel
        -   **Strictures, fissures, fistulas**
    -   **Microscopic:**
        -   **Transmural inflammation**
        -   **Non-caseating granulomas** in ~30% of cases
        -   Crypt abscesses, architectural distortion
-   **Clinical Features:**
    -   Abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss, fever
    -   Extraintestinal manifestations: arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, primary sclerosing cholangitis (less common than UC)
    -   Can mimic acute appendicitis when terminal ileum involved

### Tropical Sprue
-   Acquired malabsorptive disorder in individuals living in or visiting **tropical regions**
-   Resembles coeliac disease morphologically (villous atrophy), but responds to **antibiotics**
-   Pathogenesis unclear, likely infectious aetiology
-   Clinical features: diarrhoea, weight loss, anaemia (B12 deficiency)

### Whipple Disease
-   Rare systemic disease caused by bacillus **_Tropheryma whipplei_**
-   Affects small intestine, CNS, joints, heart
-   **Pathogenesis:** bacteria engulfed by macrophages → accumulation in lamina propria
-   **Morphology:**
    -   Small intestine: lamina propria distended by **foamy macrophages** containing PAS-positive material (bacterial remnants)
    -   Macrophages impair lymphatic drainage and villous function
-   **Clinical Features:** diarrhoea, malabsorption, arthralgia, neurological symptoms, lymphadenopathy

## 4.4 Infectious Enterocolitis

### Cholera
-   Caused by **_Vibrio cholerae_** (Gram-negative bacterium)
-   Transmission: faecal-oral route, contaminated water/food
-   Incubation: **1–5 days**
-   **Pathogenesis:**
    -   Colonises small intestine, does not invade mucosa
    -   Produces **cholera toxin (CT)**: irreversibly activates adenylate cyclase → ↑cAMP in enterocytes → massive Cl⁻ secretion (via CFTR) → passive Na⁺ and water movement into lumen
-   **Clinical Features:**
    -   **Abrupt onset of watery diarrhoea** (rice-water stools)
    -   Severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, hypovolemic shock
    -   Fluid replacement is life-saving; mortality <1% with adequate treatment
    -   Antibiotics (e.g., tetracycline) shorten duration

### Campylobacter Enterocolitis
-   Common cause of bacterial gastroenteritis worldwide
-   Caused by **_Campylobacter jejuni_** (Gram-negative, curved rod)
-   Transmission: contaminated poultry, raw milk, unpurified water
-   **Pathogenesis:** invades intestinal epithelium; produces toxins (not as potent as cholera/shiga)
-   **Clinical Features:** bloody diarrhoea, fever, abdominal pain
-   **Complications:**
    -   **Guillain-Barré syndrome:** autoimmune demyelinating neuropathy (post-infection)
    -   Reactive arthritis

### Shigellosis
-   Gram-negative bacilli; encapsulated, nonmotile, facultative anaerobes
-   One of most common causes of **bloody diarrhoea**; **humans only known reservoir**
-   Estimated **165 million cases worldwide annually**
-   Highly transmissible by **faecal-oral route** or contaminated water/food
-   **Infective dose: fewer than 100 organisms** (extremely low)
-   Each gram of stool contains up to **10⁹ organisms** in acute phase
-   Most infections and deaths in **children <5 years**

**Pathogenesis:**
-   Resistant to **acidic stomach environment** (explains very low infective dose)
-   Taken up by **M (microfold) epithelial cells** → intracellular proliferation → escape into lamina propria
-   Infect colonic/small intestinal epithelial cells through **basolateral membranes** (express bacterial receptors)
-   Shigella dysenteriae serotypes release **Shiga toxin (Stx)** → inhibits eukaryotic protein synthesis → host cell death

**Morphology:**
-   Most prominent in **left colon**; ileum may also be involved (abundance of M cells over Peyer patches)
-   Early: similar to acute self-limited colitis
-   Severe: mucosa haemorrhagic and ulcerated; **pseudomembranes may be present**
-   Aphthous ulcers similar to Crohn disease (tropism for M cells) → potential confusion with IBD
-   Confirmation requires **stool culture**

**Clinical Features:**
-   Incubation: **1–7 days**; self-limited ~**6 days** of diarrhoea, fever, abdominal pain
-   Watery diarrhoea → **dysenteric phase in ~50%**; constitutional symptoms persist up to 1 month
-   Antibiotic treatment shortens course; **antidiarrhoeal medications contraindicated** (prolong symptoms by delaying bacterial clearance)
-   **Complications:**
    -   Reactive arthritis (sterile arthritis + urethritis + conjunctivitis) — **HLA-B27 positive men aged 20–40**
    -   **Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)** from Shiga toxin (also seen with EHEC)

### Escherichia coli — Pathogenic Subsets

| Subset                  | Key Features                                                                                                                                                                    |
| :---------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **ETEC** (Enterotoxigenic)    | Principal cause of **traveller's diarrhoea**; faecal-oral spread; heat labile toxin (LT) similar to cholera toxin; heat stable toxin (ST) increases intracellular cGMP           |
| **EHEC** (Enterohemorrhagic)  | O157:H7 and non-O157:H7; inadequately cooked ground beef, milk, vegetables; produces **Shiga-like toxins** → dysentery + **haemolytic uraemic syndrome**                    |
| **EIEC** (Enteroinvasive)     | Resembles Shigella bacteriologically; no toxins; invades gut epithelium → **bloody diarrhoea**                                                                                |
| **EAEC** (Enteroaggregative)  | Attaches to enterocytes by adherence fimbriae; produces LT and Shiga-like toxins; **minimal histologic damage**                                                                |

### Salmonellosis
-   Gram-negative bacilli; **Salmonella typhi** (typhoid fever) and **nontyphoid Salmonella** (gastroenteritis)
-   Nontyphoid: most often **Salmonella enteritidis**; most common in **young children and elderly**
-   Transmission: contaminated food — raw/undercooked meat, poultry, **eggs**, milk
-   Very few organisms needed; atrophic gastritis/acid-suppressive therapy reduces required inoculum
-   **Type III secretion system** transfers bacterial proteins into M cells and enterocytes → activates Rho GTPases → actin rearrangement → bacterial uptake into phagosomes

### Typhoid Fever (Enteric Fever)
-   Caused by **Salmonella typhi** and **Salmonella paratyphi**
-   Strictly human pathogen
-   Transmission: ingestion of food/water contaminated by human faeces
-   **Pathogenesis:**
    -   Bacteria taken up by M cells over Peyer patches → invade lymphoid follicles
    -   Reaches mesenteric lymph nodes → thoracic duct → bloodstream (primary bacteraemia)
    -   Disseminates to liver, spleen, bone marrow, gallbladder
    -   Secondary bacteraemia → systemic illness
    -   Gallbladder is key site for chronic carriage (often asymptomatic)
-   **Morphology:**
    -   Peyer patches: lymphoid hyperplasia → ulceration (oval-shaped)
    -   **Typhoid nodules** in liver (foci of necrosis and macrophage aggregates)
    -   Splenomegaly; bone marrow contains macrophages with ingested bacteria
-   **Clinical Features:**
    -   Incubation: 1–3 weeks
    -   Gradual onset: fever, headache, anorexia, constipation (early) or pea-soup diarrhoea (late)
    -   **"Rose spots"** on trunk (transient erythematous macules)
    -   Complications: intestinal haemorrhage/perforation, cholecystitis, osteomyelitis (especially in sickle cell patients)
    -   Diagnosis: blood culture (early), stool/urine culture (late)
    -   Treatment: antibiotics

### Pseudomembranous Colitis
-   Acute colitis with adherent inflammatory pseudomembranes on mucosa
-   Caused by **_Clostridioides difficile_** (formerly _Clostridium difficile_)
-   Associated with **antibiotic use** (disruption of normal gut flora)
-   **Pathogenesis:**
    -   _C. difficile_ overgrowth → produces **toxins A and B**
    -   Toxins cause epithelial cell necrosis, inflammation, fluid secretion
-   **Morphology:**
    -   Mucosa covered by yellow-white plaques (pseudomembranes)
    -   Microscopy: **"volcano lesion"** — erupting pseudomembrane with necrotic debris, neutrophils, fibrin
-   **Clinical Features:**
    -   Diarrhoea (watery to bloody), abdominal pain, fever
    -   Can range from mild to fulminant colitis with toxic megacolon
    -   Diagnosis: stool PCR for toxin genes
    -   Treatment: discontinue inciting antibiotic; oral metronidazole or vancomycin; faecal microbiota transplant for recurrent cases
    -   **Antidiarrhoeal agents contraindicated**

### Viral Gastroenteritis

**Rotavirus:**
-   Most common cause of **severe childhood diarrhoea** (worldwide)
-   Peak incidence: **6–24 months of age**
-   Transmission: faecal-oral
-   **Pathogenesis:** selectively destroys mature enterocytes in small intestine → impaired absorption + increased secretion
-   **Clinical Features:** vomiting, watery diarrhoea, dehydration; usually self-limited
-   Vaccination available

**Norovirus:**
-   Major cause of non-bacterial gastroenteritis in **all age groups** (especially older children and adults)
-   Highly contagious; outbreaks in crowded settings (cruise ships, schools)
-   **Clinical Features:** acute onset vomiting, diarrhoea; usually self-limited

### Parasitic Diseases

**Giardiasis:**
-   Caused by **_Giardia lamblia_** (flagellated protozoan)
-   Transmission: contaminated water (cysts resistant to chlorine), faecal-oral
-   **Pathogenesis:** trophozoites attach to brush border of small intestine → structural changes in villi, decreased lactase activity
-   **Clinical Features:** asymptomatic to chronic diarrhoea, malabsorption, bloating, steatorrhoea
-   Diagnosis: stool O&P (cysts/trophozoites) or antigen detection

**Cryptosporidiosis:**
-   Caused by **_Cryptosporidium parvum_** (protozoan)
-   Transmission: contaminated water (oocysts), faecal-oral
-   **Pathogenesis:** obligate intracellular parasite; causes villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, inflammation
-   **Clinical Features:** watery diarrhoea; severe and chronic in immunosuppressed patients (e.g., HIV/AIDS)

**Amoebiasis:**
-   Caused by **_Entamoeba histolytica_** (protozoan)
-   Transmission: contaminated food/water (cysts)
-   **Pathogenesis:** trophozoites invade colonic mucosa → flask-shaped ulcers
-   Can disseminate to liver (amoebic liver abscesses), lungs, brain
-   **Clinical Features:** asymptomatic, dysentery (bloody diarrhoea), abdominal pain
-   Diagnosis: stool O&P (trophozoites with ingested RBCs), serology for invasive disease

**Hookworm:**
-   **_Ancylostoma duodenale_** and **_Necator americanus_**
-   Transmission: larvae penetrate skin (barefoot walking)
-   Migrate to lungs → swallowed → mature in small intestine
-   Hookworms attach to intestinal mucosa and feed on blood
-   **Clinical Features:** pruritic rash ("ground itch"), pneumonitis, **iron deficiency anaemia** (major cause in developing world)

**Strongyloidiasis:**
-   **_Strongyloides stercoralis_**
-   Transmission: larvae penetrate skin
-   Unique ability for **autoinfection** (larvae mature in intestine, reinfect host) → chronic infection
-   **Hyperinfection syndrome** in immunosuppressed (life-threatening dissemination)
-   **Clinical Features:** abdominal pain, diarrhoea, rash, eosinophilia

## 4.5 Inflammatory Intestinal Disease

### Acute Appendicitis
-   Inflammation of the vermiform appendix
-   Most common in **adolescents and young adults**
-   **Pathogenesis:** typically obstruction of appendiceal lumen (faecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia, foreign body, tumour) → increased intraluminal pressure → ischaemia → bacterial overgrowth → inflammation
-   **Morphology:**
    -   Gross: swollen, congested, covered by fibrinous exudate
    -   Microscopic: **neutrophil infiltration of the muscularis propria** is diagnostic
    -   Progression: suppurative appendicitis → gangrenous appendicitis → perforation → peritonitis
-   **Clinical Features:**
    -   **Periumbilical pain** (visceral), then localises to **right lower quadrant** (somatic)
    -   **McBurney's sign:** tenderness at a specific point in RLQ
    -   Nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever, leukocytosis
    -   Complications: perforation, peritonitis, appendiceal abscess, pylephlebitis (septic portal vein thrombosis)
-   Treatment: surgical appendectomy

### Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) — Overview
-   Chronic, relapsing inflammatory disorders of uncertain aetiology
-   **Crohn Disease (CD) ** and **Ulcerative Colitis (U

C)** are the major forms
-   Genetic susceptibility, dysregulated immune response to gut microbiota, and environmental factors are involved
-   Both associated with extraintestinal manifestations (arthritis, skin lesions, eye involvement, primary sclerosing cholangitis)

### Crohn Disease (CD) — Revisited
-   **Key features:**
    -   **Discontinuous ("skip lesions")**
    -   **Transmural inflammation**
    -   **Any part of GI tract** (most commonly terminal ileum, colon)
    -   **Non-caseating granulomas** (30-50%)
    -   **Fistulas, strictures, "creeping fat," "cobblestoning"**
-   **Microscopic:** deep linear ulcers, lymphoid aggregates, granulomas

### Ulcerative Colitis (UC)
-   Chronic inflammatory disease restricted to the **colon and rectum**
-   Affects mucosa and submucosa, generally **continuous**
-   **Pathogenesis:** similar genetic, immune, environmental factors to CD, but distinct presentation
-   **Morphology:**
    -   **Gross:**
        -   Starts in rectum, extends proximally in a **continuous** fashion
        -   No skip lesions
        -   Mucosa is granular, friable, often haemorrhagic
        -   **Pseudopolyps** (islands of regenerating mucosa amidst ulceration)
        -   No strictures, fistulas (rarely toxic megacolon)
    -   **Microscopic:**
        -   **Mucosal and submucosal inflammation** only (not transmural)
        -   **Crypt abscesses** (neutrophils in crypts)
        -   Architectural distortion (branched/shortened crypts)
        -   No granulomas
-   **Clinical Features:**
    -   Bloody diarrhoea, urgency, tenesmus, abdominal pain
    -   Extraintestinal manifestations similar to CD (P.S.C. more common in UC)
    -   Risk of **colorectal carcinoma** (higher than general population, proportional to duration and extent of disease)

## 4.6 Polyps and Tumours of Colon

### Colonic Polyps

**Non-Neoplastic Polyps:**
1.  **Hyperplastic polyps:**
    -   Most common type; small, sessile, typically in left colon
    -   No malignant potential
2.  **Inflammatory polyps (Pseudopolyps):**
    -   Result from cycles of ulceration and regeneration in IBD (especially UC)
3.  **Hamartomatous polyps:**
    -   Juvenile polyps: occur in children, often solitary, no malignant potential; multiple juvenile polyps (Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome) associated with increased cancer risk
    -   Peutz-Jeghers polyps: characteristic arborising smooth muscle core; part of Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (autosomal dominant, mucocutaneous pigmentation, increased risk of GI and extra-GI cancers)

**Adenomatous Polyps (Adenomas):**
-   **Neoplastic polyps** with malignant potential; precursor to most colorectal adenocarcinomas
-   Classified by architecture: **tubular, villous, tubulovillous**
-   Risk of malignant transformation increases with:
    -   **Size** (>2 cm significantly increased risk)
    -   **Histology** (villous > tubulovillous > tubular)
    -   **High-grade dysplasia** (degree of cytologic atypia)
-   **Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP):**
    -   Autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutation in **APC gene** (tumour suppressor)
    -   Requires **>100 adenomatous polyps** for diagnosis (often thousands)
    -   Virtually **100% risk of colorectal carcinoma by age 30-50**
    -   Prophylactic colectomy recommended

### Colorectal Carcinoma — Pathogenesis
-   Develops via two main genetic pathways:
    1.  **APC/β-catenin pathway (Adenoma-Carcinoma Sequence):**
        -   **Most common pathway** (80% of sporadic cases)
        -   Initiated by **APC tumour suppressor gene mutation** (early event)
        -   Progresses through accumulation of additional mutations (KRAS, p53)
        -   Results in chromosomal instability
    2.  **Microsatellite Instability (MSI) pathway:**
        -   Accounts for 10-15% of sporadic cases
        -   Caused by mutations in **DNA mismatch repair genes**
        -   Leads to accumulation of errors in short tandem repeats (microsatellites)
        -   Associated with **Hereditary Nonpolyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC) / Lynch Syndrome**

### Hereditary Nonpolyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC) — Lynch Syndrome
-   Caused by mutations in **DNA mismatch repair genes**
-   **Far fewer polyps** than FAP; cancer at older age than FAP but **younger than sporadic** colon cancer
-   Example of **microsatellite instability pathway**

 FAP and HNPCC = two most common forms of familial colon cancer representing two distinct neoplastic transformation pathways — **both also contribute to sporadic colon cancer**

### Colorectal Adenocarcinoma
-   **Vast majority of colonic cancers are adenocarcinomas**
-   **Two most important prognostic factors:**
    1.  **Depth of invasion**
    2.  **Presence or absence of lymph node metastases**

### Tumours of the Appendix

**Carcinoid Tumour (Neuroendocrine Tumour):**
-   Most common tumour of the appendix
-   Majority are **benign** and discovered incidentally during appendectomy
-   Typically located at the **distal tip**
-   Small, indolent; rarely metastasize
-   **Carcinoid syndrome** (flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm) is rare unless extensive liver metastases or extra-GI primary

**Mucinous Adenocarcinoma / Pseudomyxoma Peritonei:**
-   Rare, but important, tumour type
-   If perforated, can cause **pseudomyxoma peritonei** (mucinous ascites, widespread peritoneal tumour implants)
-   Often originates from appendix or ovary

## 4.7 Inflammatory Bowel Disease and Cancer

-   Increased risk of colorectal carcinoma in IBD, especially **Ulcerative Colitis** and extensive/long-standing Crohn's colitis
-   Risk factors: duration of disease, extent of involvement, severity of inflammation, presence of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)
-   Dysplasia-associated lesion or mass (DALM) → surveillance endoscopy with biopsies is critical

## SECTION 7: PERITONEAL CAVITY

**Conditions covered:** Ascites

## 7.1 Ascites

-   Abnormal excessive accumulation of **fluid in peritoneal cavity**
-   **Most common** of the three major complications of cirrhosis (ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, bleeding varices)
-   One of **5 parameters of Child-Pugh score** — most widely used system for liver function assessment
-   Presence of ascites associated with poorer survival in cirrhosis: **1-year survival 85%; 5-year survival 56%**; and in hepatocellular carcinoma

**Pathophysiology — Four Reinforcing Mechanisms:**
1.  **Elevated hydrostatic pressure** from portal hypertension
2.  **Reduced osmotic pressure** from hypoalbuminaemia
3.  **Renal retention of sodium and water** from activation of **RAAS (renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system)**
4.  **Decreased effective circulatory volume** due to ascites itself
-    These factors reinforce each other in a vicious cycle

GASTROINTESTINAL PATHOLOGY (Part 1)

## Summary
This document provides essential notes on **gastrointestinal pathology**, focusing on the **oral cavity**, **oesophagus**, and **stomach**. It covers common inflammatory lesions in the oral cavity, such as **aphthous ulcers**, **HSV infections**, and **candidiasis**, alongside proliferative and neoplastic lesions like **leukoplakia**, **erythroplakia**, and **oral squamous cell carcinoma**. Diseases of the salivary glands, including **xerostomia**, **mumps**, **mucoceles**, and **bacterial sialadenitis**, are also addressed. For the oesophagus, conditions discussed range from congenital anomalies and motility disorders (e.g., **achalasia**, **hiatal hernia**) to inflammatory oesophagitis (**infectious**, **reflux**, **eosinophilic**) and the premalignant **Barrett oesophagus**. The section on the stomach details **acute and chronic gastritis** (**H. pylori** and **autoimmune**), **peptic ulcer disease**, and various gastric tumours, including **adenocarcinomas**, **lymphomas**, **carcinoid tumours**, and **gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs)**.

## Key Points

### Oral Inflammatory Lesions
**Aphthous ulcers** (canker sores) are common, painful, recurrent, and of unknown cause. **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)** infections (cold sores) are reactivations, showing **intranuclear inclusions** and **multinucleated giant cells**. **Oral Candidiasis** (thrush) is a fungal infection, typically appearing as grey-to-white membranes that **can be scraped off**, distinguishing it from leukoplakia.

### Oral Proliferative and Neoplastic Lesions
**Leukoplakia** is a white patch that **cannot be scraped off** and is considered precancerous (5-25% progress to SCC) . **Erythroplakia** is a red, velvety area with a **much greater risk of malignant transformation** (>50%). **Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)** accounts for 95% of oral cancers, is aggressive, and is linked to "**field cancerisation**." It has two main pathways: tobacco/alcohol (**TP53 mutations**) and **HPV-related** (**HPV-16**, **p16 overexpression**, better prognosis).

### Salivary Gland Diseases
**Xerostomia** (dry mouth) is common, often drug-induced or seen in **Sjögren syndrome**. **Mumps** is a viral sialadenitis (paramyxovirus), primarily affecting parotids, and can cause **pancreatitis** or **orchitis** in adults. A **mucocele** is the most common inflammatory salivary lesion, resulting from duct blockage/rupture, typically on the lower lip.

### Oesophageal Motility and Congenital Disorders
**Oesophageal atresia** is a congenital anomaly (blind pouch), often with a **tracheoesophageal fistula**, posing an aspiration risk. **Achalasia** involves incomplete LES relaxation, increased LES tone, and aperistalsis, characterized by a "**bird's beak**" appearance on barium swallow.

### Oesophageal Inflammation
**Infectious oesophagitis** affects immunocompromised patients: **HSV** causes "**punched-out**" ulcers with viral inclusions and giant cells; **CMV** causes shallower ulcers with nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions; **Candida** causes adherent grey-white pseudomembranes. **Reflux Oesophagitis (GERD)** is the most frequent cause, leading to mucosal injury from gastric acid; histology shows **eosinophils**, **basal zone hyperplasia** (>20%), and elongated papillae. **Eosinophilic Oesophagitis** is characterized by large numbers of eosinophils in the oesophageal epithelium (especially superficially and away from the GEJ), often resistant to PPIs and associated with **atopy**.

### Barrett Oesophagus
A complication of chronic GERD, **Barrett oesophagus** is defined by **intestinal metaplasia** within the oesophageal squamous mucosa, significantly increasing the risk of **oesophageal adenocarcinoma**.

### Gastritis
**Acute gastritis** involves inflammation without mucosal injury (e.g., NSAIDs, alcohol, stress); severe cases can lead to **acute haemorrhagic erosive gastropathy**. **Chronic gastritis** is characterized by mucosal inflammation, atrophy, and metaplasia.

**H. pylori Gastritis:** This is the most common chronic gastritis, predominantly affects the **antrum**, is associated with increased acid secretion, and can lead to **PUD**, **MALT lymphoma**, and **adenocarcinoma**.

**Autoimmune Gastritis:** This affects the **body and fundus**, is associated with **anti-parietal cell** and **anti-intrinsic factor antibodies**, leading to **achlorhydria** (decreased acid) and **hypergastrinemia**. It is a major cause of **pernicious anaemia** and increases gastric cancer risk.

### Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD) **Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)** is most often associated with **H. pylori infection** or **NSAID use**, commonly found in the gastric antrum and first portion of the duodenum (**duodenal ulcers are 4x more common**). It is characterized by "**punched-out**" defects, pain relieved by alkali or food, and complications including haemorrhage and perforation. **Zollinger-Ellison syndrome** causes multiple, severe ulcers due to excessive gastrin.

### Gastric Tumours
**Gastric Adenocarcinoma:** This has highly variable incidence worldwide; **H. pylori** is the most common etiologic agent. It is classified into **intestinal pattern** (bulky, ulcerated) and **diffuse pattern** (**signet ring cells**, **linitis plastica**).

**Primary Gastric Lymphoma (MALT):** Often induced by chronic **H. pylori** gastritis; **H. pylori eradication can lead to regression** of early MALT lymphoma.

**Carcinoid Tumour:** These arise from endocrine cells, are most common in the GI tract (small intestine most aggressive, appendix almost always benign). **Carcinoid syndrome** involves flushing, diarrhoea, and **right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis**.

**Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumour (GIST):** This is the most common mesenchymal tumour of the abdomen, primarily in the stomach. It arises from **interstitial cells of Cajal** and often has activating mutations in **c-KIT** or **PDGFRA**, making them **responsive to kinase inhibitors like imatinib**.

## Detailed Notes

SECTION 1: ORAL CAVITY

## 1.1 Oral Inflammatory Lesions

### Aphthous Ulcers (Canker Sores)
**Aphthous ulcers** are the most common superficial mucosal ulcerations, affecting up to **40% of the population**. They are more common in the **first two decades of life**, are extremely painful, and recurrent. The cause is **unknown**, but they are associated with **coeliac disease**, **IBD**, and **Behçet disease**, and may be familial. Lesions can be solitary or multiple, appearing as shallow hyperaemic ulcerations covered by a thin exudate, rimmed by a narrow zone of erythema. They resolve spontaneously in **7–10 days** but recur. There is no specific proven treatment, only supportive care.

### Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Infections
Most orofacial infections are caused by **HSV-1**, though **HSV-2** is increasingly common with changing sexual practices. Primary infection typically occurs in children aged **2–4 years** and is usually **asymptomatic**. However, **10–20%** manifest as **acute herpetic gingivostomatitis**, characterized by the abrupt onset of vesicles and ulcerations. Most adults harbour latent HSV-1, leading to reactivation known as a "**cold sore**" or **herpes labialis**. Reactivation can be triggered by trauma, UV light, URTI, pregnancy, menstruation, immunosuppression, temperature extremes, or allergies. Common sites include the lips, nasal orifices, buccal mucosa, gingiva, and hard palate. These lesions resolve in **7–10 days** but can persist in immunocompromised individuals, requiring **systemic antiviral therapy**.

**Morphology:** Infected cells balloon, forming **large eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions**. Adjacent cells fuse to create **large multinucleated polykaryons** (giant cells). The lesions resemble those found in oesophageal and genital herpes.

### Oral Candidiasis (Thrush)
**Oral candidiasis** is the most common **fungal** infection of the oral cavity. **Candida albicans** is a normal oral flora, causing disease only under unusual circumstances. Predisposing factors include **immunosuppression**, specific strains of *C. albicans*, altered oral microbiota from broad-spectrum antibiotics, diabetes, and a debilitated state.

There are three clinical forms:
*   **Pseudomembranous (thrush)** – the most common form.
*   Erythematous.
*   Hyperplastic.

**Pseudomembranous thrush** presents as a superficial curd-like **grey-to-white** inflammatory membrane of matted organisms enmeshed in fibrinosuppurative exudate. This membrane can be **easily scraped off**, revealing an erythematous base. In cases of mild immunosuppression (e.g., diabetics), the infection is usually superficial; however, in severe immunosuppression, it can spread to deeper sites. A key distinction in examination is that thrush **scrapes off**, whereas leukoplakia does **NOT**.

## 1.2 Proliferative and Neoplastic Lesions

### Fibrous Proliferative Lesions

**Fibromas**
**Fibromas** are submucosal nodular fibrous tissue masses resulting from **chronic irritation**, leading to reactive connective tissue hyperplasia. They are most often found on the **buccal mucosa along the bite line**. Treatment involves complete surgical excision and removal of the irritant source.

**Pyogenic Granulomas**
**Pyogenic granulomas** are pedunculated masses typically found on the **gingiva** of children, young adults, and **pregnant women**. They are richly vascular and typically ulcerated, giving them a **red to purple colour**. Their rapid growth can raise concern for malignancy, but histology reveals dense immature vessel proliferation, resembling granulation tissue. These lesions can regress, mature into a dense fibrous mass, or develop into a **peripheral ossifying fibroma**. Treatment involves complete surgical excision.

### Leukoplakia and Erythroplakia

**Leukoplakia**
The WHO defines **leukoplakia** as a white patch or plaque that **cannot be scraped off** AND cannot be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other disease. The term is reserved for lesions with **no known aetiologic factor**. Approximately **3% of the world population** has leukoplakic lesions. Importantly, **5–25% are premalignant** and may progress to **SCC**, meaning **ALL leukoplakias must be considered precancerous** until proved otherwise by histologic evaluation.

**Erythroplakia**
**Erythroplakia** is a red, velvety, possibly eroded area that is flat or slightly depressed relative to the surrounding mucosa. It carries a **much greater risk of malignant transformation than leukoplakia**, with **>50%** of cases undergoing malignant transformation. This makes erythroplakia a higher risk lesion than leukoplakia, a critical point for examination.

**Both lesions:**
Both leukoplakia and erythroplakia typically affect adults **40–70 years** of age, with a **2:1 male preponderance**. The most common risk factor is **tobacco use** (cigarettes, pipes, cigars, chewing tobacco).
**Morphology:** The lesions exhibit a spectrum ranging from hyperkeratosis/acanthosis with orderly mucosa to marked dysplasia and carcinoma in situ. The most severe dysplastic changes are typically seen in erythroplakia. Increasing dysplasia is often accompanied by a subjacent **lymphocyte and macrophage infiltrate**.

### Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Oral SCC) **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)** accounts for **95% of oral cavity cancers**, with the remainder largely being salivary gland adenocarcinomas. It is the **6th most common neoplasm worldwide** and an aggressive malignancy. The overall long-term survival has remained **<50% for the past 50 years**, often due to diagnosis at an advanced stage. Multiple primary tumours are detected at a rate of **3–7% per year** after an initial diagnosis. Patients surviving 5 years have up to a **35% chance** of developing a new primary within that interval, and may die of a second primary tumour despite a small initial tumour. Therefore, surveillance and early detection of new premalignant lesions are **critical for long-term survival**. This phenomenon is known as "**field cancerisation**," where multiple independent primary tumours arise from years of chronic mucosal carcinogen exposure (alcohol, tobacco).

**Two Pathogenic Pathways:**

| Pathway           | Features                                                                         |
| :---------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Tobacco/alcohol** | Chronic users; mutations in **TP53**, **p63**, **NOTCH1**; molecular signature of tobacco carcinogens |
| **HPV-related**   | Tonsillar crypts/base of tongue; oncogenic **HPV-16**; fewer mutations; overexpress **p16**; **better prognosis**; not accessible to cytologic screening unlike cervix |

HPV-associated oropharyngeal SCC is predicted to **surpass cervical cancer incidence** in the next decade, with the HPV vaccine offering hope for prevention. In India and Southeast Asia, **betel quid and paan** (areca nut + slaked lime + tobacco in betel leaf) are important predisposing factors, following a similar pathway to tobacco-associated tumours.

**Morphology:** The most common locations for oral SCC are the **ventral surface of the tongue, floor of the mouth, lower lip, soft palate, and gingiva**. Early lesions appear as raised firm pearly plaques or irregular roughened/verrucous mucosal thickenings, which may be on a background of leukoplakia/erythroplakia. Late-stage lesions present as ulcerated protruding masses with **irregular indurated or rolled borders**. Histologically, they range from well-differentiated keratinizing tumours to anaplastic sarcomatoid tumours; the degree of differentiation does **NOT** correlate with biologic behaviour. The cancer spreads by infiltrating locally first, then to **cervical lymph nodes** (the most common regional metastasis), and finally to distant metastases in mediastinal lymph nodes.

## 1.3 Diseases of Salivary Glands

### Xerostomia
**Xerostomia**, defined as **dry mouth**, results from decreased saliva production. The most frequent cause is **medications**, including anticholinergic, antidepressant/antipsychotic, diuretic, antihypertensive, sedative, muscle relaxant, analgesic, and antihistaminic agents. It affects **>20% of individuals above age 70**. Xerostomia is a **major feature of Sjögren syndrome**, where it is usually accompanied by dry eyes (sicca syndrome). It is also a major complication of **radiation therapy** to the head and neck. Oral findings include dry mucosa, atrophy of tongue papillae, fissuring, and ulcerations. In Sjögren syndrome, concomitant inflammatory salivary gland enlargement may be present. Complications include increased dental caries, candidiasis, and difficulty swallowing and speaking.

### Sialadenitis

**Viral Sialadenitis — Mumps**
**Mumps** is the most common form of viral sialadenitis, caused by a **paramyxovirus** (related to influenza/parainfluenza). It predominantly involves the **parotid glands**, though all glands may enlarge. Histologically, it shows interstitial inflammation with a **mononuclear infiltrate**. In children, it is a self-limited benign condition. In adults, it can cause **pancreatitis** or **orchitis**, with orchitis sometimes leading to sterility.

**Mucocele**
A **mucocele** is the **most common inflammatory lesion of salivary glands**. It results from the **blockage or rupture of a salivary gland duct**, causing saliva to leak into the surrounding connective tissue stroma. Mucoceles are most common in toddlers, young adults, and the aged. They typically present as a **fluctuant swelling of the lower lip**, which changes size, especially around meals. Histology reveals a cyst-like space lined by inflammatory granulation tissue or fibrous connective tissue, filled with mucin and macrophages. Treatment involves complete excision of the cyst **and** the associated minor salivary gland lobule.

**Bacterial Sialadenitis**
**Bacterial sialadenitis** most often involves the **major salivary glands**, particularly the **submandibular glands**. The most frequent pathogens are **Staphylococcus aureus** and **Streptococcus viridans**. A common antecedent is **duct obstruction by stones (sialolithiasis)**, but it can also be caused by impacted food debris or injury-related oedema. Dehydration and decreased secretory function (e.g., in Sjögren syndrome) predispose individuals to bacterial sialadenitis, which is often seen in elderly, debilitated patients.

SECTION 2: OESOPHAGUS

## 2.1 Congenital and Motility Disorders

### Oesophageal Atresia and Tracheoesophageal Fistula
**Oesophageal atresia** is an abnormal developmental condition characterized by a **blind upper oesophageal pouch**, with the **distal oesophagus often arising from the trachea** (tracheoesophageal fistula being the most common variant). Infants present with regurgitation during feeding and aspiration. Surgery is curative.

### Achalasia
**Achalasia** is defined by incomplete LES relaxation, increased LES tone, and oesophageal aperistalsis. This leads to functional obstruction with proximal oesophageal dilatation.

**Primary achalasia** is the most common form, being idiopathic and involving the loss of inhibitory neurons (nitric oxide, VIP) in the oesophageal wall.

**Secondary achalasia** is less common and can be caused by:
*   **Chagas disease**, where *Trypanosoma cruzi* infection destroys enteric plexuses.
*   **Diabetic neuropathy, amyloidosis, polio, or autonomic neuropathy**.
*   **Malignancy**, such as infiltration of the myenteric plexus by SCC of the oesophagus, gastric carcinoma, or lymphoma.

**Clinical Features:**
*   **Dysphagia** to both solids and liquids.
*   Regurgitation of undigested food, which can cause aspiration.
*   Chest pain.
*   Weight loss.

**Diagnosis:** A barium swallow shows a "**bird's beak**" appearance of the narrowed LES. Manometry confirms aperistalsis and a non-relaxing LES.

**Complications:** These include oesophagitis, oesophageal ulceration, diverticula, and an increased risk of **oesophageal SCC** (5%).

Treatment options include Botox injection, pneumatic dilation, surgical myotomy, and calcium channel blockers (CCBs).

## 2.2 Oesophagitis

### Infectious Oesophagitis
**Infectious oesophagitis** most commonly affects **immunocompromised patients** (e.g., those with AIDS, transplant recipients, malignancy, or undergoing chemotherapy).

*   **HSV** causes "**punched-out ulcers**" with nuclear viral inclusions within a rim of degenerating epithelial cells at the ulcer edge, along with multinucleated giant cells.
*   **CMV** leads to **shallower ulcerations** with characteristic nuclear AND cytoplasmic inclusions within capillary endothelium and stromal cells.
*   **Candida** is the most common fungal pathogen, presenting in advanced form as adherent grey-white pseudomembranes of densely matted fungal hyphae and inflammatory cells over the oesophageal mucosa. Mucormycosis and aspergillosis are also possible.

Immunohistochemical staining for viral antigens serves as an ancillary diagnostic tool. Nonpathogenic oral bacteria are frequently found in ulcer beds, while pathogenic organisms account for approximately 10% of infectious oesophagitis cases.

### Reflux Oesophagitis (GERD) **Reflux oesophagitis (GERD)** is the **most frequent cause of oesophagitis** and the most common outpatient GI diagnosis. The stratified squamous epithelium of the oesophagus is resistant to abrasion but **sensitive to acid**. Normal protection is provided by mucin and bicarbonate from submucosal glands, and constant LES tone prevents reflux.

**Pathogenesis:** Reflux of gastric juices (and duodenal bile in severe cases) leads to mucosal injury. Factors that reduce LES tone or increase abdominal pressure include alcohol and tobacco use, obesity, CNS depressants, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, delayed gastric emptying, and increased gastric volume.

**Morphology (mild → severe):**
*   In mild GERD, the only alteration may be simple **hyperaemia** (redness on endoscopy), and mucosal histology is often unremarkable.
*   In more significant disease, **eosinophils are recruited** into the squamous mucosa, followed by **neutrophils** in cases of more severe injury.
*   Histological hallmarks include **basal zone hyperplasia** exceeding **20% of total epithelial thickness** and **elongation of lamina propria papillae** extending into the upper third of the epithelium.

**Clinical Features:** GERD is most common in **adults >40 years** but also occurs in infants and children. Symptoms include **heartburn, dysphagia**, and less often, regurgitation of sour-tasting gastric contents. Rarely, severe chest pain mimicking heart disease can occur. The severity of symptoms is **NOT closely related** to the degree of histologic damage. Treatment with **proton pump inhibitors** reduces gastric acidity and provides symptomatic relief. Complications include oesophageal ulceration, haematemesis, melena, stricture, and **Barrett oesophagus**.

### Hiatal Hernia
A **hiatal hernia** involves the separation of the diaphragmatic crura and protrusion of the stomach into the thorax through the resulting gap. It can be congenital (in infants/children) or acquired. It is **asymptomatic in >90% of adult cases**. When symptomatic, symptoms are similar to GERD and are associated with other causes of LES incompetence.

### Eosinophilic Oesophagitis
**Eosinophilic oesophagitis** presents in **adults** with food impaction and dysphagia, and in **children** with feeding intolerance or GERD-like symptoms. The **cardinal histologic feature** is epithelial infiltration by **large numbers of eosinophils**, particularly superficially and at sites **far from the gastroesophageal junction**, which helps distinguish it from GERD, Crohn's disease, and other forms of oesophagitis. The incidence is markedly increasing.

**Typical clinical characteristics:**
*   Failure of high-dose PPI treatment.
*   Absence of acid reflux.
*   The **majority are atopic**, presenting with atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, asthma, and peripheral eosinophilia.

Treatment involves dietary restrictions (avoiding cow milk, soy products) and topical and systemic corticosteroids.

## 2.3 Barrett Oesophagus

**Barrett oesophagus** is a complication of **chronic GERD**, characterized by **intestinal metaplasia** within the oesophageal squamous mucosa. Its incidence is rising, estimated in up to **10% of persons with symptomatic GERD**. **White males** are most often affected, typically presenting between **40 and 60 years of age**. Diagnosis requires **endoscopic evidence of columnar mucosa** above the GEJ AND **histologic evidence of intestinal metaplasia** (goblet cells are key). Barrett oesophagus is a significant **risk factor for oesophageal adenocarcinoma**, with a 30- to 40-fold increased risk compared to the general population. Surveillance endoscopy with biopsies is standard for the detection of **dysplasia**. Low-grade dysplasia warrants surveillance, while high-grade dysplasia requires endoscopic ablation (radiofrequency, photodynamic therapy).

Grossly, it appears as patchy, tongues of red, velvety mucosa extending proximally from the GEJ, alternating with pale, smooth squamous mucosa. Histologically, the squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar cells containing **goblet cells** (intestinal metaplasia). Genetic changes include **p53 mutations**, aneuploidy, and increased proliferation.

SECTION 3: STOMACH

## 3.1 Acute Gastritis

**Acute gastritis** is an acute mucosal inflammatory process, usually transient. It involves inflammation without mucosal injury (erosion). When severe erosions and haemorrhage occur, it is termed **acute haemorrhagic erosive gastropathy**.

**Pathogenesis:** It results from an imbalance between mucosal protective factors (mucin, bicarbonate, blood flow, prostaglandins, epithelial regeneration) and damaging factors (acid, pepsin).

**Risk factors:**
*   **NSAIDs:** The most common cause; they inhibit COX, leading to decreased prostaglandins, which in turn reduces mucin, bicarbonate, and blood flow.
*   **Alcohol:** Disrupts the mucosal barrier.
*   **Stress:** Severe trauma, burns, sepsis, shock, surgery, and increased intracranial pressure can lead to "stress ulcers."
*   **Ischaemia/shock**.
*   **H. pylori infection:** In its acute phase.
*   **Direct mucosal injury:** Bile reflux, irradiation, cytotoxic chemotherapy.

**Clinical Features:** These are variable, ranging from asymptomatic to mild epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Severe cases can present with haematemesis ("coffee-ground emesis"), melena, or even massive haemorrhage.

**Morphology:** Histology shows oedema, hyperaemia, and scattered neutrophils in the mucosa. Erosions (loss of epithelium) and haemorrhage are characteristic of acute haemorrhagic erosive gastropathy.

## 3.2 Chronic Gastritis

**Chronic gastritis** is characterized by chronic mucosal inflammation, leading to mucosal atrophy and intestinal metaplasia.

The **most important causes** are:
*   **H. pylori infection:** The most common cause worldwide.
*   **Autoimmune gastritis:** Accounts for <10% of cases.

### H. pylori Gastritis
**H. pylori gastritis** is the most common cause of chronic gastritis. **H. pylori** is a spiral-shaped, flagellated, gram-negative bacterium. It is associated with **PUD**, **gastric adenocarcinoma**, and **MALT lymphoma**. Infection is typically acquired in childhood and often persists lifelong.

**Virulence factors:**
*   **Urease:** Converts urea to ammonia, which neutralizes gastric acid locally and protects the bacteria.
*   **Flagella:** Allow movement in viscous mucus.
*   **Adhesins:** Bind to gastric epithelial cells.
*   **Toxins:** CagA (cytotoxin-associated gene A) and VacA (vacuolating cytotoxin A) contribute to host cell injury.

**Pathogenesis:** *H. pylori* induces intense inflammatory and immune responses.

**Morphology:** It typically affects the **antrum predominantly**. There is an intense inflammatory infiltrate, including neutrophils (indicating active inflammation), plasma cells, lymphocytes, and macrophages. **Intestinal metaplasia** is frequently present.

**Clinical Features:** Most individuals are asymptomatic.
**Diagnosis:** This can be made via urea breath test, stool antigen test, serology (antibodies), or endoscopic biopsy (histology, rapid urease test, culture).
**Treatment:** Antibiotics combined with proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy lead to eradication, which reverses gastritis and prevents recurrence of PUD.

### Autoimmune Gastritis
**Autoimmune gastritis** accounts for <10% of chronic gastritis cases. It involves **immune-mediated destruction of parietal cells** (located in the body/fundus) and is associated with other autoimmune diseases (e.g., Hashimoto thyroiditis, Addison disease). The **hallmark** is the presence of antibodies to parietal cells (H+/K+-ATPase) and/or intrinsic factor.

**Pathogenesis:** The loss of parietal cells leads to:
*   **Achlorhydria** (lack of gastric acid), which stimulates gastrin release from G cells, resulting in **hypergastrinemia**.
*   **Lack of intrinsic factor**, leading to impaired vitamin B12 absorption and subsequently **pernicious anaemia**.

**Morphology:** There is diffuse mucosal damage in the **body and fundus**. Histology shows a deep lympho-plasmacytic infiltrate and loss of parietal and chief cells. **Intestinal metaplasia** and **endocrine cell hyperplasia** (due to hypergastrinemia) are common.

**Clinical Features:** It often presents in older adults (median age 60) and progresses over decades. Symptoms include anaemia (fatigue, weakness) and neurological symptoms (due to B12 deficiency).
**Complications:** These include pernicious anaemia and a significantly increased risk of **gastric adenocarcinoma** and **carcinoid tumours**.

### Gastric Atrophy (Atrophic Gastritis)
**Gastric atrophy** is the end stage of chronic gastritis (both *H. pylori* and autoimmune). It is characterized by a marked reduction in mucosal thickness and glandular elements. It is associated with **intestinal metaplasia**, where gastric mucosa transforms into intestinal-type epithelium. This condition carries an increased risk of **dysplasia and adenocarcinoma**. Parietal and chief cell loss are prominent, and intestinal metaplasia may develop.

### H. pylori vs Autoimmune Gastritis — Comparison

| Feature           | H. pylori                                | Autoimmune                               |
| :---------------- | :--------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------- |
| Location          | **Antrum** (predominantly)                   | **Body and fundus**                          |
| Acid secretion    | **Increased** (antral)                       | **Decreased (achlorhydria)**                 |
| Gastrin levels    | **Low (hypogastrinemia)**                    | **High (hypergastrinemia)**                  |
| Antibodies        | None specific                            | **Anti-parietal cell, anti-intrinsic factor** |
| Pernicious anaemia | No                                       | **Yes**                                      |
| Atrophic gastritis | Yes (multifocal)                         | Yes (diffuse, body/fundus)               |
| Intestinal metaplasia | Yes                                      | Yes                                      |
| Gastric cancer risk | Increased                                | Increased                                |
| Inflammatory pattern | Superficial; **neutrophils + plasma cells** | Deep; **lymphocytes + macrophages**          |

## 3.4 Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD) **Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)** is most often associated with **H. pylori infection** or **NSAID use**. It is most commonly found in the **gastric antrum and first portion of the duodenum**. PUD can also occur in the oesophagus (from GERD/ectopic gastric mucosa) or small intestine (gastric heterotopia in Meckel diverticulum). The lifetime risk is approximately **10% for males** and **4% for females**.

**Pathogenesis:** PUD results from an imbalance between mucosal defences and damaging forces, often on a background of chronic gastritis. **>70% of PUD cases are associated with H. pylori**, but only **5–10% of H. pylori-infected persons** develop ulcers, indicating that host factors and strain variation determine the outcome. Gastric hyperacidity is fundamental, caused by *H. pylori* infection, parietal cell hyperplasia, excessive secretory responses, or impaired inhibition of gastrin release. **Zollinger-Ellison syndrome**, characterized by uncontrolled gastrin release from a gastrinoma, leads to massive acid production and multiple peptic ulcerations in the stomach, duodenum, and even the **jejunum**. Cofactors include chronic NSAID use, cigarette smoking, and high-dose corticosteroids. PUD is also more frequent in individuals with alcoholic cirrhosis, COPD, chronic renal failure, and hyperparathyroidism (where hypercalcaemia stimulates gastrin, increasing acid). Psychological stress may exacerbate PUD.

**Morphology:** **Duodenal ulcers** are **4 times more common** than gastric ulcers, typically found within a few centimetres of the pyloric valve, often on the **anterior duodenal wall**. Gastric peptic ulcers predominantly occur near the **interface of the body and antrum**. They are **solitary in >80%** of patients. The classic appearance is a **round to oval, sharply punched-out defect** with a **smooth, clean base** due to peptic digestion of exudate. Lesions less than 0.3 cm are considered shallow, while those greater than 0.6 cm are likely deeper. Histologically, the base consists of richly vascular **granulation tissue**. Ongoing bleeding can lead to life-threatening haemorrhage, and perforation demands emergent surgical intervention.

**Clinical Features:** PUD involves chronic, recurring lesions, typically affecting middle-aged to older adults. The primary symptom is **epigastric burning or aching pain**, which occurs **1–3 hours after meals**, is worse at night, and is **relieved by alkali or food**. Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, bloating, and belching. Complications include iron-deficiency anaemia, frank haemorrhage, and perforation. The tendency to develop ulcers remains even after healing. Treatment involves **H. pylori eradication (antibiotics + PPI)**; surgery is reserved for bleeding or perforated ulcers. PUD causes much more **morbidity than mortality**.

## 3.5 Gastric Tumours

### Gastric Polyps
**Inflammatory and hyperplastic polyps** are reactive lesions associated with chronic gastritis; the risk of dysplasia increases with polyp size. **Gastric adenomas** develop in the background of chronic gastritis, particularly associated with intestinal metaplasia and mucosal atrophy. **Adenocarcinoma frequently arises in gastric adenomas**, requiring **complete excision and surveillance**.

### Gastric Adenocarcinoma
The incidence of **gastric adenocarcinoma** varies markedly with geography and is more common in lower socioeconomic groups. **H. pylori infection** is the most common aetiologic agent. Other associations include chronic atrophic gastritis and **EBV infection**, which can lead to multiple pathways of neoplastic transformation.

**Classification:**

| Type                       | Features                                                                         |
| :------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Intestinal pattern**     | Forms bulky tumours; may be ulcerated                                            |
| **Diffuse (signet ring cells)** | Diffuse infiltrative growth → thickens gastric wall without discrete mass = **linitis plastica** |

**Clinical Features:** These include abdominal swelling, abdominal pain, vomiting, and gastric outlet obstruction.

### Primary Gastric Lymphoma
**Primary gastric lymphoma** is most often derived from **MALT** (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue). MALT development is induced by **chronic gastritis** (H. pylori). Importantly, **H. pylori eradication can lead to regression of early MALT lymphoma**.

### Carcinoid Tumour
**Carcinoid tumours** arise from diffuse components of the endocrine system. They are most common in the **gastrointestinal tract**, particularly the **small intestine**. The **most important prognostic factor is location**: small intestine tumours are the most aggressive, while appendix tumours are almost always benign. **Carcinoid syndrome**, caused by vasoactive substances released by the tumour, involves cutaneous flushing, sweating, bronchospasm, colicky abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and **right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis**.

### Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumour (GIST)
A **Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumour (GIST)** is the **most common mesenchymal tumour of the abdomen**. It occurs most often in the **stomach** and arises from **interstitial cells of Cajal** (pacemaker cells). The **majority have activating mutations in c-KIT or PDGFRA tyrosine kinases**, making them **responsive to kinase inhibitors** (e.g., imatinib). A key examination point is that GISTs with a **c-KIT mutation** respond to **imatinib**.
