**Q2. Discuss classes of fungi based on reproduction (20 marks)** *(2 repeats)*
**Introduction:**
- Fungi reproduce both sexually and asexually
- Classification based on sexual reproduction structures
- Four major classes recognized
**1. Ascomycota:**

- Largest class of fungi
- Named for sac-like structure called **ascus** that contains sexual spores
- **Sexual reproduction:**
 - Produce **ascospores** — contained within ascus

- Ascus forms within fruiting body called ascocarp
- Typically 8 ascospores per ascus
- **Asexual reproduction:**
 - Produce **conidia** — most common asexual spores

- Conidiophores bear conidia
- **Characteristics:**
 - Septate hyphae

- Cell wall contains chitin and glucans
- Reproduce both sexually and asexually
- **Medical examples:**
 - *Aspergillus* spp — aspergillosis

- *Candida albicans* — candidiasis
- *Histoplasma capsulatum* — histoplasmosis
- *Coccidioides immitis* — coccidioidomycosis
- *Blastomyces dermatitidis* — blastomycosis
**2. Basidiomycota:**
- Named for club-shaped structure called **basidium**
- **Sexual reproduction:**
 - Produce **basidiospores** on surface of basidium

- Typically 4 basidiospores per basidium
- Basidium borne on fruiting body — mushroom
- **Asexual reproduction:**
 - Produce conidia

- Some reproduce by budding
- **Characteristics:**
 - Septate hyphae

- Clamp connections — unique feature
- Fruiting bodies — mushrooms, bracket fungi
- **Medical examples:**
 - *Cryptococcus neoformans* — meningitis (basidiomycete yeast)

- Mushroom poisoning — *Amanita* spp
- *Malassezia* spp — pityriasis versicolor
**3. Deuteromycetes (Fungi Imperfecti/Mitosporic fungi):**
- Not a true taxonomic class — artificial grouping
- Fungi whose **sexual reproduction is unknown or not clearly known**
- Also called imperfect fungi — lack sexual stage
- **Reproduction:**
 - Only asexual reproduction documented

- Reproduce by conidia
- Complex reproductive mechanisms
- **Characteristics:**
 - Septate hyphae

- When sexual stage discovered → reclassified into Ascomycota or Basidiomycota
- **Medical examples:**
 - Most dermatophytes — *Trichophyton*, *Microsporum*, *Epidermophyton*

- *Candida* species (asexual form)
**4. Zygomycota:**
- Named for sexual spore — **zygospore**
- **Sexual reproduction:**
 - Two compatible mating strains fuse

- Form zygospore — thick-walled resistant spore
- Zygospores are large and thick-walled
- **Asexual reproduction:**
 - Produce **sporangiospores** within sporangium

- Sporangiophore bears sporangium at tip
- Conidia also produced
- **Characteristics:**
 - **Aseptate (coenocytic) hyphae** — distinguishing feature

- No cross walls — multinucleate cytoplasm
- Rapid growing
- Ribbon-like broad hyphae
- **Medical examples:**
 - *Rhizopus* spp — mucormycosis (most common)

- *Mucor* spp — mucormycosis
- *Cunninghamella* — rare mucormycosis
- Cause life-threatening infections in immunocompromised — diabetics especially

**Q3. Discuss the clinical manifestation and treatment of candidiasis (20 marks)** *(2 repeats)*
**Introduction:**
- Candidiasis is an opportunistic mycosis caused by *Candida albicans* (most common)
- Other species: *C. tropicalis*, *C. glabrata*, *C. parapsilosis*, *C. krusei*
- Normal commensal of GIT, mouth, vagina — becomes pathogenic when host defenses fail
**Predisposing Factors:**

- HIV/AIDS, diabetes, prolonged antibiotics, corticosteroids
- Pregnancy, extremes of age, indwelling catheters
- Chemotherapy, organ transplantation
**Clinical Manifestations:**

*Mucocutaneous Manifestations:*
**Oral Candidiasis (Thrush):**
- White, creamy plaques on oral mucosa, tongue, palate
- Plaques can be wiped off — leaving red, bleeding base
- Painful — difficulty swallowing (odynophagia)
- Common in neonates, HIV patients, denture wearers
- Pseudomembranous type most common
**Oesophageal Candidiasis:**

- Extension of oral thrush downward
- Severe dysphagia and odynophagia
- Retrosternal chest pain
- AIDS-defining illness when CD4 count very low
**Vulvovaginal Candidiasis:**

- Intense itching and burning of vulva and vagina
- Thick, white, cottage cheese-like discharge
- Erythema and swelling of vulva
- Dyspareunia — painful intercourse
- Dysuria — painful urination
- Very common — 75% of women experience at least once
**Cutaneous Candidiasis:**

- **Intertriginous candidiasis:** Skin folds — groin, axilla, under breasts — red, moist, macerated patches
- **Diaper rash:** Infants — erythematous papular eruption in diaper area
- **Paronychia:** Nail fold infection — painful, swollen nail fold
- **Onychomycosis:** Nail plate infection — discoloured, thickened nails
**Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis:**

- Persistent *Candida* infection of skin, nails, mucous membranes
- Associated with T-cell immunodeficiency
- Granulomatous lesions on skin
- Very difficult to treat
*Systemic/Invasive Candidiasis:*

**Candidemia (Candida in blood):**
- Most serious form
- High mortality — up to 40%
- Fever not responding to antibiotics in hospitalised patient
- Risk: central venous catheters, abdominal surgery, ICU admission
**Disseminated Candidiasis:**

- Spreads from blood to multiple organs:
 - **Endocarditis** — especially prosthetic valves

- **Meningitis** — headache, neck stiffness, altered consciousness
- **Endophthalmitis** — eye pain, visual disturbance — important clue to diagnosis
- **Osteomyelitis** — bone infection
- **Hepatosplenic candidiasis** — liver and spleen abscesses
**Urinary Candidiasis:**
- Associated with urinary catheters
- Candiduria — Candida in urine
- Can ascend to cause pyelonephritis
**Pulmonary Candidiasis:**

- Rare — usually via haematogenous spread
- Cough, fever, infiltrates on chest X-ray
**Treatment:**

*Mucocutaneous:*
- **Oral thrush:** Nystatin suspension (swish and swallow), Fluconazole oral
- **Oesophageal:** Fluconazole oral/IV — first line
- **Vaginal:** Clotrimazole pessary, Miconazole cream, single dose Fluconazole oral
- **Skin:** Topical Clotrimazole, Miconazole, Nystatin cream
*Systemic/Invasive:*

- **Fluconazole** — first line for susceptible *Candida* species
- **Amphotericin B** — severe systemic, CNS candidiasis
- **Echinocandins (Caspofungin, Micafungin)** — *C. glabrata*, *C. krusei* resistant to fluconazole
- **5-Flucytosine** — combined with Amphotericin B for CNS candidiasis
- Remove predisposing factors — catheters, stop antibiotics if possible
- Duration: minimum 2 weeks after last positive blood culture for candidemia

# HIV / AIDS — Complete Study Notes
## 1. The Virus
HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) is a retrovirus that progressively destroys the immune system, ultimately leading to Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS).
- **Family:** Retroviridae
- **Genus:** Lentivirus
- **Genome:** Single-stranded RNA (two identical copies — diploid)
- **Type:** Enveloped virus
---
## 2. Structure
**Envelope glycoproteins:**
- **gp120** — surface unit; binds CD4 receptor on target cells
- **gp41** — transmembrane unit; mediates fusion with host cell membrane
- Together they form the precursor **gp160**
**Core proteins:**
- **p24** — capsid protein; major diagnostic marker detected by ELISA
- **p17** — matrix protein
- **p7/p9** — nucleocapsid proteins
**Enzymes packaged inside the virion:**
- Reverse transcriptase
- Integrase
- Protease
---
## 3. Transmission
- Sexual contact — anal, vaginal (most common globally)
- Blood and blood products — transfusions, sharing needles
- Mother to child (vertical) — pregnancy, delivery, breastfeeding
- Needlestick injuries in healthcare workers
HIV is NOT transmitted by casual contact, mosquitoes, saliva, tears, or shared utensils.
---
## 4. Target Cells
HIV infects cells that express the **CD4 receptor:**
- CD4+ T-helper lymphocytes — primary target
- Macrophages
- Dendritic cells
- Microglial cells (CNS)
**Co-receptors required for entry:**
- **CCR5** — used by macrophage-tropic strains (early infection)
- **CXCR4** — used by T-cell tropic strains (late infection)
---
## 5. Pathogenesis — The Most Examined Topic
### Step 1: Attachment and Entry
- gp120 binds CD4 receptor
- Co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4) binding causes conformational change
- gp41 inserts into host membrane → fusion → viral core enters cytoplasm
### Step 2: Reverse Transcription
- Reverse transcriptase converts viral RNA → single-stranded DNA
- RNase H activity degrades the original RNA strand
- Second DNA strand synthesized → double-stranded DNA (dsDNA)
- High error rate — no proofreading — causes mutations and drug resistance
### Step 3: Integration
- dsDNA transported into nucleus
- Integrase cuts host DNA and inserts viral dsDNA → **provirus**
- Provirus remains permanently in host genome
- This is why HIV infection is lifelong and cannot be cured
### Step 4: Transcription and Translation
- Host RNA polymerase transcribes proviral DNA → viral mRNA and genomic RNA
- Viral proteins synthesized by host ribosomes
- Protease cleaves large polyprotein precursors into functional proteins
### Step 5: Assembly and Budding
- New viral particles assemble at the cell membrane
- Virus buds off, acquiring its envelope from the host cell membrane
- Mature, infectious virions released
---
## 6. The Three Key Enzymes — Highest Yield
### Reverse Transcriptase
- Converts RNA → DNA (unique to retroviruses)
- Has RNase H activity
- No proofreading → high mutation rate
- Drug targets: NRTIs (e.g., Zidovudine/AZT, Tenofovir) and NNRTIs (e.g., Nevirapine, Efavirenz)
### Integrase
- Integrates viral dsDNA into host chromosome as provirus
- Provirus is permanent — basis of lifelong infection
- Drug targets: Integrase strand transfer inhibitors — Raltegravir, Dolutegravir, Elvitegravir (drugs ending in -tegravir)
### Protease
- Cleaves Gag and Gag-Pol polyproteins into functional structural proteins and enzymes
- Required for viral maturation — without it, virions are non-infectious
- Drug targets: Protease inhibitors — Lopinavir, Ritonavir, Atazanavir (drugs ending in -navir)
**Why these enzymes make antiretrovirals selectively toxic:**
These enzymes are unique to HIV and have no equivalent in normal human cells. Drugs targeting them therefore kill or inhibit virus-infected cells specifically without harming uninfected human cells — this is the definition of selective toxicity.
---
## 7. Clinical Stages of HIV Infection
### Stage 1: Acute HIV Infection (Primary Infection)
- Occurs 2–4 weeks after exposure
- High viral load, rapid drop in CD4 count
- Symptoms: fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, rash, myalgia — resembles glandular fever
- Highly infectious at this stage
- Body mounts immune response → viral load falls, CD4 count partially recovers
### Stage 2: Chronic HIV Infection (Clinical Latency)
- Can last years (average 10 years without treatment)
- Patient may be asymptomatic or have mild symptoms
- Virus still replicating slowly
- CD4 count gradually declining
### Stage 3: AIDS
- Defined as CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ OR development of AIDS-defining illness
- Severe immunodeficiency → opportunistic infections and malignancies
---
## 8. AIDS-Defining Conditions
**Opportunistic infections:**
- Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) — most common
- Toxoplasmosis (brain)
- Cryptococcal meningitis
- CMV retinitis
- Candidiasis (oesophageal, tracheal)
- Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC)
- Tuberculosis (TB) — especially in Sub-Saharan Africa
**Malignancies:**
- Kaposi's sarcoma (caused by HHV-8)
- Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma
- Cervical cancer (caused by HPV)
---
## 9. Diagnosis
**Direct detection:**
- HIV RNA by PCR — detects viral load; used in early infection and monitoring
- p24 antigen — detectable before antibodies appear
**Antibody detection:**
- ELISA — screening test (sensitive)
- Western Blot — confirmatory test (specific)
**CD4 count:**
- Monitors immune status and guides when to start treatment
- Normal: 500–1500 cells/mm³
- Start ART: below 500 cells/mm³ (or any count in current guidelines)
- AIDS: below 200 cells/mm³
**Window period:**
- The gap between infection and detectable antibodies (2–12 weeks)
- Patient is infectious but tests negative during this period
---
## 10. Antiretroviral Therapy (ART)
Treatment uses combination therapy (at least 3 drugs from 2 different classes) — called HAART (Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy).
**Drug classes and mechanisms:**
| Class | Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| NRTIs | Block reverse transcriptase (competitive inhibition) | Zidovudine (AZT), Tenofovir, Lamivudine |
| NNRTIs | Block reverse transcriptase (non-competitive) | Nevirapine, Efavirenz |
| Protease Inhibitors | Block viral protease | Lopinavir, Ritonavir, Atazanavir |
| Integrase Inhibitors | Block integrase | Raltegravir, Dolutegravir |
| Fusion Inhibitors | Block gp41-mediated fusion | Enfuvirtide (Fuzeon) |
| CCR5 Antagonists | Block CCR5 co-receptor | Maraviroc |
**Goals of ART:**
- Suppress viral load to undetectable levels
- Preserve and restore CD4 count
- Prevent opportunistic infections
- Reduce transmission
---
## 11. Prevention
- Consistent condom use
- ART for HIV-positive individuals (Treatment as Prevention — TasP)
- Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) — Tenofovir/Emtricitabine for high-risk individuals
- Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) — within 72 hours of exposure
- Safe blood transfusion practices
- Needle exchange programmes
- Prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) — ART during pregnancy
---
# Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1 and HSV-2) — Complete Study Notes
## 1. The Virus
Herpes Simplex Virus causes lifelong latent infections with periodic reactivation. It is one of the most clinically important herpesviruses.
- **Family:** Herpesviridae
- **Subfamily:** Alphaherpesvirinae
- **Genome:** Double-stranded DNA (dsDNA)
- **Enveloped virus**
- **Two serotypes:** HSV-1 and HSV-2
---
## 2. Structure
- Large, complex enveloped virus
- Icosahedral capsid surrounded by a **tegument** layer (unique to herpesviruses)
- Envelope studded with glycoproteins (gB, gC, gD, gH, gL) — used for attachment and fusion
- **gC** and **gB** — bind heparan sulphate on host cells
- **gD** — binds specific entry receptors (HVEM, nectin)
- **gH/gL** — mediate fusion
---
## 3. Differences Between HSV-1 and HSV-2
| Feature | HSV-1 | HSV-2 |
|---|---|---|
| Primary site | Orolabial (mouth, lips) | Genital area |
| Portal of entry | Oral mucosa, skin | Genital mucosa, skin |
| Latency site | Trigeminal ganglion | Sacral dorsal root ganglion |
| Transmission | Direct contact, saliva | Sexual contact |
| Reactivation triggers | Stress, fever, UV light, illness | Stress, menstruation, immunosuppression |
Note: HSV-1 can cause genital herpes (increasingly common), and HSV-2 can cause oral lesions — the distinction is not absolute.
---
## 4. Portal of Entry — High Yield
**HSV-1:**
- Oral and labial mucosa
- Conjunctiva
- Skin (abraded)
- Respiratory mucosa (rare)
**HSV-2:**
- Genital mucosa
- Perianal skin
- Mucous membranes
Both viruses enter through **mucosal surfaces and broken skin** — they cannot penetrate intact skin.
---
## 5. Pathogenesis
### Primary Infection
- Virus enters via mucosa or abraded skin
- Replicates locally at the entry site → causes vesicular lesions
- Travels **retrograde** along sensory nerve axons to the **sensory ganglion**
- Establishes **latency** in the ganglion — viral DNA maintained as circular episome
- Immune response limits primary infection but cannot clear latent virus
### Latency
- Virus becomes latent in sensory ganglia
- Only LAT (Latency-Associated Transcripts) expressed — virus is invisible to immune system
- No viral replication during latency
- Cell remains alive — virus does not destroy the neuron during latency
### Reactivation
- Triggered by: stress, fever, UV light, menstruation, immunosuppression, trauma
- Virus travels **anterograde** back down the axon to the skin/mucosa
- Replication resumes → new lesions (recurrent herpes)
- Reactivation may be symptomatic (lesions) or asymptomatic (silent shedding)
- Silent shedding is a major source of transmission
---
## 6. Diseases Caused — High Yield
**HSV-1:**
- Herpes labialis — cold sores (most common)
- Gingivostomatitis — primary oral infection in children
- Keratoconjunctivitis — eye infection; can cause corneal scarring and blindness
- Herpes encephalitis — most common cause of fatal sporadic encephalitis
- Herpetic whitlow — infection of the finger
**HSV-2:**
- Genital herpes — painful vesicular ulcers on genitalia
- Neonatal herpes — acquired during delivery through infected birth canal; can be fatal
- Aseptic meningitis
**Both HSV-1 and HSV-2:**
- Encephalitis
- Disseminated infection in immunocompromised patients
- Erythema multiforme (hypersensitivity reaction triggered by HSV)
---
## 7. Neonatal Herpes — Special Importance
- Neonate acquires HSV-2 (rarely HSV-1) during passage through infected birth canal
- Risk highest when mother has primary genital herpes at time of delivery
- Three forms:
  - Localized skin, eye, mouth (SEM disease)
  - CNS disease — encephalitis
  - Disseminated disease — involves multiple organs; highest mortality
- Management: Caesarean section if active genital lesions at term; IV Acyclovir for infected neonates
---
## 8. HSV Encephalitis — Special Importance
- Most common cause of fatal sporadic (non-epidemic) viral encephalitis worldwide
- Caused predominantly by HSV-1
- Affects the **temporal lobe** preferentially
- Clinical features: fever, headache, altered consciousness, seizures, focal neurological deficits
- Diagnosis: MRI (temporal lobe changes), PCR of CSF (gold standard)
- Treatment: IV Acyclovir — must be started early
---
## 9. Diagnosis
- **Tzanck smear** — multinucleated giant cells seen on smear from lesion base (not specific for HSV vs VZV)
- **PCR** — gold standard; detects HSV DNA in CSF, swabs, tissue
- **Viral culture** — from vesicle fluid; definitive but slow
- **Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA)** — rapid, from lesion swab
- **Serology** — IgM (acute), IgG (past infection/latency); type-specific serology distinguishes HSV-1 from HSV-2
---
## 10. Treatment — Why Acyclovir is Selectively Toxic (High Yield)
**Acyclovir** is the drug of choice for HSV infections.
**Mechanism of selective toxicity — step by step:**
1. Acyclovir enters all cells (infected and uninfected)
2. In HSV-infected cells only, viral thymidine kinase (TK) phosphorylates acyclovir → acyclovir monophosphate
3. Host cell kinases add two more phosphates → acyclovir triphosphate (active form)
4. Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral DNA polymerase competitively
5. It is also incorporated into viral DNA as a chain terminator — DNA synthesis stops
6. Human DNA polymerase has very low affinity for acyclovir triphosphate — human cells are spared
**Why it is selective:**
- Normal uninfected cells lack viral thymidine kinase — they cannot activate acyclovir
- Only virus-infected cells activate the drug
- Therefore acyclovir is toxic only to HSV-infected cells — this is the definition of selective toxicity
**Drugs in the acyclovir family:**
| Drug | Notes |
|---|---|
| Acyclovir | IV or oral; first-line for HSV and VZV |
| Valacyclovir | Oral prodrug of acyclovir; better bioavailability |
| Famciclovir | Oral prodrug of penciclovir; used for genital herpes and zoster |
| Ganciclovir | Used for CMV (not HSV first-line) |
**Resistance:**
- Occurs through mutation of viral thymidine kinase (most common) or viral DNA polymerase
- Resistant strains treated with Foscarnet or Cidofovir (do not require TK activation)
---
## 11. Prevention
- Avoid direct contact with active lesions
- Suppressive acyclovir therapy — reduces frequency of recurrences and asymptomatic shedding
- Condom use — reduces but does not eliminate transmission (virus shed from areas not covered)
- Caesarean section for mothers with active genital lesions at term
- No licensed vaccine currently available
---
## 12. Immune Evasion by HSV
HSV has developed multiple strategies to evade the immune system:
- **Latency** — virus hides in neurons where immune surveillance is limited
- **Downregulation of MHC class I** — infected cells become less visible to cytotoxic T cells
- **Blocking complement** — gC binds complement component C3b, blocking complement activation
- **Blocking antibody-dependent cytotoxicity** — gE/gI complex acts as Fc receptor, binding IgG and blocking immune recognition
---

# Part 1: Influenza Virus

## 1. Introduction

Influenza is an acute respiratory illness caused by Influenza viruses. It is one of the most clinically and epidemiologically important viruses in medicine, responsible for seasonal epidemics and occasional global pandemics. Its unique ability to change its surface antigens — antigenic drift and antigenic shift — is why it remains a major global health threat and why the influenza vaccine must be reformulated every year.

At MKU, influenza is examined almost every year, primarily through the essay question on antigenic shift versus antigenic drift and their clinical significance.

---

## 2. Classification and Structure

- **Family:** Orthomyxoviridae
- **Genome:** Single-stranded, negative-sense RNA — segmented into 8 segments
- **Enveloped virus**
- **Types:** Influenza A, B, and C
  - Influenza A — causes epidemics and pandemics; infects humans, birds, pigs
  - Influenza B — causes epidemics; infects humans only; less severe
  - Influenza C — causes mild illness; not clinically significant

**Surface glycoproteins — the two most important structures:**

- **Haemagglutinin (H or HA)**
  - Binds sialic acid receptors on respiratory epithelial cells
  - Mediates viral attachment and fusion with host cell
  - Target of neutralizing antibodies — antibodies against H prevent infection
  - 18 subtypes identified (H1 to H18)

- **Neuraminidase (N or NA)**
  - Cleaves sialic acid to release newly formed virions from infected cells
  - Prevents viral aggregation
  - Facilitates spread through mucus
  - Target of neuraminidase inhibitor drugs
  - 11 subtypes identified (N1 to N11)

**Internal proteins:**
- **M2 protein** — ion channel; involved in uncoating; target of adamantane drugs
- **Nucleoprotein (NP)** — determines type (A, B, or C)
- **RNA polymerase complex** — error-prone; no proofreading; drives antigenic drift

---

## 3. Antigenic Variation — The Highest Yield Topic

This is the single most important concept in influenza and has appeared as an essay question in multiple MKU past papers.

### Antigenic Drift — Minor Antigenic Change

**Definition:** Small, gradual, cumulative changes in the H or N antigens caused by point mutations in the viral RNA during replication.

**Mechanism:**
- The RNA polymerase of influenza has no proofreading ability
- Random point mutations accumulate in the genes encoding H and N
- Over time, the surface antigens change enough that existing antibodies no longer recognize them
- The immune system is partially but not fully effective against the new strain

**Clinical significance:**
- Occurs continuously and gradually
- Responsible for seasonal influenza epidemics every year
- Explains why the influenza vaccine must be updated annually
- Affects both Influenza A and Influenza B

### Antigenic Shift — Major Antigenic Change

**Definition:** Sudden, dramatic change in the H or N antigens resulting from genetic reassortment between two different influenza A strains infecting the same host simultaneously.

**Mechanism:**
- Influenza A infects multiple species — humans, birds, pigs
- When two different Influenza A strains infect the same cell simultaneously (e.g., a human strain and a bird strain infecting a pig)
- The 8 RNA segments from each strain mix randomly during replication — reassortment
- A new hybrid virus emerges with a completely new combination of H and N antigens
- Human population has no pre-existing immunity to the new H or N subtype

**Clinical significance:**
- Occurs suddenly and unpredictably
- Produces a completely new subtype that the human population has never encountered
- No existing immunity in the population
- Responsible for influenza pandemics
- Only affects Influenza A — because only Influenza A infects multiple species
- Historical pandemics caused by antigenic shift:
  - 1918 Spanish flu — H1N1 — killed 50 million people
  - 1957 Asian flu — H2N2
  - 1968 Hong Kong flu — H3N2
  - 2009 Swine flu pandemic — H1N1 (new reassortant)

### Key Comparison

| Feature | Antigenic Drift | Antigenic Shift |
|---|---|---|
| Type of change | Minor, gradual | Major, sudden |
| Mechanism | Point mutations | Genetic reassortment |
| Viruses affected | Influenza A and B | Influenza A only |
| Result | New variant of same subtype | Entirely new subtype |
| Immunity | Partial pre-existing immunity | No pre-existing immunity |
| Consequence | Seasonal epidemics | Pandemics |
| Vaccine impact | Annual reformulation needed | Existing vaccine ineffective |

---

## 4. Replication Cycle

1. Haemagglutinin binds sialic acid receptors on respiratory epithelial cells
2. Virus enters by endocytosis
3. Low pH in endosome activates H — triggers fusion of viral and endosomal membranes
4. M2 ion channel allows H+ ions into virion — acidifies interior — uncoating occurs
5. 8 RNA segments released into cytoplasm, transported to nucleus
6. Viral RNA polymerase transcribes RNA segments → mRNA → viral proteins
7. Genome RNA also replicated in nucleus
8. New virions assembled and bud from cell surface
9. Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid — releases new virions

---

## 5. Transmission

- Respiratory droplets — primary route
- Airborne transmission in enclosed spaces
- Fomites — virus survives on surfaces for several hours
- Direct contact with infected secretions

---

## 6. Clinical Features

**Incubation period:** 1–4 days

**Typical influenza:**
- Sudden onset — distinguishes it from common cold
- High fever (38–40°C)
- Severe myalgia and arthralgia
- Headache
- Dry cough
- Sore throat
- Nasal congestion
- Fatigue and malaise — can be severe and prolonged

**Complications:**
- Primary viral pneumonia — most serious
- Secondary bacterial pneumonia — Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, H. influenzae
- Myocarditis
- Encephalitis
- Reye's syndrome — in children given aspirin during influenza infection (avoid aspirin in children)

**High-risk groups for severe disease:**

- Elderly (over 65)
- Young children
- Pregnant women
- Immunocompromised
- Chronic cardiopulmonary disease

---

## 7. Diagnosis

- **Clinical diagnosis** — typical presentation during epidemic season
- **Rapid antigen test** — nasal swab; quick but less sensitive
- **RT-PCR** — gold standard; detects viral RNA; highly sensitive and specific
- **Viral culture** — from nasopharyngeal swab; slow but definitive
- **Serology** — four-fold rise in antibody titres between acute and convalescent samples

---

## 8. Treatment

### Neuraminidase Inhibitors — First Line
- **Oseltamivir (Tamiflu)** — oral; most widely used
- **Zanamivir** — inhaled
- **Mechanism:** Block neuraminidase → new virions cannot be released from infected cells → spread is halted
- **Effective against:** Influenza A and B
- Must be started within 48 hours of symptom onset for maximum benefit

### Adamantanes — Second Line
- **Amantadine** and **Rimantadine**
- **Mechanism:** Block M2 ion channel → prevent uncoating of virus inside endosome → virus cannot release its RNA into the cell
- **Effective against:** Influenza A only — Influenza B has no M2 protein
- High resistance rates — not recommended as monotherapy currently

### Supportive Treatment
- Rest, hydration, antipyretics (paracetamol — not aspirin in children)

---

## 9. Vaccines

**Seasonal influenza vaccine:**
- Reformulated annually based on WHO predictions of circulating strains
- Contains H and N antigens from predicted strains — usually 3 or 4 strains (trivalent or quadrivalent)
- Two types available:
  - **Inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV)** — killed virus; injected; suitable for all including immunocompromised
  - **Live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV)** — weakened live virus; nasal spray; not for immunocompromised

**Why the vaccine does not confer lifelong protection:**
- Antigenic drift continuously changes the surface antigens
- Antibodies from last year's vaccine may not recognize this year's strains
- Annual reformulation and revaccination required
---
# Part 2: Viral Receptors and Spikes

## 1. Introduction

Viral receptors and spikes are among the most clinically important concepts in virology. Every virus must attach to a specific receptor on a host cell before it can infect it — this step is called adsorption or attachment, and it is the first and most critical step in viral pathogenesis. The viral surface proteins (spikes) that mediate this attachment are also the primary targets of the host immune system and of antiviral drugs. Understanding viral receptors and spikes explains tissue tropism, disease manifestations, transmission routes, and the basis of antiviral therapy and vaccines.

At MKU, this topic has appeared as a major Section C essay question multiple times, asking students to discuss the clinical importance of viral receptors and spikes with specific examples.

---

## 2. What Are Viral Spikes

Viral spikes are glycoprotein projections that extend from the surface of enveloped viruses. They are encoded by the viral genome and inserted into the viral envelope. They serve as the primary means by which a virus recognizes and binds to host cell receptors.

**Functions of viral spikes:**
- Attachment to specific host cell receptors — determines which cells can be infected
- Fusion with host cell membrane — allows viral genome to enter the cell
- Immune evasion — some spikes help virus evade antibody recognition
- Targets of neutralizing antibodies — antibodies against spikes can block infection
- Targets of antiviral drugs

---

## 3. What Are Viral Receptors

Viral receptors are normal host cell surface molecules — proteins, glycoproteins, carbohydrates, or lipids — that viruses have evolved to exploit for entry. The virus does not create these receptors — it hijacks molecules that the cell uses for its own normal functions.

**The receptor determines:**
- Which cell types can be infected — tissue tropism
- Which species can be infected — host range
- Which route of transmission is possible
- What disease the virus causes

---

## 4. Clinical Importance of Viral Receptors and Spikes — With Examples

### HIV — gp120 and CD4

- **Viral spike:** gp120 (surface) and gp41 (transmembrane) — together form the envelope glycoprotein complex
- **Host receptor:** CD4 molecule on T-helper lymphocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells
- **Co-receptors:** CCR5 (macrophage-tropic strains) and CXCR4 (T-cell tropic strains)
- **Clinical importance:**
  - HIV can only infect CD4+ cells — explains selective destruction of T-helper cells
  - Loss of CD4+ cells → immunodeficiency → AIDS
  - Individuals with CCR5 deletion mutation (CCR5-delta32) are naturally resistant to HIV infection
  - Maraviroc (CCR5 antagonist) blocks the co-receptor — used as an antiretroviral drug
  - Enfuvirtide (Fuzeon) blocks gp41-mediated fusion — another drug target at this step

### Influenza — Haemagglutinin and Sialic Acid

- **Viral spike:** Haemagglutinin (H)
- **Host receptor:** Sialic acid residues on respiratory epithelial cells
  - Human influenza strains bind alpha-2,6-linked sialic acid — found in human upper respiratory tract
  - Avian influenza strains bind alpha-2,3-linked sialic acid — found in human lower respiratory tract and bird intestines
- **Clinical importance:**
  - Explains why human influenza primarily causes upper respiratory symptoms
  - Explains why avian influenza (H5N1) causes severe pneumonia — it infects deep lung tissue
  - Pigs have both receptor types — can be infected by both human and avian strains simultaneously — this is why pigs are mixing vessels for antigenic shift
  - Neutralizing antibodies against H prevent attachment — basis of influenza vaccine

### Rabies — Glycoprotein G and Acetylcholine Receptor

- **Viral spike:** Glycoprotein G
- **Host receptor:** Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at neuromuscular junctions; also NCAM (neural cell adhesion molecule) and p75 neurotrophin receptor
- **Clinical importance:**
  - Explains why rabies virus infects neurons specifically — neurotropism
  - Virus travels along peripheral nerves to the CNS — explains the pathogenesis of rabies
  - Explains why bite wounds near the CNS (face, neck) cause faster disease progression than distal wounds (feet)
  - Glycoprotein G is the target of rabies vaccine — induces protective neutralizing antibodies

### Epstein-Barr Virus — gp350 and CD21

- **Viral spike:** gp350/220
- **Host receptor:** CD21 (complement receptor 2, CR2) on B lymphocytes and epithelial cells
- **Clinical importance:**
  - EBV specifically infects B cells — explains B cell immortalization and lymphoma development
  - Explains why EBV causes infectious mononucleosis — massive B cell proliferation
  - CD21 is also involved in complement regulation — virus exploits this normal immune molecule
  - EBV latency in B cells is the basis of Burkitt's lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma

### Rhinovirus — Viral Protein and ICAM-1

- **Viral spike:** VP1, VP2, VP3 capsid proteins forming a canyon structure
- **Host receptor:** ICAM-1 (Intercellular Adhesion Molecule 1) on upper respiratory epithelial cells
- **Clinical importance:**
  - Explains why rhinovirus causes common cold — ICAM-1 is abundant in nasal epithelium
  - ICAM-1 is also a normal immune cell adhesion molecule — virus exploits it
  - Attempts to develop drugs blocking ICAM-1 binding have been explored

### Poliovirus — Viral Protein and PVR

- **Viral spike:** VP1 capsid protein
- **Host receptor:** PVR (Poliovirus Receptor — CD155) on motor neurons and intestinal cells
- **Clinical importance:**
  - Explains why poliovirus specifically destroys anterior horn motor neurons → flaccid paralysis
  - Virus enters via gut but travels to CNS via bloodstream and neural routes
  - Only primates express PVR — explains host range of poliovirus

---

## 5. Tissue Tropism

Tissue tropism means the preference of a virus for specific tissues or cell types. It is determined almost entirely by the match between the viral spike and the host receptor.

| Virus | Receptor | Tissue Tropism | Disease |
|---|---|---|---|
| HIV | CD4 / CCR5 / CXCR4 | T-helper cells, macrophages | AIDS |
| Influenza | Sialic acid (alpha-2,6) | Respiratory epithelium | Flu |
| Rabies | Acetylcholine receptor | Neurons | Encephalitis |
| EBV | CD21 | B lymphocytes | Mononucleosis, lymphoma |
| Poliovirus | CD155 (PVR) | Motor neurons | Paralysis |
| Rhinovirus | ICAM-1 | Nasal epithelium | Common cold |
| Hepatitis B | NTCP receptor | Hepatocytes | Hepatitis |

---

## 6. Receptors as Drug and Vaccine Targets

Because viral spikes and host receptors mediate the first and most critical step of infection, they are prime targets for antiviral strategies:

- **Vaccines** — most viral vaccines work by inducing antibodies against surface spike proteins, which block receptor binding and prevent infection
- **Fusion inhibitors** — Enfuvirtide blocks HIV gp41 fusion
- **CCR5 antagonists** — Maraviroc blocks HIV co-receptor
- **Neuraminidase inhibitors** — Oseltamivir blocks influenza NA, preventing viral release
- **Monoclonal antibodies** — can be designed to block specific spike-receptor interactions
---
# Part 3: Interferons

## 1. Introduction

Interferons are a family of signalling proteins produced by host cells in response to viral infection. They are part of the innate (non-specific) immune system — the body's first line of defence against viruses. They do not directly kill viruses but instead create an antiviral state in surrounding cells, slow viral replication, and activate immune cells to destroy infected cells. Interferons are critically important in limiting the spread of viral infection in the early days before the adaptive immune response (antibodies and T cells) has time to develop.

At MKU, interferons have appeared as a standalone essay question in almost every past paper — typically asking students to explain how interferons help virus-infected cells fight back the infection.

---

## 2. Types of Interferons

**Type I Interferons — Antiviral Interferons**
- **Interferon-alpha (IFN-α)**
  - Produced by: infected leukocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells
  - Main antiviral interferon
  - Multiple subtypes (IFN-α1, IFN-α2, etc.)
- **Interferon-beta (IFN-β)**
  - Produced by: infected fibroblasts and epithelial cells
  - Also antiviral
- Both IFN-α and IFN-β bind the same receptor — IFNAR (Type I interferon receptor)

**Type II Interferon — Immune Interferon**
- **Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ)**
  - Produced by: activated T lymphocytes and NK cells
  - Primarily an immune activator rather than direct antiviral
  - Activates macrophages to kill intracellular pathogens
  - Binds a different receptor — IFNGR

**Type III Interferons**
- **IFN-lambda (IFN-λ)**
  - Produced at mucosal surfaces — especially respiratory and gastrointestinal tract
  - Important in antiviral defence at mucosal barriers

---

## 3. How Interferons Are Produced — The Trigger

1. Virus infects a cell
2. Viral components — particularly double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), a byproduct of viral replication — are detected by pattern recognition receptors inside the cell
3. Key receptors: **TLR3** (in endosomes), **RIG-I** and **MDA5** (in cytoplasm)
4. These receptors trigger signalling cascades → activation of transcription factors **IRF3, IRF7, and NF-κB**
5. These transcription factors enter the nucleus and switch on **IFN-α and IFN-β genes**
6. Interferons are synthesized and secreted from the infected cell

---

## 4. How Interferons Work — Mechanism of Action

Interferons do not directly destroy viruses. Instead they act on both infected and neighbouring uninfected cells to create an antiviral state.

### Step 1: Interferon Secretion
- Infected cell secretes IFN-α and IFN-β
- These act in an autocrine manner (on the infected cell itself) and paracrine manner (on neighbouring cells)

### Step 2: Receptor Binding and Signalling
- IFN-α/β binds IFNAR on the surface of target cells
- Triggers JAK-STAT signalling pathway:
  - JAK1 and TYK2 (kinases) are activated
  - They phosphorylate STAT1 and STAT2
  - Phosphorylated STATs form a complex with IRF9 → called ISGF3
  - ISGF3 enters the nucleus → binds ISRE (Interferon Stimulated Response Element) sequences in DNA
  - Switches on hundreds of Interferon Stimulated Genes (ISGs)

### Step 3: Antiviral Proteins Produced

The ISGs encode several key antiviral proteins:

**Protein Kinase R (PKR):**
- Activated by double-stranded RNA
- Phosphorylates eIF2-alpha → blocks protein synthesis in the cell
- Stops viral protein production — also stops host protein production (cell accepts this sacrifice to stop viral spread)

**2'-5' Oligoadenylate Synthetase (OAS) and RNase L:**
- OAS activated by dsRNA → produces 2'-5' oligoadenylates
- These activate RNase L — an enzyme that degrades all RNA in the cell, both viral and host
- Destroys viral mRNA → stops viral replication

**Mx Proteins (Myxovirus Resistance Proteins):**
- GTPases that specifically interfere with viral RNA synthesis
- Particularly effective against influenza and other RNA viruses
- Block transport of viral components within the cell

**TRIM proteins and ISG15:**

- Further restrict viral replication through multiple mechanisms

### Step 4: Activation of Immune Cells
- Interferons activate **Natural Killer (NK) cells** — NK cells kill virus-infected cells directly
- Interferons increase **MHC class I expression** on infected cells — makes them more visible to cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8+ T cells)
- Interferons activate macrophages — enhance phagocytosis of infected cells and viral debris
- Interferons promote maturation of dendritic cells — bridge innate and adaptive immunity

### Step 5: Apoptosis of Infected Cells
- Interferons can trigger apoptosis (programmed cell death) in heavily infected cells
- This is a sacrifice — the infected cell destroys itself to prevent further viral spread
- Neighbouring cells are warned and enter antiviral state before they get infected

---

## 5. Summary — How Interferons Fight Viral Infection

| Action | Effect |
|---|---|
| Block protein synthesis (PKR) | Stops viral protein production |
| Degrade RNA (OAS/RNase L) | Destroys viral genome and mRNA |
| Mx proteins | Interfere with viral RNA synthesis |
| Activate NK cells | Kill infected cells directly |
| Upregulate MHC I | Infected cells targeted by CD8+ T cells |
| Activate macrophages | Enhanced clearance of infected cells |
| Trigger apoptosis | Infected cells self-destruct |
| Warn neighbouring cells | Create antiviral state before infection spreads |

---

## 6. Viral Evasion of Interferons

Many viruses have evolved mechanisms to block interferon production or action:

- **Influenza NS1 protein** — blocks RIG-I sensing of viral RNA; prevents IFN production
- **Hepatitis C virus** — blocks JAK-STAT signalling; interferons cannot activate ISGs
- **Adenovirus VA RNA** — blocks PKR activation
- **HIV Vif protein** — degrades host antiviral proteins
- **Herpesviruses** — multiple mechanisms including blocking IRF3 activation

This is why some viral infections are severe — the virus disables the first line of defence before the adaptive immune system can respond.

---

## 7. Clinical Use of Interferons

Interferons are used therapeutically:

- **IFN-α (Pegylated)** — treatment of chronic Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C (now largely replaced by direct-acting antivirals for HCV)
- **IFN-β** — treatment of Multiple Sclerosis (reduces relapse frequency)
- **IFN-γ** — treatment of chronic granulomatous disease
- **IFN-α** — treatment of certain malignancies (hairy cell leukaemia, Kaposi's sarcoma)

# Part 4: Viral Pathogenesis

## 1. Introduction

Viral pathogenesis refers to the sequence of events that occur from the moment a virus enters the host body to the point where disease is produced. Understanding pathogenesis explains why different viruses cause different diseases, why some infections are mild and others fatal, why some viruses are localized while others spread throughout the body, and how the host immune system responds. It also forms the scientific basis for designing antiviral drugs, vaccines, and other prevention strategies.

At MKU, the stages of viral pathogenesis have appeared as both MCQ and essay questions repeatedly — it is one of the most fundamental topics in the entire virology course.

---

## 2. Stages of Viral Pathogenesis — The Core Framework

### Stage 1: Entry and Inoculation

The virus must first gain access to the body through a portal of entry.

**Portals of entry:**
- **Respiratory tract** — most common; influenza, measles, mumps, RSV, rhinovirus, adenovirus
- **Gastrointestinal tract** — fecal-oral route; poliovirus, hepatitis A, rotavirus, adenovirus
- **Genital/urogenital mucosa** — sexual transmission; HIV, HSV-2, HPV, HBV
- **Skin** — through breaks, bites, or injections; rabies (animal bite), arbovirus (insect bite), HIV (needlestick)
- **Conjunctiva** — adenovirus, HSV
- **Transplacental** — vertical transmission; CMV, rubella, HIV, HSV

**The portal of entry influences:**
- Which tissues are first infected
- How the disease begins
- What prevention strategies are possible

---

### Stage 2: Primary Replication

- After entry, the virus replicates locally at the site of entry
- This is called primary replication or local infection
- Produces the initial viral load
- May cause local symptoms — e.g., sore throat in influenza, vesicles in HSV, diarrhea in rotavirus
- Some viruses remain localized here and never spread further — e.g., rhinovirus (common cold), HPV (warts)
- Other viruses use this as a launching pad for systemic spread

---

### Stage 3: Spread to Regional Lymph Nodes

- Virus drains from local site to regional lymph nodes via lymphatics
- Replicates further in lymph nodes
- Lymph nodes may become enlarged — lymphadenopathy
- Some viruses are cleared here by the immune system — infection remains localized

---

### Stage 4: Primary Viremia

- Virus escapes lymph nodes and enters the bloodstream — **viremia**
- This is called primary viremia — usually a brief, low-level phase
- Allows virus to reach distant organs
- Patient may have non-specific symptoms — fever, malaise, myalgia
- Virus may be carried by:
  - Free in plasma
  - Inside blood cells — HIV in CD4+ cells, EBV in B cells, CMV in monocytes

---

### Stage 5: Replication in Target Organs

- Virus leaves bloodstream and infects specific target organs — determined by receptor expression
- Extensive replication in target organs produces high viral loads
- This is where organ-specific disease develops
- Examples:
  - Poliovirus — anterior horn cells of spinal cord → paralysis
  - Hepatitis viruses — hepatocytes → hepatitis
  - HIV — CD4+ T cells → immunodeficiency
  - Rabies — neurons → encephalitis
  - Influenza — lower respiratory epithelium → pneumonia

---

### Stage 6: Secondary Viremia

- After replication in target organs, virus may re-enter bloodstream — secondary viremia
- Usually higher viral loads than primary viremia
- Spreads to even more distant organs
- Responsible for disseminated disease — e.g., CMV dissemination in immunocompromised

---

### Stage 7: Disease and Tissue Damage

Tissue damage in viral infections occurs through several mechanisms:

**Direct viral cytopathic effect:**
- Virus kills infected cells directly during replication
- Cell lysis when new virions burst out
- Examples: poliovirus, influenza, herpes viruses

**Immune-mediated damage:**
- The host immune response itself causes much of the damage
- Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells — necessary but causes tissue destruction
- Inflammatory response — cytokines cause fever, tissue damage
- Immune complexes deposited in tissues — complement activation → damage
- Examples: hepatitis B liver damage is primarily immune-mediated

**Inclusion bodies:**
- Accumulations of viral components inside infected cells
- Visible on microscopy — useful for diagnosis
- Examples: Negri bodies in rabies (in neurons), owl-eye inclusions in CMV, Cowdry type A bodies in HSV

**Transformation:**
- Some viruses do not kill the cell but instead transform it into a cancer cell
- Examples: EBV, HPV, HBV, HCV, HTLV-1

---

### Stage 8: Resolution or Persistence

**Resolution:**
- Immune system clears the virus
- Adaptive immunity — neutralizing antibodies and cytotoxic T cells eliminate infected cells
- Patient recovers
- Immunological memory established — protection against reinfection

**Persistent Infection:**
Some viruses are not cleared and establish persistent infection:

- **Latent infection** — virus remains in host cells in a dormant state, no active replication
  - Examples: HSV in sensory ganglia, VZV in dorsal root ganglia, EBV in B cells
  - Reactivation possible when immunity drops

- **Chronic infection** — virus continues replicating at low levels indefinitely
  - Examples: Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, HIV
  - Ongoing immune activation → chronic liver damage, immunodeficiency

- **Slow infection** — very long incubation period, then progressive fatal disease
  - Examples: HIV (years before AIDS), prion diseases (decades)

- **Transforming infection** — virus integrates and transforms cells into tumour cells
  - Examples: HPV (cervical cancer), EBV (Burkitt's lymphoma), HTLV-1 (T-cell leukaemia)

---

## 3. Factors Determining Disease Outcome

**Viral factors:**
- Virulence — ability to cause disease
- Inoculum size — larger dose → more severe disease
- Tissue tropism — determined by receptor-spike interaction
- Rate of replication

**Host factors:**
- Age — extremes of age more susceptible
- Immune status — immunocompromised patients get severe disease
- Nutritional status
- Genetic factors — e.g., CCR5-delta32 mutation in HIV resistance
- Prior immunity — vaccines or prior infection

---

## 4. Host Defenses Against Viral Infection

**Non-specific (Innate) defenses:**
- Physical barriers — skin, mucus, cilia
- Fever — high temperature inhibits viral replication
- Interferons — create antiviral state in neighbouring cells
- Natural Killer cells — kill infected cells without prior sensitization
- Macrophages and dendritic cells — phagocytosis, antigen presentation
- Complement system — direct viral lysis, opsonization

**Specific (Adaptive) defenses:**
- **Humoral immunity (antibodies):**
  - Neutralizing antibodies bind viral spikes → block attachment to host receptors
  - Opsonizing antibodies enhance phagocytosis of virions
  - Complement-fixing antibodies activate complement → viral lysis
  - Most effective against extracellular virus — before it enters cells

- **Cell-mediated immunity:**
  - Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8+ T cells) — kill infected cells directly
  - Helper T cells (CD4+) — coordinate and amplify immune response
  - Most effective against intracellular virus — kills infected cells

- **Immunological memory:**
  - Long-lived memory B and T cells
  - Rapid, amplified response on re-exposure
  - Basis of vaccination

---

## 5. Persistent Viral Infections — Summary Table

| Type | Characteristics | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Latent | Dormant; no active replication; periodic reactivation | HSV, VZV, EBV, CMV |
| Chronic | Ongoing low-level replication; not cleared | HBV, HCV, HIV |
| Slow | Very long incubation; progressive fatal disease | Prions, HIV |
| Transforming | Integration; cell transformation to tumour | HPV, EBV, HTLV-1 |

# Part 1: Vaccines and Antivirals

## 1. Introduction

Vaccines and antiviral drugs are the two primary strategies for controlling viral infections. Vaccines work by preparing the immune system before infection occurs — they are preventive. Antiviral drugs work by interfering with specific steps in the viral replication cycle — they are therapeutic. Both strategies depend on understanding viral structure, replication, and the host immune response. These topics are among the most consistently examined at MKU, appearing in essays across virtually every past paper, particularly questions on OPV vs IPV, active vs passive immunization, and the mechanism of selective toxicity of antivirals.

---

## 2. Vaccines

### What is a Vaccine

A vaccine is a biological preparation that induces active immunity against a specific pathogen by stimulating the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells without causing the disease itself.

### Mechanism of Protection

1. Vaccine antigen is administered
2. Antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages) process the antigen
3. Presented to CD4+ T-helper cells via MHC class II
4. T-helper cells activate B cells → differentiate into plasma cells
5. Plasma cells produce specific antibodies against the viral antigen
6. CD8+ cytotoxic T cells also activated — important for live vaccines
7. Long-lived memory B and T cells formed
8. On exposure to real virus — rapid, amplified secondary immune response
9. Virus neutralized before disease can develop

### Types of Vaccines

**1. Live Attenuated Vaccines**
- Contain weakened but living virus — reduced virulence, retained antigenicity
- Produced by: repeated passage of virus in non-human cells until it loses ability to cause disease in humans
- Advantages:
  - Strongest and most durable immunity — mimics natural infection
  - Both humoral and cell-mediated immunity induced
  - Single dose often sufficient
  - Mucosal immunity produced (especially important for gut/respiratory viruses)
- Disadvantages:
  - Risk of reversion to virulence — attenuated virus can mutate back
  - Cannot be given to immunocompromised patients — can cause disease
  - Requires cold chain — heat sensitive
  - Cannot be given in pregnancy
- Examples: OPV (oral polio), MMR (measles, mumps, rubella), Yellow fever vaccine, Varicella vaccine, LAIV (live attenuated influenza)

**2. Inactivated (Killed) Vaccines**
- Contain killed virus — treated with heat, formalin, or beta-propiolactone
- Virus cannot replicate but antigens are preserved
- Advantages:
  - Cannot cause disease — safer
  - Can be given to immunocompromised patients
  - Stable — does not revert to virulence
- Disadvantages:
  - Weaker immunity — mainly humoral, less cell-mediated
  - Multiple doses required (boosters needed)
  - Adjuvant often needed to boost response
  - No mucosal immunity
- Examples: IPV (injected polio), inactivated influenza vaccine, Hepatitis A vaccine, Rabies vaccine

**3. Subunit Vaccines**
- Contain only specific viral proteins — not whole virus
- Examples: Hepatitis B vaccine (HBsAg), HPV vaccine (L1 capsid protein)
- Very safe — no viral genetic material
- Requires adjuvant and boosters

**4. Toxoid Vaccines**
- Not strictly viral — used for bacterial toxins
- Inactivated toxin — cannot cause disease but induces antitoxin antibodies

**5. mRNA Vaccines**
- Deliver mRNA encoding viral antigen into host cells
- Host cells produce the antigen → immune response
- Examples: COVID-19 vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna)
- Advantages: rapid production, no live virus needed

---

### OPV vs IPV — The Most Examined Vaccine Comparison

This comparison has appeared in essay form multiple times at MKU.

| Feature | OPV (Oral Polio Vaccine) | IPV (Inactivated Polio Vaccine) |
|---|---|---|
| Type | Live attenuated | Killed/inactivated |
| Route | Oral (swallowed) | Injected (intramuscular) |
| Developed by | Albert Sabin | Jonas Salk |
| Immunity type | Humoral + cell-mediated + mucosal (gut IgA) | Humoral only |
| Herd immunity | Yes — vaccine virus shed in stool, spreads to contacts | No — does not spread |
| Dose | Single dose effective | Multiple doses required |
| Cost | Cheaper | More expensive |
| Risk | Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) — rare but real | No risk of VAPP |
| Use in immunocompromised | Contraindicated — can cause disease | Safe |
| Cold chain | Required | Required |
| Why some countries prefer IPV | Eliminate risk of VAPP, especially in countries with low polio burden | Safer for immunocompromised populations |

**Why OPV produces better gut immunity:**
- OPV is swallowed → replicates in gut epithelium → stimulates local mucosal IgA production
- Gut IgA blocks poliovirus entry at the primary site of infection
- IPV injected → only systemic IgG produced → no gut mucosal immunity
- This is why OPV is better at preventing transmission — it blocks infection at the gut

**Why some countries prefer IPV:**
- Risk of VAPP — approximately 1 in 2.4 million doses causes vaccine-associated paralysis
- Countries that have already eliminated wild poliovirus use IPV to avoid the risk of introducing vaccine-derived poliovirus into a susceptible population

---

### Active vs Passive Immunization — High Yield

| Feature | Active Immunization | Passive Immunization |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Stimulating the host immune system to produce its own antibodies | Administering pre-formed antibodies directly |
| Onset | Slow — days to weeks | Immediate — within hours |
| Duration | Long-lasting — months to years (memory cells) | Short-lived — weeks (antibodies degraded) |
| Source | Vaccine or natural infection | Human or animal serum, immunoglobulins |
| Memory | Yes — immunological memory formed | No memory cells produced |
| Use | Prevention before exposure | Treatment after exposure, or in immunocompromised |
| Examples | All standard vaccines | Rabies immunoglobulin, tetanus immunoglobulin, HNIG, anti-D |

**How an attenuated vaccine protects a child:**
1. Attenuated virus administered — cannot cause disease in immunocompetent child
2. Virus replicates minimally — enough to stimulate immune response
3. B cells produce antibodies against viral antigens
4. Memory B and T cells formed
5. On exposure to wild virus — memory cells activated rapidly
6. Large amounts of antibody produced within days — neutralize virus before disease develops
7. Child is protected

---

## 3. Antiviral Drugs

### Introduction

Antiviral drugs work by targeting specific steps in the viral replication cycle. Unlike antibiotics, antivirals must be selectively toxic — they must inhibit viral replication without significantly harming host cells. This selectivity is achieved by targeting viral enzymes or processes that are unique to the virus or significantly different from host cell equivalents.

### The Viral Replication Cycle and Drug Target Sites

Antiviral drugs can target any of the following stages:

**Stage 1: Attachment/Adsorption**
- Target: viral spike — host receptor interaction
- Drugs: Maraviroc (blocks CCR5 co-receptor — HIV), Monoclonal antibodies against viral spikes

**Stage 2: Penetration and Fusion**
- Target: membrane fusion
- Drugs: Enfuvirtide/Fuzeon (blocks HIV gp41 fusion), Amantadine (blocks influenza M2 ion channel — prevents uncoating)

**Stage 3: Uncoating**
- Target: release of viral genome inside the cell
- Drugs: Amantadine, Rimantadine (influenza M2 channel blockers)

**Stage 4: Replication of Viral Genome**
- Target: viral polymerases — most important drug target stage
- Drugs:
  - NRTIs — Zidovudine, Tenofovir, Lamivudine (HIV reverse transcriptase)
  - NNRTIs — Nevirapine, Efavirenz (HIV reverse transcriptase)
  - Acyclovir triphosphate (HSV DNA polymerase)
  - Ganciclovir (CMV DNA polymerase)
  - Sofosbuvir (HCV RNA polymerase)
  - Oseltamivir — technically targets release but also reduces replication efficiency

**Stage 5: Transcription and Translation**
- Less commonly targeted
- Drugs: Fomivirsen (antisense oligonucleotide — CMV)

**Stage 6: Assembly**
- Target: viral protease — processing of polyproteins into functional proteins
- Drugs: Protease inhibitors — Lopinavir, Ritonavir, Atazanavir (HIV)

**Stage 7: Release/Budding**
- Target: neuraminidase — release of influenza virions
- Drugs: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu), Zanamivir — neuraminidase inhibitors

---

### Selective Toxicity — How Antivirals Spare Host Cells

Selective toxicity means a drug is toxic to the virus or virus-infected cells but not to normal host cells. This is achieved through:

**1. Targeting virus-specific enzymes not present in host cells:**
- HIV reverse transcriptase — host cells do not reverse transcribe RNA into DNA
- HIV integrase — host cells do not integrate foreign DNA via viral integrase
- Influenza neuraminidase — host cells do not express neuraminidase

**2. Targeting viral enzymes that differ sufficiently from host equivalents:**
- Viral DNA polymerases (HSV, CMV) differ from human DNA polymerase in structure
- Acyclovir triphosphate has much higher affinity for HSV DNA polymerase than human DNA polymerase

**3. Requiring virus-specific activation:**
- Acyclovir requires viral thymidine kinase for first phosphorylation
- Only HSV-infected cells contain viral TK → only infected cells activate acyclovir
- Uninfected cells cannot activate acyclovir → spared

---

### Key Antiviral Drugs Summary

| Drug | Virus Target | Mechanism | Stage Blocked |
|---|---|---|---|
| Acyclovir | HSV, VZV | Inhibits viral DNA polymerase after activation by viral TK | Replication |
| Ganciclovir | CMV | Inhibits CMV DNA polymerase | Replication |
| Zidovudine (AZT) | HIV | NRTI — inhibits reverse transcriptase | Replication |
| Nevirapine | HIV | NNRTI — inhibits reverse transcriptase | Replication |
| Raltegravir | HIV | Integrase inhibitor | Integration |
| Lopinavir/Ritonavir | HIV | Protease inhibitor | Assembly |
| Enfuvirtide (Fuzeon) | HIV | Fusion inhibitor — blocks gp41 | Penetration/Fusion |
| Maraviroc | HIV | CCR5 antagonist | Attachment |
| Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) | Influenza A and B | Neuraminidase inhibitor | Release |
| Amantadine | Influenza A only | M2 channel blocker | Uncoating |
| Sofosbuvir | HCV | NS5B RNA polymerase inhibitor | Replication |
| Ribavirin | Broad spectrum | Multiple mechanisms | Replication |

# Part 2: Rabies Virus

## 1. Introduction

Rabies is an acute, progressive, invariably fatal viral encephalitis caused by the Rabies virus. It is one of the oldest known infectious diseases and remains a significant public health problem in Africa and Asia. Despite being almost universally fatal once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is completely preventable through vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis. This stark contrast — preventable yet fatal — makes it one of the most clinically important viruses to understand. At MKU, rabies has appeared in essay questions asking students to describe its pathogenesis and the management of an exposed patient.

---

## 2. Classification and Structure

- **Family:** Rhabdoviridae
- **Genus:** Lyssavirus
- **Genome:** Single-stranded, negative-sense RNA
- **Enveloped virus**
- **Shape:** Bullet-shaped — distinctive, unique among human viruses
- **Key surface protein:** Glycoprotein G — mediates attachment to host receptors; target of neutralizing antibodies; basis of rabies vaccine

**Internal proteins:**
- **N protein (nucleoprotein)** — encapsidates RNA genome; used in diagnosis
- **L protein** — RNA-dependent RNA polymerase
- **P protein** — polymerase cofactor
- **M protein** — matrix protein; links envelope to nucleocapsid

---

## 3. Transmission

- **Animal bite** — primary route; infected saliva introduced into wound
- **Scratch** — if contaminated with infected saliva
- **Licking of broken skin or mucous membranes** — by infected animal
- **Aerosol transmission** — very rare; reported in bat caves with high bat density
- **Transplantation** — extremely rare; infected cornea or organ transplant

**Reservoir animals:**
- Dogs — most common source of human rabies globally, especially in Africa and Asia
- Bats — main reservoir in Americas
- Foxes, raccoons, skunks — in specific geographic regions
- Wild animals — jackals, mongooses, wolves

**Important:** Virus is present in saliva of infected animals. Animals are infectious before showing symptoms — in the prodromal phase.

---

## 4. Pathogenesis — High Yield

The pathogenesis of rabies is one of the most distinctive in virology and explains all the clinical features.

### Step 1: Inoculation
- Infected animal bites → virus deposited in wound
- Virus remains at the wound site, replicating in local muscle cells
- **Incubation at wound site:** days to weeks — this is the window for post-exposure prophylaxis

### Step 2: Peripheral Nerve Entry
- Virus binds to **nicotinic acetylcholine receptors** at neuromuscular junctions
- Also binds NCAM (neural cell adhesion molecule) and p75 neurotrophin receptor
- Virus enters peripheral nerve endings at the wound site

### Step 3: Retrograde Axonal Transport

- Virus travels **retrograde** (from nerve ending toward cell body) along peripheral sensory and motor nerves
- Travels inside axons — protected from immune system
- Rate of travel: approximately 50–100 mm per day
- This is why wounds closer to the CNS (face, neck) cause faster disease — shorter journey
- Wounds on feet or hands cause slower disease — longer journey to CNS

### Step 4: CNS Entry and Spread
- Virus reaches the spinal cord and brain
- Spreads rapidly throughout CNS — infects neurons extensively
- Primarily infects the **limbic system, brainstem, and cerebellum**
- No inflammatory destruction of neurons — virus causes functional disruption rather than cell death
- This explains why there is little structural damage on pathology despite severe clinical disease

### Step 5: Centrifugal Spread

- Virus spreads **centrifugally** (outward from CNS) along peripheral nerves to many organs
- Reaches salivary glands → virus present in saliva — this is how transmission occurs
- Also reaches cornea, skin, heart, adrenal glands, kidneys

### Step 6: Death
- Death from respiratory failure, cardiovascular collapse, or brainstem dysfunction
- Almost 100% fatal once clinical symptoms appear

---

## 5. Clinical Features

**Incubation period:**
- Average: 1–3 months
- Range: 4 days to several years (rare)
- Shorter with: head/neck bites, severe wounds, large inoculum

### Phase 1: Prodromal Phase (2–10 days)
- Non-specific symptoms — fever, malaise, headache, fatigue
- Paraesthesia or pain at the wound site — highly specific early sign
- Anxiety, agitation, irritability

### Phase 2: Acute Neurological Phase (2–7 days)

**Furious (Encephalitic) Rabies — 80% of cases:**
- Hydrophobia — fear of water; attempts to swallow trigger violent pharyngeal spasms — pathognomonic of rabies
- Aerophobia — fear of air/drafts; similar spasms triggered by air on skin
- Hypersalivation — virus in salivary glands; swallowing painful
- Hyperexcitability, agitation, aggression
- Hallucinations, confusion
- Autonomic dysfunction — tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia
- Periods of calm between episodes of spasm

**Paralytic (Dumb) Rabies — 20% of cases:**
- Ascending flaccid paralysis — resembles Guillain-Barré syndrome
- Less dramatic — often misdiagnosed
- Eventually progresses to coma

### Phase 3: Coma and Death (days)
- Progressive coma
- Respiratory failure
- Death — virtually 100% once symptomatic

---

## 6. Diagnosis

- **Clinical diagnosis** — in endemic areas, classic presentation is sufficient
- **Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test** — gold standard; detects rabies antigen in brain tissue (post-mortem) or skin biopsy (corneal epithelium)
- **Negri bodies** — eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies in neurons (especially Purkinje cells of cerebellum and hippocampal neurons); pathognomonic on histology
- **RT-PCR** — detects viral RNA in saliva, CSF, skin
- **Serology** — antibody detection; useful in vaccinated individuals

---

## 7. Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) — High Yield

PEP is effective because of the long incubation period before virus reaches the CNS. Once the virus enters peripheral nerves and travels to the brain, PEP is no longer effective.

### Wound Management — First and Most Critical Step

- Immediate and thorough washing of wound with soap and water for at least 15 minutes
- Apply antiseptic — povidone iodine or alcohol
- Do not suture wound primarily if possible — suturing can push virus deeper
- This simple step significantly reduces viral inoculum

### Passive Immunization — Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG)
- Administered once — at the time of first presentation
- Infiltrated directly into and around the wound — neutralizes virus locally
- Remaining dose given intramuscularly at a distant site
- Human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG) — preferred; 20 IU/kg
- Equine rabies immunoglobulin (ERIG) — cheaper alternative; test for allergy first
- Purpose — provides immediate protection while active immunity develops

### Active Immunization — Rabies Vaccine
- Modern cell-culture rabies vaccines — HDCV (Human Diploid Cell Vaccine), PCECV (Purified Chick Embryo Cell Vaccine)
- Schedule for unvaccinated person: days 0, 3, 7, 14 (and sometimes day 28)
- Schedule for previously vaccinated person: days 0 and 3 only — no RIG needed
- Vaccine induces active immunity — antibodies against glycoprotein G
- Takes 7–14 days to produce protective antibody levels

### Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP)
- For high-risk groups — veterinarians, wildlife workers, laboratory workers, travellers to endemic areas
- Three doses — days 0, 7, 21 or 28
- Simplifies PEP if exposed — only 2 booster doses needed, no RIG
---
# Part 3: CMV and EBV

## 1. Introduction

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) are both members of the Herpesviridae family and share the fundamental herpesvirus property of establishing lifelong latent infection. However, they differ significantly in their target cells, clinical manifestations, and oncogenic potential. CMV is the most important cause of congenital viral infection worldwide and is a major pathogen in immunocompromised patients. EBV is the cause of infectious mononucleosis and is strongly associated with several malignancies including Burkitt's lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Both are high-yield topics at MKU, appearing in MCQs and essays.

---

## 2. Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

### Classification
- **Family:** Herpesviridae
- **Subfamily:** Betaherpesvirinae
- **Genome:** Double-stranded DNA — largest herpesvirus genome
- **Enveloped virus**
- Characteristic **owl-eye inclusion bodies** in infected cells — large intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo

### Epidemiology
- Ubiquitous — infects 50–90% of adults worldwide
- Transmitted through: saliva, urine, breast milk, sexual contact, blood transfusion, organ transplantation, transplacental
- Primary infection usually asymptomatic in immunocompetent individuals
- Establishes latency in monocytes, macrophages, and endothelial cells

### Target Cells
- Virtually all nucleated cells — explains why CMV causes disseminated disease
- Latency in: monocytes and their precursors in bone marrow
- Reactivation when cell-mediated immunity falls

### CMV in Immunocompetent Patients
- Usually asymptomatic
- Can cause a mononucleosis-like syndrome — fever, fatigue, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis
- Distinguished from EBV mononucleosis by negative monospot test (heterophile antibody negative)

### Congenital CMV — Highest Yield

Congenital CMV is the most common congenital viral infection worldwide.

**Transmission:**
- Transplacental — primary maternal infection during pregnancy most dangerous
- Risk of transmission: 30–40% if primary infection in pregnancy
- Secondary infection (reactivation) can also transmit but causes less severe disease

**Clinical features — the congenitally infected neonate:**
- 90% asymptomatic at birth — but 10–15% develop late sequelae
- 10% symptomatic at birth:
  - **Microcephaly** — small head; most serious sequela
  - **Periventricular calcifications** — on CT scan; pathognomonic
  - Hepatosplenomegaly
  - Jaundice
  - Petechiae and purpura — blueberry muffin appearance
  - Chorioretinitis — can cause blindness
  - Sensorineural hearing loss — most common long-term sequel
  - Mental retardation
  - Seizures

**Diagnosis of congenital CMV:**
- **Urine culture or PCR** — within first 3 weeks of life; virus shed in urine
- Blood PCR — detects CMV DNA
- Serology — IgM in neonate (IgM does not cross placenta — presence confirms active neonatal infection)

**Treatment:**
- Ganciclovir (IV) or Valganciclovir (oral prodrug)
- Given to symptomatic neonates — reduces hearing loss progression
- Mechanism: Ganciclovir inhibits CMV DNA polymerase

### CMV in Immunocompromised Patients

In transplant recipients and HIV/AIDS patients, CMV causes severe disease:
- **CMV retinitis** — most common in AIDS; causes progressive blindness; treated with ganciclovir
- **CMV pneumonitis** — severe, life-threatening pneumonia in bone marrow transplant patients
- **CMV colitis** — bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain
- **CMV encephalitis** — in advanced AIDS
- **CMV hepatitis**

**Treatment of CMV disease:**
- **Ganciclovir** (IV) — first-line
- **Valganciclovir** (oral) — prodrug; used for maintenance
- **Foscarnet** — used when resistance to ganciclovir
- **Cidofovir** — second-line

### Diagnosis
- **Owl-eye inclusions** — histology of infected tissue
- **PCR** — most sensitive; detects CMV DNA in blood, urine, CSF
- **Shell vial culture** — rapid culture method
- **pp65 antigenemia** — detects CMV antigen in leukocytes; used to monitor transplant patients

---

## 3. Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)

### Classification
- **Family:** Herpesviridae
- **Subfamily:** Gammaherpesvirinae
- **Genome:** Double-stranded DNA
- **Enveloped virus**

### Transmission
- Saliva — primary route; kissing disease
- Blood transfusion — rare
- Organ transplantation

### Target Cells
- **B lymphocytes** — primary target; EBV binds CD21 (complement receptor 2)
- Epithelial cells of oropharynx and nasopharynx
- Latency in B lymphocytes — lifelong

### Infectious Mononucleosis (Glandular Fever)

**Pathogenesis:**
- EBV infects oropharyngeal epithelial cells → spreads to B lymphocytes in tonsillar tissue
- B cells become immortalized and proliferate massively
- CD8+ cytotoxic T cells respond aggressively to destroy infected B cells
- The reactive T cells are the atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells) seen on blood film
- Clinical disease is largely immune-mediated — the T cell response causes symptoms

**Clinical features:**
- Affects adolescents and young adults predominantly
- **Triad:** fever, pharyngitis (exudative tonsillitis), lymphadenopathy (especially posterior cervical)
- Splenomegaly — in 50%; risk of splenic rupture — avoid contact sports
- Hepatomegaly and mild hepatitis
- Periorbital oedema
- Maculopapular rash — especially if ampicillin/amoxicillin given — characteristic drug reaction
- Fatigue — can persist for weeks to months

**Diagnosis:**
- **Monospot test (Paul-Bunnell test)** — detects heterophile antibodies; positive in 85–90% of cases
- **Blood film** — atypical lymphocytes (large, activated CD8+ T cells)
- **EBV-specific serology** — VCA IgM (acute infection), VCA IgG (past infection), EA antibodies (active replication), EBNA antibodies (appear late, confirm past infection)
- **PCR** — detects EBV DNA; used in immunocompromised
- **FBC** — lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes

**Treatment:**
- Supportive — rest, analgesia, adequate hydration
- Avoid ampicillin/amoxicillin — causes rash in EBV infection
- Avoid contact sports until splenomegaly resolves — risk of splenic rupture
- Steroids — for severe airway obstruction from tonsillar enlargement
- No specific antiviral — acyclovir has limited benefit

### EBV and Oncogenesis — High Yield

EBV is one of the most important oncogenic viruses. It causes malignancy through:
- B cell immortalization via latent gene expression
- Integration of viral DNA near oncogenes
- Immunosuppression in host allows uncontrolled B cell proliferation

**EBV-associated malignancies:**

| Malignancy | Key Facts |
|---|---|
| Burkitt's lymphoma | B cell lymphoma; jaw mass in African children; t(8;14) translocation — c-myc oncogene activation; endemic in malaria belt of Africa |
| Nasopharyngeal carcinoma | Common in Southern China and Southeast Asia; EBV in virtually all cases |
| Hodgkin's lymphoma | EBV in 40–50% of cases; Reed-Sternberg cells contain EBV |
| Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) | Uncontrolled EBV-driven B cell proliferation in immunosuppressed transplant recipients |
| Primary CNS lymphoma | In AIDS patients with very low CD4 counts |
