## 4. Liver Disease
### Functions of the Liver
- Detoxification of drugs, alcohol, and metabolic waste
- Synthesis of plasma proteins (albumin, clotting factors)
- Bile production for fat digestion
- Carbohydrate and lipid metabolism
- Iron storage (ferritin)
### Types of Liver Disease
**Hepatitis (Inflammation):**
- **Acute** — sudden onset; causes: viral (Hep A, B, C), toxins, alcohol, autoimmune
- **Chronic** — >6 months; causes: Hep B, Hep C, autoimmune hepatitis
**Fatty Liver Disease:**
- **NAFLD** — fat accumulation unrelated to alcohol; associated with obesity, diabetes, metabolic syndrome. Can progress to NASH → cirrhosis
- **Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD)** — spectrum: fatty liver → alcoholic hepatitis → cirrhosis
**Cirrhosis:**
- End-stage scarring from chronic liver damage; irreversible; causes: viral hepatitis, alcohol, NAFLD
- Complications: portal hypertension, ascites, varices, hepatic encephalopathy, HCC
**Liver Cancer:**
- **Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)** — most common primary liver cancer; arises on background of cirrhosis or viral hepatitis
- **Cholangiocarcinoma** — bile duct cancer
**Genetic Liver Diseases:**
- **Haemochromatosis** — iron overload → liver damage, diabetes, cardiomyopathy; diagnose with ferritin + transferrin saturation
- **Wilson's Disease** — copper accumulation (defective ATP7B gene) → liver disease, neuropsychiatric symptoms, Kayser-Fleischer rings; diagnose with caeruloplasmin + 24-hr urinary copper
- **Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency** — can cause cirrhosis and emphysema
**Autoimmune:**
- **Autoimmune Hepatitis** — immune attack on hepatocytes; ANA/SMA positive
- **Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)** — bile duct destruction; AMA (anti-mitochondrial antibody) positive; causes pruritus
- **Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)** — bile duct scarring; associated with IBD
**Biliary:**
- **Gallstones** — obstruct bile flow → jaundice, cholecystitis
- **Biliary Atresia** — congenital absence/closure of bile ducts in infants
### Clinical Features of Liver Disease
| Feature | Explanation |
|---|---|
| Jaundice | Elevated bilirubin → yellowing of skin and sclera |
| Dark urine | Conjugated bilirubin excreted in urine |
| Pale stools | Bile not reaching intestine (obstructive) |
| Ascites | Portal hypertension + low albumin → fluid in abdomen |
| Hepatic Encephalopathy | Ammonia accumulation → confusion, flap (asterixis) |
| Spider angiomata / Palmar erythema | Oestrogen accumulation in cirrhosis |
| Pruritus | Bile salt deposition in skin (PBC especially) |
| Fatigue | Chronic disease, anaemia |
### Laboratory Diagnosis of Liver Disease
| Test | Significance |
|---|---|
| **ALT** | Most liver-specific; elevated in hepatitis, hepatocellular damage |
| **AST** | Elevated in liver + heart + muscle damage; AST:ALT >2 suggests alcoholic hepatitis |
| **ALP** | Elevated in cholestatic disease (bile duct obstruction, PBC, PSC) |
| **GGT** | Sensitive for biliary/liver disease; elevated with alcohol |
| **Bilirubin (total, direct, indirect)** | Direct ↑ → obstructive/conjugated; indirect ↑ → pre-hepatic (haemolysis) |
| **Albumin** | Low → chronic liver failure (poor synthetic function) |
| **PT/INR** | Prolonged → liver can't synthesise clotting factors; severity marker |
| **Viral hepatitis serology** | HBsAg, anti-HCV, HBV DNA PCR, HCV RNA PCR |
| **ANA, SMA, AMA** | Autoimmune hepatitis (ANA/SMA), PBC (AMA) |
| **Caeruloplasmin + urinary copper** | Wilson's disease |
| **Ferritin + transferrin saturation** | Haemochromatosis (ferritin high, sat >60%) |
| **Liver biopsy** | Grade and stage fibrosis; confirm diagnosis where uncertain |
| **FibroScan (Elastography)** | Non-invasive assessment of liver stiffness/fibrosis |

## 5. Body Fluid Cytology
### Types of Body Fluids
- **Pleural** — chest cavity; tapped by thoracentesis
- **Peritoneal/Ascitic** — abdomen; tapped by paracentesis
- **Pericardial** — around heart; pericardiocentesis
- **CSF** — surrounds brain/spinal cord; lumbar puncture
- **Synovial** — joint cavities; arthrocentesis
- **Urine, bile, gastric juice, saliva, sweat** — other analysable fluids
### Transudate vs Exudate (Light's Criteria)
| Feature | Transudate | Exudate |
|---|---|---|
| Protein | <2.5 g/dL | >2.5 g/dL |
| Specific gravity | <1.012 | >1.020 |
| LDH | Low | High |
| Appearance | Clear, pale yellow | Turbid, cloudy, may be bloody |
| Nature | Non-inflammatory | Inflammatory |
| Causes | Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome | Infection, malignancy, TB, pneumonia |
**Light's Criteria formally classifies exudate if any of:** pleural fluid protein/serum protein >0.5, pleural LDH/serum LDH >0.6, pleural LDH >2/3 upper normal serum LDH.
### Body Fluid Cytology Processing
1. **Sample collection** — method depends on fluid type; immediate fixation if needed to preserve cells
2. **Cytocentrifugation** — concentrates sparse cells onto a slide in a uniform thin layer
3. **Smearing** — if cytocentrifuge not used; thin smear made manually
4. **Fixation** — methanol or alcohol-based fixative applied immediately to preserve morphology
5. **Staining** — Pap stain (detailed nuclear morphology), Wright's stain (blood/marrow), Diff-Quik (rapid)
6. **Drying and coverslipping**
7. **Microscopy and interpretation** — look for malignant cells, inflammatory cells (neutrophils → bacterial infection; lymphocytes → viral/TB/malignancy), organisms, crystals (e.g., urate in gout for synovial fluid)
### Clinical Significance of Body Fluid Cytology
- **Malignant effusions** — detect cancer cells in pleural/peritoneal fluid (lung, ovarian, breast cancer commonly shed cells)
- **Infectious** — organisms identified in CSF (bacteria, fungi) or stool
- **Inflammatory** — WBC differential helps identify cause (neutrophilia → bacterial; lymphocytosis → viral, TB, lymphoma)
- **CSF analysis specifically:** cell count, protein, glucose (CSF glucose normally 60–70% of serum; low glucose → bacterial/fungal meningitis), Gram stain, culture

## 1. Cytology vs Cytopathology

**Cytology:** The branch of biology studying cell structure, function, and chemistry in both normal and pathological states.

**Cytopathology:** A subspecialty of pathology that diagnoses disease by examining cells from body fluids or tissue samples — looking for changes in cell morphology that indicate cancer, infection, or inflammation.

**Key distinction:** Cytology is the broader science; cytopathology is the clinical diagnostic application.

### Cytology Slide Preparation — Steps
1. **Sample collection** — scraping, brushing, aspiration, or fluid collection
2. **Fixation** — alcohol or methanol immediately applied to prevent degradation
3. **Smearing** — thin uniform layer spread on a glass slide
4. **Staining** — Pap stain (gynaecological/general), Wright's/Giemsa (haematology), H&E (general)
5. **Air drying and coverslipping**
6. **Microscopic examination** — low to high magnification
7. **Interpretation and reporting** — cytopathologist identifies abnormalities, issues a diagnostic report

### Advantages of Cytopathology
- Minimally invasive compared to surgical biopsy
- Cost-effective and relatively quick
- Used in screening programmes (e.g., cervical cancer via Pap smear)

### Limitations
- No tissue architecture — only individual cells are seen
- May miss disease if sample is non-representative
- False negatives possible in early or focal disease

---

## 2. Exfoliative Cytology (Topic VII)

**Definition:** Examination of cells that have been naturally shed from body surfaces or collected by scraping/washing from mucosal surfaces.

### Techniques and Applications

**Pap Smear (Papanicolaou Smear):**
- Purpose: Cervical cancer screening
- Procedure: Spatula or brush scrapes cells from the cervical transformation zone; spread on a slide and stained with Pap stain
- Detects: Cervical dysplasia (pre-cancer) and invasive cervical cancer
- Reporting system: Bethesda system — NILM (normal), ASCUS, LSIL, HSIL, carcinoma

**Sputum Cytology:**
- Purpose: Diagnose lung disease, mainly cancer
- Procedure: Patient expectorates sputum; cells examined for malignant changes
- Detects: Squamous cell carcinoma of lung (most amenable to sputum cytology)

**Urine Cytology:**
- Purpose: Urinary tract evaluation
- Procedure: Voided urine or catheter specimen processed, concentrated, and stained
- Detects: Transitional (urothelial) cell carcinoma of the bladder

**FNA (as an exfoliative technique):**
- Aspirates cells from a mass using a thin needle
- Used for thyroid, lymph nodes, breast, salivary glands

**Body Fluid Cytology:**
- Examines cells in pleural, peritoneal, pericardial, CSF, synovial fluids
- Detects: Malignant effusions, infections, inflammatory conditions

### Principles of Exfoliative Cytology
- Cells collected from where they naturally shed or are accessible
- Fixed, stained, then examined for changes in: cell size, shape, nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, nuclear hyperchromasia, abnormal mitoses, and arrangement

---

## 3. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) — Detailed

**Definition:** A laboratory technique using antigen-antibody binding to detect specific proteins (antigens) in tissue sections, allowing their localisation to be visualised under a microscope.

### Core Principle
- A **primary antibody** binds specifically to the target antigen in the tissue
- A **secondary antibody** (conjugated to an enzyme or fluorophore) binds to the primary antibody to amplify and visualise the signal
- **Detection:** Enzyme-based (HRP + DAB substrate → brown precipitate) or fluorescent (fluorophore emits light)
- **Counterstain:** Haematoxylin applied to show tissue architecture in blue/purple contrast

### Full IHC Process (Step by Step)

| Step | Detail |
|---|---|
| 1. Fixation | Formalin (10% NBF) — preserves morphology |
| 2. Embedding | Paraffin wax blocks |
| 3. Sectioning | Microtome, 3–5 µm sections on glass slides |
| 4. Deparaffinisation | Heated + xylene to remove wax; rehydrated through alcohol series |
| 5. Antigen retrieval | HIER (heat in buffer — microwave or water bath) or enzymatic retrieval — unmasks antigens masked by fixation |
| 6. Blocking | Serum applied to prevent non-specific antibody binding |
| 7. Primary antibody | Applied and incubated (1 hour to overnight) |
| 8. Washing | Buffer (PBS or TBS) to remove unbound antibody |
| 9. Secondary antibody | Conjugated antibody applied; shorter incubation |
| 10. Detection | DAB substrate → brown colour where antigen present |
| 11. Counterstaining | Haematoxylin → blue nuclei for background |
| 12. Dehydration & mounting | Alcohol series, xylene, coverslip applied |
| 13. Microscopy | Analysis and image capture |

### Types of IHC

**By detection method:**
- **Chromogenic** — enzyme-linked (HRP/AP + substrate); produces coloured precipitate; used in routine diagnostics
- **Fluorescent** — fluorophore-conjugated; allows multiplexing (multiple targets simultaneously)

**By antibody type:**
- **Monoclonal** — single clone, highly specific, one epitope (e.g., ER, HER2)
- **Polyclonal** — multiple clones, higher sensitivity, less specific

**By target:**
- **Tumour markers** — Ki-67 (proliferation), p53 (tumour suppressor), HER2 (breast cancer)
- **Cell lineage markers** — cytokeratins (epithelial), CD34 (haematopoietic stem cells), CD68 (macrophages), CD markers (lymphocytes)

**Special methods:**
- **Dual/multiplex IHC** — detects multiple antigens on same section
- **Tissue Microarray (TMA)** — many tissue cores on one slide; high-throughput analysis
- **ISH (In Situ Hybridisation)** — detects RNA/DNA targets in tissue; often combined with IHC

### Quality Control in IHC

| QC Area | Key Requirement |
|---|---|
| Antibody validation | Characterised, validated antibodies with correct specificity |
| Fixation consistency | Standardised formalin time (over-fixation blocks antigen retrieval) |
| Antigen retrieval | Standardised HIER protocol — same buffer, temperature, time |
| Controls | Positive and negative control slides on every run |
| Sectioning | Uniform 3–5 µm thickness; no folds/tears |
| Blocking | Effective blocking to eliminate background |
| Documentation | SOPs, lot numbers, incubation times all recorded |
| Staff | Trained personnel; periodic competency assessment |
| Equipment | Regular microtome and microscope calibration/maintenance |
| Interpretation | Blinded scoring where possible; consistent microscopy settings |

---

## 4. Special Techniques in Cytology (Topic X)

### Liquid-Based Cytology (LBC)
- Cells collected into a liquid preservative medium (e.g., ThinPrep, SurePath) instead of directly smeared
- Advantages: Better preservation, less obscuring debris, reduced cellular overlap, residual sample available for ancillary tests (HPV testing, ICC)
- Replaces conventional Pap smears in many modern cervical screening programmes

### Immunocytochemistry (ICC)
- Same principle as IHC but applied to cytology preparations (smears, LBC, cell blocks)
- Identifies specific antigens in individual cells
- Used to determine cell lineage (e.g., carcinoma vs lymphoma vs mesothelioma in effusions)

### Fluorescence In Situ Hybridisation (FISH)
- Uses fluorescent DNA probes that bind to complementary sequences on specific chromosomes
- Detects chromosomal abnormalities: deletions, amplifications, translocations
- Applications:
  - HER2 amplification in breast cancer
  - BCR-ABL translocation (Philadelphia chromosome) in CML
  - ALK rearrangement in lung adenocarcinoma
  - Urine FISH for bladder cancer detection
- **Dual-colour FISH** — two different probes simultaneously detect two targets; identifies specific rearrangements

### Comparative Genomic Hybridisation (CGH)
- Detects gains and losses of chromosomal DNA across the entire genome
- Used in cancer genetics and investigation of genetic disorders

### Karyotyping / Cytogenetic Analysis
- Examines number and structure of chromosomes
- Identifies aneuploidy, translocations, inversions
- Useful in haematological malignancies, genetic disorders, prenatal diagnosis

### Papanicolaou (Pap) Stain
- Multi-chromatic stain giving excellent nuclear detail
- Stains: nuclei dark blue/black (haematoxylin); cytoplasm shades of pink, green, orange depending on cell type and maturity
- Widely used in gynaecological cytology and body fluids

### Giemsa Stain
- Air-dried preparations; stains cytoplasm well
- Used in FNA, blood films, bone marrow smears
- Excellent for haematological cells and identifying microorganisms

### Rapid On-Site Evaluation (ROSE)
- Cytologist assesses FNA samples immediately during the procedure
- Confirms adequate cellularity before the patient leaves
- Reduces non-diagnostic rates and need for repeat procedures

### Electron Microscopy (EM)
- Ultra-high resolution imaging of cellular ultrastructure
- Visualises organelles at nm resolution — not achievable with light microscopy
- Applications in cytology:
  - Diagnosis of tumours with specific ultrastructural features (e.g., Weibel-Palade bodies in angiosarcoma, neurosecretory granules in neuroendocrine tumours)
  - Viral identification (virus morphology)
  - Ciliary defects (primary ciliary dyskinesia)
  - Renal biopsy interpretation (podocyte effacement in nephrotic syndrome)

### Flow Cytometry

**Principle:**
- Cells suspended in fluid stream pass single-file through a laser beam
- **Forward scatter (FSC)** — correlates with cell size
- **Side scatter (SSC)** — correlates with internal granularity/complexity
- Fluorescent-labelled antibodies bind surface/intracellular markers; lasers excite fluorophores → emitted light detected and analysed

**Key Applications:**
- **Immunophenotyping** — identify and classify cell populations (B vs T cells, mature vs immature) — essential for leukaemia/lymphoma diagnosis and classification
- **Cell counting** — rapid; used in haematology analysers
- **Cell cycle analysis** — determines proportion of cells in G0/G1, S, G2/M phases
- **Apoptosis detection** — Annexin V staining
- **CD4 counting** — monitors HIV disease progression and treatment
- **Stem cell identification** — CD34+ cells for transplant
- **Transplant monitoring** — immune cell populations post-transplant
- **Vaccine research** — measures immune response to vaccination

### Image Analysis Systems
- Automated algorithms analyse cytological slides
- Improve throughput and consistency; reduce inter-observer variability
- Used in cervical screening programmes (liquid-based cytology automation)

## 5. Vitamins — Deficiencies

### Water-Soluble Vitamins

| Vitamin | Deficiency Disease | Key Features |
|---|---|---|
| B1 (Thiamine) | Beriberi / Wernicke-Korsakoff | Wet beriberi: cardiac failure; Dry beriberi: peripheral neuropathy; Wernicke's: confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia |
| B2 (Riboflavin) | Ariboflavinosis | Angular stomatitis, cheilosis, glossitis |
| B3 (Niacin) | Pellagra | 3 Ds: Dermatitis, Diarrhoea, Dementia |
| B6 (Pyridoxine) | Peripheral neuropathy | Especially in INH (anti-TB drug) use |
| B9 (Folate) | Megaloblastic anaemia | Neural tube defects in pregnancy |
| B12 (Cobalamin) | Megaloblastic anaemia + subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord | Neurological damage; causes: pernicious anaemia, strict veganism |
| C (Ascorbic acid) | Scurvy | Perifollicular haemorrhages, gum disease, poor wound healing, corkscrew hairs |

### Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, K)

| Vitamin | Deficiency | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| A (Retinol) | Night blindness, xerophthalmia, Bitot's spots | Increased susceptibility to infections |
| D (Calciferol) | Rickets (children), Osteomalacia (adults) | Defective bone mineralisation; low Ca²⁺, low PO₄³⁻, raised ALP |
| E (Tocopherol) | Haemolytic anaemia, neuropathy | Rare; seen in fat malabsorption |
| K (Phylloquinone) | Bleeding tendency | Impaired clotting factor synthesis (II, VII, IX, X); prolonged PT |

### Etiology of Vitamin Deficiencies
- Inadequate dietary intake (poor diet, poverty, famine)
- Malabsorption (coeliac disease, Crohn's, chronic pancreatitis)
- Increased requirements (pregnancy, lactation, rapid growth)
- Chronic disease (liver, kidney, cancer)
- Alcoholism (especially B vitamins)
- Drug interactions (e.g., methotrexate → folate; INH → B6; anticonvulsants → D and K)

### Laboratory Evaluation
- Serum vitamin levels (B12, folate, vitamin D, vitamin A)
- CBC — macrocytic anaemia (B12/folate); normocytic or haemolytic (Vit E)
- Prothrombin time — prolonged in vitamin K deficiency
- Homocysteine and methylmalonic acid — elevated in B12 deficiency (functional tests)
- 24-hour urine — for B6 assessment
- Bone profile (Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻, ALP) — for vitamin D deficiency

## 6. Trace Elements

### Types and Disorders

| Element | Deficiency | Excess |
|---|---|---|
| **Iron** | Iron deficiency anaemia — fatigue, pallor, koilonychia, low ferritin, high TIBC | Haemochromatosis — liver disease, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, bronze skin; ferritin very high, transferrin saturation >60% |
| **Zinc** | Impaired wound healing, immune dysfunction, taste/smell loss, skin lesions, growth retardation | Interferes with copper absorption → copper deficiency |
| **Copper** | Anaemia, connective tissue abnormalities, neurological symptoms | Wilson's disease — liver + brain damage, Kayser-Fleischer rings, psychiatric symptoms; low caeruloplasmin |
| **Selenium** | Keshan disease (cardiomyopathy), impaired immunity | Selenosis — GI, neurological, respiratory symptoms |
| **Iodine** | Goitre, hypothyroidism, cretinism (congenital) | Hyperthyroidism, thyroiditis |
| **Manganese** | Bone and glucose metabolism defects | Neurological symptoms resembling Parkinson's disease |

### Lab Evaluation of Trace Element Disorders
- **Iron:** Serum iron, ferritin, TIBC, transferrin saturation
- **Copper:** Serum caeruloplasmin (low in Wilson's), 24-hour urinary copper (high in Wilson's), liver biopsy copper quantification
- **Zinc:** Serum zinc
- **Selenium:** Serum selenium
- **Genetic testing** — Wilson's disease (ATP7B mutation), haemochromatosis (HFE gene — C282Y)
- **Tissue biopsy** — copper or iron quantification in liver

## 7. Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM)

### Types

**Kwashiorkor:**
- Cause: Severe protein deficiency with near-adequate calorie intake
- Common in: regions of Africa and Asia with low-quality protein diets
- Pathophysiology: Hypoalbuminaemia → reduced oncotic pressure → oedema; fatty liver from impaired lipoprotein synthesis
- Clinical features: Bilateral pitting oedema (hallmark), distended abdomen, hepatomegaly, skin changes (flaky paint dermatosis — hypo and hyperpigmentation patches), thin brittle hair that may depigment, growth retardation
- Labs: Low serum albumin; electrolyte imbalances; low pre-albumin

**Marasmus:**
- Cause: Severe deficiency of both calories AND protein (total starvation)
- Common in: extreme poverty, famine, neglect, chronic illness
- Pathophysiology: Body catabolises fat and muscle for energy; metabolic adaptation to conserve vital organs
- Clinical features: Severe generalised wasting — "skin and bones" appearance; loss of subcutaneous fat; muscle wasting; old man facies (loss of buccal fat pad); no oedema; growth failure, weakness
- Labs: Serum albumin often normal (unlike kwashiorkor); other markers of starvation

**Marasmic Kwashiorkor:**
- Combined — wasting (marasmus features) plus oedema (kwashiorkor features)
- Worst prognosis of the three types

**Secondary PEM:**
- Results from chronic illness, infection, GI malabsorption rather than dietary inadequacy alone

### Management Principles
- Gradual nutritional rehabilitation (refeeding syndrome risk if too rapid — hypophosphataemia, cardiac failure)
- Correct underlying infection or disease
- Micronutrient supplementation (zinc, potassium, magnesium, vitamins)
- Monitor electrolytes closely during refeeding

# MBPA 3413 & MBPA 3412 — Exam Crash Course Notes
*General Pathology II & III | Point-form, comprehensive*
## Section One: Genetic Disorders (MBPA 3413)
*Mutations, Mendelian Disorders, Molecular Diagnosis, Chromosomal Disorders, Complex Multigenic Disorders*
### 1.1 Key Definitions
- **Genetics** — study of individual genes and heredity
- **Genomics** — study of the entire genome (all genes + interactions)
- **Genetic disorder** — disease caused by abnormality in an individual's DNA
- **DNA (Deoxyribonucleic acid)** — double-stranded molecule carrying genetic instructions
- **Exons** — coding sequences of DNA that are expressed into protein
- **Introns** — non-coding sequences within a gene; spliced out before translation
- **Intergenic regions** — DNA between genes; mostly non-coding
- **SNP (Single Nucleotide Polymorphism)** — variation at a single base pair; occurs ~every 1,000 bp; used as genetic markers
- **Epigenetics** — heritable changes in gene expression without altering DNA sequence
- **Proteomics** — large-scale study of all proteins expressed by a genome
- **Bioinformatics** — use of computational tools to analyse biological data (e.g., genome sequences)
- **Genotype** — the genetic makeup of an individual
- **Phenotype** — observable characteristics resulting from genotype + environment
- **Gene therapy** — treatment of disease by correcting/replacing defective genes
- **Hereditary** — passed from parent to child through the germline
- **Familial** — runs in families but not necessarily purely genetic
- **Congenital** — present at birth (may or may not be genetic)
- **Mutation** — permanent change in DNA sequence
- **DNA microarray analysis** — "gene chip" technology; interrogates thousands of genes simultaneously on a single platform
- **Recombinant DNA technology** — lab technique of joining DNA from different sources to produce new genetic combinations
### 1.2 Mutations
**Definition:** permanent change in the DNA; can be inherited (germline) or acquired (somatic)
**Categories of mutations**
- **Genome mutations** — loss/gain of whole chromosomes → monosomies / trisomies
- **Chromosome mutations** — visible structural rearrangements of chromosomes
- **Gene mutations** — partial/complete deletion of a gene or single base pair change
**Types of gene mutations**
- **Point mutations (substitutions)**
  - *Missense* — changes one amino acid to another (conservative or non-conservative, e.g. sickle cell anaemia)
  - *Nonsense* — changes an amino acid codon to a stop codon → truncated, non-functional protein
- **Frameshift mutations** — insertion/deletion of 1 or 2 base pairs → shifts the entire reading frame → abnormal protein
- **Deletions / insertions**
  - < 3 base pairs → frameshift
  - Multiples of 3 → missing amino acid(s) but frame intact → abnormal protein
- **Trinucleotide repeat mutations** — dynamic amplification of a 3-nucleotide sequence (e.g. Huntington's disease)
- **Promoter/enhancer mutations** — disrupt transcription factor binding → reduced or absent gene expression (e.g. some hereditary haemolytic anaemias)
**How mutations cause genetic disease** — through:
- Enzyme defects → failure of metabolic pathways
- Enzyme inhibitor defects
- Defective receptors → impaired cell signalling
- Defective transport systems
- Abnormal structural proteins (e.g. collagen disorders)
- Defects in haemostasis
- Defects in growth regulation
- Adverse drug reactions (pharmacogenomics)
### 1.3 Mendelian Disorders & Transmission Patterns
**Key facts**
- Every person carries 5–8 deleterious genes (mostly recessive)
- 80% of mutations are familial; the remainder are de novo
- **Pleiotropism** — one mutant gene produces many effects
- **Genetic heterogeneity** — mutations at different loci produce the same phenotype
**Autosomal Dominant (AD)**
- At least one parent usually affected (de novo possible in older fathers)
- Affects males and females equally
- Both sexes can transmit the disorder
- 50% risk per pregnancy
- Features: reduced penetrance, variable expressivity, often delayed onset
- Mechanisms: reduced gene product production, or production of an inactive/abnormal protein
**Autosomal Recessive (AR)**
- Largest category of Mendelian disorders
- Parents usually unaffected (carriers); siblings may be affected
- 25% recurrence risk per birth
- More uniform expression than AD; complete penetrance common
- Onset frequently early in life
- Includes nearly all inborn errors of metabolism
- Consanguinity increases risk
**X-Linked Disorders**
- Almost all X-linked disorders are recessive
- Affected males do not transmit to sons — daughters become carriers
- Carrier females may show mild features
- X-linked dominant is rare (e.g. vitamin D-resistant rickets)
### 1.4 Molecular Diagnosis of Mendelian & Complex Disorders
**Background**
- Field emerged in the latter 20th century via karyotyping and Southern blotting
- Four advances drove expansion: ① human genome sequencing ② PCR kits ③ microarrays ④ next-generation sequencing
- Mutations tested can be germline (in every cell, e.g. CFTR in cystic fibrosis) or somatic (tissue-specific, e.g. NMYC in neuroblastoma)
**Diagnosis of copy number abnormalities**
| Method | What it detects |
|---|---|
| G-banding karyotype | Whole chromosome changes; low resolution |
| FISH | Specific chromosomal regions > 100 kb; no dividing cells needed |
| Array-CGH | Genome-wide; detects amplifications/deletions down to 10 kb resolution |
| SNP microarray | > 1 million SNPs; highest resolution; detects copy number + zygosity |
**FISH (Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization)**
- Uses fluorescent probes that bind to specific chromosomal regions
- Can be used on: amniocentesis cells, chorionic villus biopsy, peripheral blood, archival tissue
- Detects: aneuploidy, microdeletions, complex translocations, gene amplification
- Limitation: requires prior knowledge of the region being tested
**Array-Based CGH (Comparative Genomic Hybridization)**
- Test DNA + reference DNA labelled with different fluorescent dyes (Cy3 & Cy5)
- Hybridised to an array of genomic segments on a glass slide
- Gains → increased signal; losses → decreased signal vs. reference
- No prior knowledge of the mutation needed
**PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)**
- Exponentially amplifies specific DNA sequences
- Requires knowledge of the normal gene sequence
- If RNA is the starting material → reverse transcribed to cDNA first (RT-PCR)
- Mutations then identified by sequencing or hybridisation
**Sanger Sequencing**
- Reads nucleotide order in DNA; compares to wild-type sequence to identify mutations
- Fluorescent dye-based; largely automated
- Also done via gene chips (microarrays with tiled oligonucleotides)
**Next-Generation (NextGen) Sequencing**
- "Massively parallel sequencing" — millions of fragments sequenced simultaneously
- Generates > 1 gigabase of data per day at low cost
- Allows whole genome sequencing in days
- Used for: somatic tumour mutation profiling, rare Mendelian disorder identification
- Works by: fluorescently labelled nucleotides incorporated into immobilised template strands → signal read → mapped to genome using bioinformatics
**Linkage Analysis & GWAS**
- Used when the causative gene is unknown or the disease is polygenic
- Uses marker loci (especially SNPs) in linkage with disease genes
- HapMap project — divided the genome into haplotype blocks; allows efficient SNP-based gene hunting
- GWAS (Genome-Wide Association Studies) — screens millions of SNPs to find disease-associated variants in large populations
**Indications for genetic testing**
*Prenatal:*
- Advanced maternal age > 34 years (↑ trisomy risk)
- Carrier of balanced translocation/inversion
- Previous child with chromosomal abnormality
- Partner is a carrier of an X-linked disorder
*Postnatal (on peripheral blood lymphocytes):*
- Multiple congenital anomalies
- Unexplained intellectual disability / developmental delay
- Features of Down syndrome, Prader-Willi, Turner syndrome, fragile X
- Infertility (rule out sex chromosome anomaly)
- Recurrent spontaneous abortions
### 1.5 Chromosomal Disorders
**Numerical abnormalities**
- Caused by nondisjunction during meiosis → gametes with n+1 or n−1 chromosomes
- **Trisomy** (2n+1) — e.g. Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
- **Monosomy** (2n−1) — autosomal monosomy incompatible with life; sex chromosome monosomy viable (e.g. Turner syndrome, 45,X)
- **Mosaicism** — two or more cell populations with different chromosomal complements in the same individual; results from postzygotic mitotic nondisjunction
**Structural abnormalities** (after chromosomal breakage)
- **Translocation** — transfer of a chromosomal segment to another chromosome
  - *Balanced reciprocal* — exchange with no net loss/gain
  - *Robertsonian* — between two acrocentric chromosomes; one large + one tiny (lost) chromosome formed; predisposes to unbalanced gametes
- **Isochromosome** — centromere divides horizontally → chromosome with two identical arms (e.g. i(Xq), most common in live births)
- **Deletion** — loss of a chromosomal segment; an isolated fragment without a centromere is usually lost
- **Inversion** — segment re-inserted in reverse orientation after two breaks
- **Ring chromosome** — segments lost from both ends; arms join to form a ring
Notation: p = short arm (petit); q = long arm — e.g. 2q34 = chromosome 2, long arm, region 3, band 4
**General rules of chromosomal disorders**
- Loss of material is more severe than gain
- Sex chromosome imbalance is better tolerated than autosomal imbalance
- Sex chromosome disorders are often subtle; infertility may be the first sign (detected at adolescence)
- Most are de novo (parents normal, low recurrence risk) — exception: translocation Down syndrome
### 1.6 Complex Multigenic (Multifactorial) Disorders
- Also called polygenic or multifactorial disorders
- Caused by interactions between variant genes and environmental factors
- A **polymorphism** = a genetic variant with ≥ 2 alleles occurring in ≥ 1% of the population
- **Common disease–common variant hypothesis** — many polymorphisms, each with modest effect and low penetrance, are co-inherited to produce disease
**Key points**
- Different polymorphisms vary in significance — e.g. in type 1 diabetes, 6–7 of 20–30 implicated genes are most important; a few HLA alleles contribute > 50% of risk
- Some polymorphisms are shared across similar diseases; others are disease-specific
- **Quantitative trait loci (QTLs)** — traits like height, skin colour, and intelligence follow multigenic inheritance with continuous variation
- Environment significantly modifies expression — e.g. obesity unmasks the type 2 diabetes genetic trait
- Diagnosis of multifactorial inheritance requires familial clustering + exclusion of Mendelian and chromosomal modes of transmission
- A variable severity range is suggestive — but variable expressivity of single-gene disorders must be excluded

## Section Two: Neoplasia & Oncology (MBPA 3412)
*Introduction to Neoplasia, Tumour Nomenclature, TNM Staging, Carcinogenic Agents, Viral Oncogenesis*
### 2.1 Key Definitions
- **Neoplasia** — formation of new, abnormal tissue growth
- **Neoplasm / Tumour** — abnormal mass of tissue; growth exceeds and is uncoordinated with normal tissue; persists after the initiating stimulus ceases
- **Mesenchymal tissue** — connective tissue origin (fat, muscle, bone, cartilage)
- **Epithelial tissue** — tissue lining surfaces and glands
- **Cancer** — common term for all malignant neoplasms
- **Benign** — localised, non-invasive tumour; does not metastasise
- **Malignant** — invasive tumour capable of metastasis; life-threatening
- **Clonal proliferation** — tumour arising from a single transformed precursor cell
- **Differentiation** — degree to which tumour cells resemble their normal cell of origin
- **Anaplasia** — lack of differentiation; a hallmark of malignancy
### 2.2 Tumour Nomenclature & Classification
**Benign tumours**
- Named by cell/tissue of origin + suffix "-oma"
- Mesenchymal origin → fibroma, chondroma, lipoma, leiomyoma
- Glandular epithelial → adenoma (solid mass) or cystadenoma (cyst-forming)
- Finger-like projections → papilloma
**Malignant tumours**
- Mesenchymal origin → sarcomas (e.g. liposarcoma, fibrosarcoma, osteosarcoma)
- Epithelial origin → carcinomas (e.g. squamous cell carcinoma)
- Glandular epithelial → adenocarcinoma
- Oddly named exceptions: melanoma, seminoma, mesothelioma (don't follow the standard rules)
### 2.3 TNM Staging System
Published by the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) — in use for over 70 years.
- **T** — Primary Tumour: size and local extent
- **N** — Regional lymph Nodes: involvement and extent
- **M** — Distant Metastases: present (1) or absent (0)
**Importance of TNM**
- Guides treatment planning
- Indicates prognosis
- Evaluates treatment outcomes
- Facilitates information exchange between treatment centres
- Supports cancer registries and national cancer control planning
- Internationally standardised "common language" for oncology professionals
### 2.4 Carcinogenic Agents
Core principle: genetic damage is the foundation of carcinogenesis. Three classes of agents cause this.
**Chemical carcinogens**
*Direct-acting agents* — require no metabolic conversion to be carcinogenic
- Generally weak carcinogens
- Examples: alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil), acylating agents
- Note: anticancer drugs (e.g. in Hodgkin lymphoma treatment) can themselves cause secondary leukaemia
*Indirect-acting agents (procarcinogens)* — require metabolic activation
- Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (e.g. benzo[a]pyrene in cigarette smoke, charbroiled meat)
- Aromatic amines & azo dyes (e.g. β-naphthylamine → 50× increased bladder cancer in dye workers)
- Natural products: aflatoxin B1 (Aspergillus mould → hepatocellular carcinoma in Africa/Asia)
- Others: vinyl chloride, arsenic, nickel, chromium, nitrosamines
*Mechanism of chemical carcinogenesis*
- Most are mutagens → form covalent adducts with DNA
- Common targets: RAS oncogene, TP53 tumour suppressor
- Aflatoxin B1 produces a "signature mutation" in TP53
- **Initiation** → mutation of an oncogene (e.g. RAS activation)
- **Promotion** → subsequent exposure to promoters (e.g. phorbol esters, hormones) → clonal expansion of initiated cells → accumulation of further mutations → malignancy
- Cytochrome P-450 enzyme polymorphisms affect individual susceptibility to chemical carcinogens
**Radiation carcinogenesis**
- UV rays, X-rays, and nuclear radiation are all established carcinogens
- Ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma) → chromosome breaks, translocations, point mutations; double-stranded DNA breaks are the most important
- Hiroshima/Nagasaki survivors → markedly increased leukaemia (especially myelogenous) after ~7-year latency; also thyroid, breast, colon, and lung cancers
- UV radiation → forms pyrimidine dimers in DNA, normally repaired by nucleotide excision repair
- Excessive UV → overwhelms repair → skin cancers (melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma)
- Xeroderma pigmentosum — inherited defect in nucleotide excision repair → greatly increased skin cancer risk
**Viral & microbial oncogenesis**
*Oncogenic RNA virus*
- **HTLV-1** (Human T-cell Lymphotropic Virus-1) → T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma
  - Endemic in Japan and the Caribbean; transmitted sexually, via blood products, or breastfeeding
  - Only 3–5% of infected persons develop leukaemia; 20–50 year latency
  - Mechanism: viral TAX protein transactivates cytokine genes (IL-2, IL-15) → autocrine T-cell proliferation; TAX also inactivates tumour suppressors (CDKN2A/p16, TP53)
  - TAX is necessary and sufficient for cellular transformation
*Oncogenic DNA viruses*
- **HPV** (Human Papillomavirus)
  - Low-risk types (6, 11) → genital warts; low malignant potential
  - High-risk types (16, 18) → cervical carcinoma, anogenital cancers
- **EBV** (Epstein-Barr Virus) → Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, some B-cell lymphomas
- **HBV & HCV** → hepatocellular carcinoma
- **HHV-8 / KSHV** → Kaposi sarcoma
- **H. pylori** (bacterium) → gastric carcinoma, MALT lymphoma
### 2.5 Cancer Burden (Statistics to Know)
- Global, 2000: 10 million new cases; 6 million deaths
- Global, 2020: 18.1 million new cases; 10 million deaths (1 in every 6 deaths globally)
- Kenya, 2018: ~47,887 new cases; ~32,987 deaths → 3rd leading cause of death

## Section Three: Specific Genetic Disorders, Cancer Biology & Advanced Oncology
*Specific Mendelian Disorders, Hallmarks of Cancer, Oncogenes & Tumour Suppressors, Metastasis, Host Response, Paraneoplastic Syndromes, Gene Therapy, Mitochondrial & Non-Mendelian Disorders*
### 3.1 Specific Mendelian Disorders — Autosomal Recessive
**Cystic Fibrosis (CF)**
- Most common lethal AR disorder in white populations
- Gene: CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) on chromosome 7
- Most common mutation: ΔF508 (deletion of phenylalanine at position 508)
- CFTR normally functions as a chloride channel regulated by cAMP
- Defective CFTR → abnormal chloride transport → thick, viscid secretions in lungs, pancreas, liver, gut, reproductive tract
- Features:
  - Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease → recurrent infections (Pseudomonas, Staph aureus)
  - Pancreatic insufficiency → malabsorption, steatorrhoea
  - Meconium ileus in neonates
  - Infertility in males (absent vas deferens)
  - Elevated sweat chloride → diagnostic (sweat chloride > 60 mEq/L)
**Phenylketonuria (PKU)**
- Deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase → cannot convert phenylalanine to tyrosine
- Accumulation of phenylalanine is toxic to the developing brain
- Features:
  - Intellectual disability (if untreated)
  - Seizures, tremors, behavioural disturbances
  - Fair skin and hair (reduced melanin — tyrosine is needed for melanin synthesis)
  - Musty/mousy body odour
- Screened at birth (Guthrie test); treated with a low-phenylalanine diet
**Sickle Cell Anaemia (SCA)**
- Point mutation (non-conservative missense): glutamic acid → valine at position 6 of the β-globin chain
- Results in haemoglobin S (HbS)
- Under low oxygen → HbS polymerises → sickling of RBCs
- Features:
  - Chronic haemolytic anaemia
  - Vaso-occlusive crises → pain, organ infarction
  - Splenic sequestration → functional asplenia → increased infection risk (encapsulated organisms)
  - Stroke, acute chest syndrome, avascular necrosis
  - Heterozygotes (HbAS) — sickle cell trait; relatively protected against malaria
**Tay-Sachs Disease**
- Deficiency of hexosaminidase A → accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neurons
- Progressive neuronal destruction
- Features: motor weakness, blindness, cherry-red spot on the macula, seizures → death by age 2–3
- Common in Ashkenazi Jewish populations
### 3.2 Specific Mendelian Disorders — Autosomal Dominant
**Huntington's Disease**
- Trinucleotide repeat mutation — CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4
- Normal: < 36 repeats; disease: > 36 repeats
- **Anticipation** — disease worsens / earlier onset in successive generations
- Features:
  - Progressive involuntary choreiform movements
  - Dementia
  - Psychiatric disturbances (depression, personality change)
  - Onset typically 35–45 years
  - No cure; uniformly fatal
**Marfan Syndrome**
- Mutation in the FBN1 gene → defective fibrillin-1 (structural glycoprotein in elastic tissue)
- Features:
  - Tall stature, long limbs, arachnodactyly (spider fingers)
  - Lens dislocation (ectopia lentis) — upward
  - Aortic aneurysm / dissection — most common cause of death
  - Mitral valve prolapse
  - High arched palate
**Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1)**
- Mutation in the NF1 gene → loss of neurofibromin (tumour suppressor / RAS-GAP)
- Features:
  - Multiple neurofibromas (benign peripheral nerve sheath tumours)
  - Café-au-lait spots (≥ 6, > 1.5 cm diameter)
  - Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas)
  - Increased risk of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours
### 3.3 Chromosomal Disorders — Specific Conditions
**Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21)**
- Most common chromosomal disorder compatible with life
- 95% → nondisjunction (extra free chromosome 21); 4% → Robertsonian translocation; 1% → mosaic
- Maternal age is strongly associated with the nondisjunction form
- Features:
  - Intellectual disability (variable severity)
  - Flat facial profile, epicanthic folds, upward slanting palpebral fissures
  - Single palmar crease (simian crease)
  - Congenital heart disease (especially ASD, VSD) — most common cause of death
  - Duodenal atresia
  - Increased risk of ALL and AML
  - Early-onset Alzheimer's disease (chromosome 21 carries the APP gene)
**Turner Syndrome (45,X)**
- Most common sex chromosome disorder in females
- 57% → complete monosomy X; the rest → mosaics or structural X abnormalities
- Features:
  - Short stature
  - Primary amenorrhoea / ovarian failure (streak gonads)
  - Webbed neck, low posterior hairline
  - Broad shield chest, widely spaced nipples
  - Bicuspid aortic valve / coarctation of the aorta
  - Normal intelligence (usually)
**Klinefelter Syndrome (47,XXY)**
- Most common cause of male hypogonadism
- Extra X chromosome in males
- Features:
  - Tall stature with long legs
  - Small, firm testes → infertility (azoospermia)
  - Gynaecomastia
  - Reduced body/facial hair
  - Mild intellectual impairment possible
### 3.4 Hallmarks of Cancer
Fundamental biological capabilities acquired during tumour development:
- Self-sufficiency in growth signals → oncogene activation (e.g. RAS, MYC)
- Insensitivity to growth-inhibitory signals → tumour suppressor loss (e.g. RB, TP53)
- Evasion of apoptosis → BCL-2 overexpression; TP53 loss
- Limitless replicative potential → telomerase reactivation
- Sustained angiogenesis → VEGF upregulation → new vessel formation feeding the tumour
- Invasion and metastasis → loss of E-cadherin; matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) activation
- Reprogramming of energy metabolism → Warburg effect (aerobic glycolysis)
- Evading immune destruction → downregulation of MHC class I; PD-L1 expression
### 3.5 Oncogenes & Tumour Suppressor Genes
**Oncogenes**
- Mutated/overactivated versions of normal proto-oncogenes
- Act in a dominant fashion — one mutant allele is sufficient
- Drive uncontrolled cell proliferation
| Oncogene | Function | Associated cancer |
|---|---|---|
| RAS | GTPase signal transduction | Lung, colon, pancreas |
| MYC | Transcription factor | Burkitt lymphoma, many others |
| HER2/NEU | Growth factor receptor | Breast, ovarian cancer |
| BCL-2 | Anti-apoptotic protein | Follicular lymphoma |
| NMYC | Transcription factor | Neuroblastoma |
**Tumour suppressor genes**
- Normal function: inhibit cell proliferation, promote apoptosis
- Act in a recessive fashion — both alleles must be lost (Knudson's two-hit hypothesis)
| Gene | Function | Associated cancer |
|---|---|---|
| TP53 | "Guardian of the genome" — apoptosis, DNA repair | Most human cancers |
| RB | Cell cycle checkpoint (G1/S) | Retinoblastoma, osteosarcoma |
| APC | Wnt signalling inhibitor | Colorectal cancer |
| BRCA1/2 | DNA repair | Breast, ovarian cancer |
| CDKN2A/p16 | CDK inhibitor → cell cycle arrest | Melanoma, many cancers |
**DNA repair genes**
- When mutated → accumulation of mutations genome-wide → "mutator phenotype"
- Examples: MLH1, MSH2 → microsatellite instability → hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC/Lynch syndrome)
### 3.6 Tumour Invasion & Metastasis
Metastasis = spread of a tumour to a site discontinuous with the primary tumour; the defining feature of malignancy.
**Steps of metastasis (the metastatic cascade)**
1. **Local invasion** — tumour cells detach from the primary mass; degrade the basement membrane using MMPs; invade surrounding stroma
2. **Intravasation** — entry into blood vessels or lymphatics
3. **Survival in circulation** — tumour cells evade immune attack; often travel as clumps with platelets
4. **Arrest at a distant site** — tumour cells adhere to endothelium at distant capillary beds
5. **Extravasation** — exit the vessel into distant tissue
6. **Colonisation** — proliferate and establish a metastatic deposit; requires a suitable microenvironment ("seed and soil" hypothesis — Paget)
**Molecular changes enabling invasion**
- Loss of E-cadherin → loss of cell-cell adhesion → cells detach
- Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) → tumour cells acquire migratory, invasive properties
- Upregulation of MMPs (matrix metalloproteinases) → ECM degradation
- Altered integrins → changed adhesion to ECM components
**Common metastatic patterns**
- Carcinomas → lymphatics first, then blood
- Sarcomas → blood first
- Colorectal → liver (portal drainage)
- Lung, breast → bone, brain, liver, adrenals
- Prostate → bone (osteoblastic)
### 3.7 Host Response to Tumours & Paraneoplastic Syndromes
**Immune response to tumours**
- Tumours express tumour-associated antigens (TAAs) → recognised by the immune system
- CD8+ cytotoxic T cells — primary anti-tumour effectors
- NK cells — kill tumour cells with low/absent MHC class I expression
- Tumours evade immunity by: downregulating MHC I, secreting immunosuppressive cytokines (TGF-β, IL-10), expressing PD-L1 (checkpoint inhibition)
**Paraneoplastic syndromes**
- Symptoms not caused by the direct tumour mass or metastasis
- Caused by tumour secretion of hormones/cytokines, or immune cross-reactivity
- Important to recognise — may be the first sign of cancer
| Syndrome | Mechanism | Associated cancer |
|---|---|---|
| Hypercalcaemia | PTHrP secretion | Squamous cell lung, renal, breast |
| SIADH | Ectopic ADH | Small cell lung cancer |
| Cushing's syndrome | Ectopic ACTH | Small cell lung cancer |
| Polycythaemia | Ectopic EPO | Renal cell carcinoma, hepatoma |
| Trousseau's sign | Hypercoagulability | Pancreatic, lung cancer |
| Acanthosis nigricans | TGF-α secretion | Gastric, lung cancer |
| Eaton-Lambert syndrome | Anti-VGCC antibodies | Small cell lung cancer |
### 3.8 Gene Therapy
**Definition:** treatment of disease by introducing, altering, or replacing genetic material within a person's cells.
**Approaches**
- Gene replacement — introduce a functional copy of a defective gene
- Gene silencing — use RNA interference (RNAi) to suppress an overactive/mutant gene
- Gene editing — CRISPR-Cas9 to precisely correct mutations at the DNA level
**Vectors used for gene delivery**
- Viral vectors (retroviruses, adenoviruses, AAV — adeno-associated virus) — most efficient
- Non-viral vectors (liposomes, naked DNA) — safer but less efficient
**Germline vs. somatic gene therapy**
- Somatic — changes only the treated individual; not heritable → ethically accepted
- Germline — changes passed to offspring → highly controversial; not currently permitted
**Clinical applications**
- SCID (Severe Combined Immunodeficiency) — ADA deficiency → one of the first successes
- Cystic fibrosis — trials ongoing
- Haemophilia A & B — promising results with AAV vectors
- Cancer — CAR-T cell therapy (chimeric antigen receptor T cells)
### 3.9 Mitochondrial Disorders
- Mitochondria have their own DNA (mtDNA) — circular, 16,569 base pairs; encodes 37 genes
- Maternal inheritance — mitochondria come exclusively from the oocyte (egg); fathers do not transmit
- **Heteroplasmy** — coexistence of normal and mutant mtDNA in the same cell; the degree determines severity
- All cells rely on mitochondria → mutations affect high-energy-demand tissues most: brain, muscle, heart, retina
**Features of mitochondrial diseases**
- Maternal inheritance pattern
- Variable severity within a family (heteroplasmy)
- Organs affected: CNS, skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, eye
- Lactic acidosis (failure of oxidative phosphorylation → anaerobic metabolism)
**Examples**
- MELAS — Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, Stroke-like episodes
- MERRF — Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged-Red Fibres
- Leber's Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON) → sudden blindness in young adults
### 3.10 Non-Mendelian Inheritance Patterns
**Genomic imprinting**
- Certain genes are expressed from only one parental allele (the other is silenced epigenetically)
- The same deletion causes a different disease depending on which parent it came from
- **Prader-Willi syndrome** — deletion of chromosome 15q11-q13 from the father → hypotonia, obesity, intellectual disability, hypogonadism
- **Angelman syndrome** — deletion of the same region from the mother → severe intellectual disability, seizures, happy affect, absent speech
**Uniparental disomy (UPD)**
- Both copies of a chromosome (or region) inherited from the same parent
- Can cause imprinting disorders without a visible deletion
**Trinucleotide repeat disorders**
- Unstable DNA sequences that expand across generations
- Anticipation — earlier onset and greater severity in successive generations
- Examples: Huntington's (CAG), Fragile X (CGG), Myotonic Dystrophy (CTG), Friedreich's Ataxia (GAA)
**Fragile X Syndrome**
- Most common inherited cause of intellectual disability
- X-linked; CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene
- Normal: < 55 repeats; premutation: 55–200; full mutation: > 200 repeats
- Full mutation → methylation and silencing of FMR1 → loss of FMRP protein
- Features: intellectual disability, macroorchidism (large testes), large ears, prominent jaw, autism-like behaviour

## SECTION 1: SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (10 Marks Each)

Question 1
Explain the role and significance of chemical mediators in the initiation and regulation of the acute inflammatory response. Illustrate your answer with two specific examples.

Model Answer:

Acute inflammation is orchestrated by a cascade of chemical mediators released from plasma and cells (mast cells, platelets, neutrophils, macrophages, endothelium) at the site of injury. They act on vessels and leukocytes to produce the cardinal signs of inflammation — redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function.

Vascular mediators:
- Histamine (from mast cell granules) — released within seconds of injury. Causes arteriolar vasodilation and increased venular permeability (endothelial gap formation), producing redness and oedema. The *immediate* mediator.
- Bradykinin (kinin system) — increases vascular permeability, causes pain, and contributes to vasodilation.

Chemotactic mediators (directing cell traffic):
- C5a (complement) and IL-8/CXCL8 (chemokine) — establish a concentration gradient that recruits neutrophils first (within hours), guiding them from the vessel lumen to the site of injury (chemotaxis).

Arachidonic acid metabolites:
- Prostaglandins (e.g. PGE2) — vasodilation, potentiate pain, fever.
- Leukotrienes (e.g. LTB4) — potent neutrophil chemoattractant, increases vascular permeability; LTC4/D4/E4 cause vasoconstriction and bronchospasm.

Cellular sequence: Neutrophils are the first cells recruited in acute inflammation (peak 6–24h), clearing bacteria and debris via phagocytosis. Macrophages follow later (24–48h+), clearing remaining debris and apoptotic neutrophils, and — together with cytokines like IL-1 and TNF-α — bridging into the repair phase by stimulating fibroblast proliferation and angiogenesis (via growth factors such as VEGF).

Two specific examples illustrated: Histamine (immediate vascular response) and C5a (chemotactic recruitment of neutrophils) — together demonstrating how mediators couple the vascular and cellular arms of acute inflammation.

---

Question 2
Describe the sequence of pathological changes that occur in pulmonary embolism starting from thrombus formation to the development of shock.

Model Answer:

1. Thrombus formation: A deep vein thrombosis (DVT) forms most commonly in the deep veins of the lower limb (femoral, popliteal, or iliac veins), favoured by Virchow's triad — stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial injury.
2. Embolization: Part or all of the thrombus dislodges (becomes an embolus) and travels via the inferior vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery.
3. Lodgement: The embolus lodges in a pulmonary artery or its branches, mechanically obstructing blood flow. (Note: a paradoxical embolism reaching systemic circulation would require a septal defect — not the typical pathway.)
4. Haemodynamic consequence: Obstruction → increased pulmonary vascular resistance → impaired gas exchange and hypoperfusion of lung parenchyma distal to the clot → hypoxaemia.
5. Right heart strain: The right ventricle must pump against a sudden rise in afterload → acute right ventricular strain ("acute cor pulmonale") → reduced right ventricular output.
6. Shock: Reduced right ventricular output → reduced left ventricular filling → decreased cardiac output → obstructive shock, with hypotension, tachycardia, and tissue hypoperfusion. If massive, this can be rapidly fatal.

## SECTION 2: LONG ESSAY QUESTION (20 Marks)

Question 1
A 4-year-old child from a resource-limited setting presents with delayed wound healing, recurrent infections, and poor growth. Discuss the pathological mechanisms by which nutritional deficiencies impair tissue repair and immune function. Include the role of protein, vitamin C, and micronutrients in the healing process and explain the environmental factors that perpetuate malnutrition.

Model Answer:

Protein deficiency:
Protein is essential for fibroblast proliferation, collagen synthesis, and production of acute-phase proteins, enzymes, and clotting factors (e.g. thrombin) needed for tissue repair. Hypoalbuminaemia reduces oncotic pressure (contributing to oedema) and impairs transport of iron and other nutrients to healing tissue. Protein is also required to build antibodies and immune cell components, so deficiency directly impairs both repair and immunity — explaining recurrent infections.

Vitamin C:
Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, enzymes required to hydroxylate proline and lysine residues during collagen synthesis. Without this, collagen is structurally weak and cannot cross-link properly, leading to fragile, slow-healing wounds. Severe deficiency causes scurvy — manifesting as poor wound healing, bleeding gums, and easy bruising (not night blindness, which is a Vitamin A deficiency sign). Vitamin C also supports neutrophil function and acts as an antioxidant, indirectly supporting immunity.

Micronutrients:
- Zinc — essential cofactor for DNA/RNA polymerases and matrix metalloproteinases involved in wound remodelling; also required for T-lymphocyte development in the thymus (Th and Tc maturation) and for normal immune regulation. Zinc deficiency is strongly linked to impaired wound healing and increased infection susceptibility.
- Iron — needed for collagen hydroxylation (alongside Vitamin C) and oxygen delivery to healing tissue via haemoglobin; deficiency causes tissue hypoxia, slowing repair.
- Vitamin A — supports epithelial differentiation and immune cell function; deficiency impairs epithelialization of wounds and increases infection risk.

Linking to immune function: B cells mature in bone marrow, T cells mature in the thymus — both processes depend on adequate protein and zinc. Deficiency in either impairs adaptive immunity, explaining the child's recurrent infections.

Environmental factors perpetuating malnutrition:
- Food insecurity and poverty — limited access to protein- and micronutrient-rich foods.
- Recurrent infections — create a vicious "malnutrition–infection cycle": infection increases metabolic demand and reduces appetite/absorption, worsening malnutrition, which further weakens immunity.
- Poor sanitation and water access — increase diarrhoeal disease burden, causing nutrient malabsorption and loss.
- Limited healthcare access — delays treatment of infections and correction of deficiencies.
- Maternal and early childhood factors — inadequate breastfeeding/weaning practices and low maternal nutritional status compound the problem in early life.

Together, these mechanisms explain the clinical triad: protein and micronutrient deficiency impair both the structural (collagen, ECM) and cellular (neutrophil, lymphocyte) machinery of healing and defence, while environmental deprivation sustains the deficient state.

---

**Acute Inflammation — Mediator Quick Recall**
| Phase | Mediator | Source | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Immediate (secs) | Histamine | Mast cells | Vasodilation + ↑permeability |
| Early | Bradykinin | Kinin system | Pain + ↑permeability |
| Chemotaxis | C5a | Complement | Neutrophil recruitment |
| Chemotaxis | IL-8 | Macrophages/endothelium | Neutrophil recruitment |
| Pain/fever | PGE2 | Arachidonic acid (COX) | Vasodilation, pain, fever |
| Chemotaxis/permeability | LTB4 | Arachidonic acid (LOX) | Neutrophil chemoattractant |
| Repair bridge | IL-1, TNF-α | Macrophages | Fibroblast + angiogenesis signal |
**Cell sequence:** Neutrophils (0–24h, first responders) → Macrophages (24–48h+, clear debris, signal repair)
---
**Nutrient Deficiency → Wound Healing/Immunity**
| Nutrient | Mechanism | Deficiency Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Protein | Fibroblast proliferation, collagen, antibodies, clotting factors | Weak repair, poor immunity, oedema |
| Vitamin C | Cofactor: prolyl/lysyl hydroxylase (collagen cross-linking) | Scurvy — fragile wounds, bleeding gums |
| Zinc | MMPs, DNA/RNA polymerase, T-cell maturation in thymus | Poor healing, ↓T-cell immunity |
| Iron | Collagen hydroxylation + O2 delivery (Hb) | Tissue hypoxia, slow healing |
| Vitamin A | Epithelial differentiation | Poor epithelialization, ↑infection |
**Memory hook:** Vitamin **A** = night blindness + epithelium. Vitamin **C** = scurvy + collagen. Don't mix these up — that was your essay's slip.
**Malnutrition-perpetuating cycle:** Poverty → poor diet → infection (↑demand, ↓absorption) → worse malnutrition → repeat. Add: poor sanitation, limited healthcare access.

# SECTION 1: SKIN PATHOLOGY (DERMATOPATHOLOGY)
**Intro:** This section covers the major disease categories of the skin — infections, chronic inflammatory dermatoses, blistering disorders, disorders of epidermal appendages, and disorders of pigmentation/melanocytes (including melanoma). Focus areas for exams: pathogenesis mechanisms, key morphological buzzwords, and distinguishing features between similar-looking conditions (e.g., pemphigus vs. pemphigoid).
---
## 1. INFECTIOUS DERMATOSES
### A. Bacterial Infections (Impetigo)
- Range: superficial (impetigo) → deep dermal abscesses (e.g., Pseudomonas, puncture wounds)
- **Organism:** *S. aureus* (most common) or *S. pyogenes*
- **Morphology:** neutrophils beneath stratum corneum → **subcorneal pustule**; Gram stain shows cocci
- **Clinical:** mainly children; starts as small macule (face/extremities) → **honey-colored crust**
- Bullous variant of childhood impetigo can mimic autoimmune blistering disease
### B. Fungal Infections
- Spectrum: superficial (Tinea, Candida) → deep/systemic (Aspergillus in immunosuppressed)
- **Morphology:** superficial → neutrophilic epidermal infiltrate; Candida → psoriasiform hyperplasia; deep → granulomatous response; Aspergillus = angioinvasive
- **Stains:** PAS and Gomori methenamine silver (GMS)
- **Clinical:** superficial = pruritic erythematous scaly macules (can mimic psoriasis — always exclude fungal cause before diagnosing new psoriasis)
### C. Viral – Verrucae (Warts)
- Caused by **HPV**; self-limited (resolve in 6 mo–2 yrs)
- Low-risk HPV → warts (no transforming potential); high-risk HPV → anogenital cancers (via E6/E7 oncoproteins)
- **Types:** Verruca vulgaris (hands, most common), Verruca plana (flat, face), Verruca plantaris/palmaris (soles/palms), Condyloma acuminatum (genital)
- **Morphology:** verrucous epidermal hyperplasia + **koilocytosis** (perinuclear vacuolization/halo)
---
## 2. CHRONIC INFLAMMATORY DERMATOSES
### A. Psoriasis
- Affects 1–2%; linked to ↑ CV risk, arthritis (10%)
- **Pathogenesis:** multifactorial immune disease — CD4+ TH17/TH1 and CD8+ T cells → keratinocyte hyperproliferation; **Koebner phenomenon** (trauma-induced lesions); HLA association
- **Morphology:** well-demarcated salmon plaque with silvery scale; **acanthosis** with "test-tube in rack" rete ridges; loss of stratum granulosum; **parakeratosis**; thin suprapapillary plates with dilated vessels → **Auspitz sign** (pinpoint bleeding); neutrophil microabscesses (Munro)
- **Clinical:** elbows, knees, scalp, lumbosacral, glans penis; nail pitting (30%)
- **Treatment:** NSAIDs, cyclosporine, TNF antagonists
### B. Lichen Planus
- Mnemonic: **"Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar Papules and Plaques"**
- **Pathogenesis:** CD8+ T cell cytotoxic response vs. basal layer antigens (post-viral/drug)
- **Morphology:** **Wickham striae** (white lines on papules); interface dermatitis; **sawtooth** rete ridges; **Civatte/colloid bodies** (necrotic basal cells); squamatization
- **Clinical:** middle-aged adults; wrists, elbows, glans penis; 70% oral mucosa (reticulate white pattern); skin lesions resolve in 1–2 yrs, oral lesions persist
### C. Lichen Simplex Chronicus
- Response to chronic rubbing/scratching; nodular form = **prurigo nodularis**
- **Morphology:** acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, dermal fibrosis (resembles thickened volar skin)
- **Clinical:** can mask underlying pruritic dermatosis — rule out cause
---
## 3. BLISTERING (BULLOUS) DISORDERS
### A. Inflammatory — Pemphigus Group
- **Common mechanism:** IgG autoantibodies vs. **desmogleins** → **acantholysis** (loss of cell-cell adhesion)
| Type | Level of blister | Key feature |
|---|---|---|
| Pemphigus vulgaris (>80%) | Suprabasal | "Row of tombstones"; oral ulcers first |
| Pemphigus vegetans | Suprabasal | Verrucous plaques, no true blisters |
| Pemphigus foliaceus | Subcorneal (superficial) | Fogo selvagem (Brazil); mucosa spared |
| Pemphigus erythematosus | Superficial | Localized, malar/lupus-like |
| Paraneoplastic pemphigus | — | Associated with NHL |
- IF: net-like intercellular IgG deposits
### B. Bullous Pemphigoid
- Elderly patients; thighs, forearms, axillae, groin
- **Pathogenesis:** autoantibodies vs. **BPAG2** (hemidesmosome component) → complement activation → eosinophil/neutrophil recruitment
- **Morphology:** **tense bullae** (don't rupture easily, unlike pemphigus); **subepidermal, nonacantholytic** blister; eosinophils beneath basal layer
### C. Dermatitis Herpetiformis
- Associated with **celiac disease**; males, 3rd–4th decade; intensely pruritic
- **Pathogenesis:** IgA anti-gliadin cross-reacts with reticulin → subepidermal blister
- **Morphology:** **microabscesses at dermal papillary tips** (fibrin + neutrophils); IF = **granular IgA** at papillary tips
- Responds to gluten-free diet
### D. Noninflammatory Blistering Disorders
- **Epidermolysis Bullosa** (defects in structural proteins; blisters at trauma sites from birth):
  - Simplex — keratin 5/14 mutation (AD, most common)
  - Junctional — laminin or BPAG2 mutation (AR), lamina lucida split
  - Dystrophic — COL7A1 mutation, beneath lamina densa
  - Mixed — multiple levels
- **Porphyria:** disturbed porphyrin metabolism; 5 types (congenital erythropoietic, erythrohepatic protoporphyria, acute intermittent, porphyria cutanea tarda, mixed); photosensitive subepidermal vesicles with vessel wall thickening
---
## 4. DISORDERS OF EPIDERMAL APPENDAGES
### A. Acne Vulgaris
- Universal in teens; worse in males; exacerbated by androgens, drugs, occlusive cosmetics
- **4 pathogenic factors:** (1) follicular keratin plug, (2) sebaceous hypertrophy (androgen-driven), (3) *Propionibacterium acnes* colonization → proinflammatory fatty acids, (4) secondary inflammation
- **Morphology:** open comedones (black, oxidized melanin) vs. closed comedones (trapped plug); severe form = acne conglobata (scarring)
- **Treatment:** antibiotics (anti-*P. acnes*), isotretinoin (antisebaceous)
### B. Rosacea
- Middle-aged females
- **4 stages:** flushing → persistent erythema/telangiectasia → papules/pustules → **rhinophyma**
- **Pathogenesis:** abnormal cathelicidin processing (via kallikrein 5, TLR2 activation)
- **Morphology:** perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate, telangiectasia; rhinophyma = sebaceous hypertrophy + keratotic plugging
---
## 5. DISORDERS OF PIGMENTATION & MELANOCYTES
### A. Freckle (Ephelis)
- Childhood; ↑ melanin in basal keratinocytes (not ↑ melanocyte number); darkens with sun, fades in winter
### B. Lentigo
- Benign melanocyte hyperplasia (linear, non-nested) just above basement membrane; does **not** darken with sun (unlike freckle)
### C. Melanocytic Nevus (Mole)
- Acquired **RAS/BRAF** activating mutations → limited by **oncogene-induced senescence** (p16/INK4a)
- **Progression:** Junctional nevus (DEJ) → Compound nevus (epidermis + dermis) → Intradermal nevus (dermis only)
- Deep cells show **neurotization** (loss of pigment, neural-like morphology) — helps distinguish from melanoma
### D. Dysplastic Nevi
- Precursor/marker of melanoma risk; **dysplastic nevus syndrome** (AD, germline **CDKN2A**/p16 or CDK4 mutation) → >50% lifetime melanoma risk
- **Morphology:** >5mm, pebbly/target lesions; **lentiginous hyperplasia**, architectural + cytologic atypia, melanin incontinence, lamellar fibrosis around rete ridges
### E. Melanoma
- Most lethal skin cancer; UV-induced (~85–90% sporadic), 10–15% familial (CDKN2A, telomerase genes)
- **Growth phases:**
  - **Radial** — horizontal spread, no metastatic potential (subtypes: lentigo maligna, superficial spreading [most common], acral/mucosal lentiginous [UV-independent])
  - **Vertical** — downward invasion, metastatic potential, heralded by a nodule
- **Morphology:** irregular borders, color variation, large nuclei with peripheral clumped chromatin, prominent nucleoli; no neurotization (unlike nevi)
- **Clinical — ABCDEs:** **A**symmetry, **B**order irregularity, **C**olor variegation, **D**iameter increase, **E**volution/change
---
## 6. PANNICULITIS
- Inflammation of subcutaneous fat (lobular and/or septal); often lower legs
| Feature | Erythema Nodosum | Erythema Induratum |
|---|---|---|
| Population | Any age | Adolescents/menopausal women |
| Cause | Hypersensitivity (strep, TB, sarcoid, IBD, drugs, malignancy) | Primary vasculitis of deep dermal vessels (TB-related historically) |
| Lesion | Tender plaques/nodules, no ulceration | Nodule that **ulcerates** |
| Histology | **Septal** panniculitis, **no vasculitis** | **Granulomatous + caseous necrosis**, **vasculitis present** |
- **Other types:** Weber-Christian disease (relapsing febrile nodular panniculitis), factitial panniculitis (self-inflicted), lymphoma-related, lupus panniculitis

# SECTION 2: BREAST PATHOLOGY
**Intro:** This section covers benign and malignant breast disease — benign epithelial lesions (and their cancer-risk stratification), inflammatory/infective breast disorders, stromal tumors, and breast carcinoma (the most clinically important topic — focus heavily here for exams).
---
## 1. BENIGN EPITHELIAL LESIONS OF THE BREAST
Classified into **3 risk groups**:
### A. Nonproliferative Changes ("Fibrocystic Changes") — *no ↑ cancer risk*
- **Cysts** — dilated lobules; lined by flattened or apocrine metaplastic epithelium; calcifications common; resolves on FNA
- **Fibrosis** — from cyst rupture → chronic inflammation
- **Adenosis** — ↑ acini/lobule; normal in pregnancy
- **Lactational adenoma** — palpable mass in pregnancy/lactation; regresses after weaning
- **Flat epithelial atypia** — earliest clonal lesion (16q deletion); mild atypia; risk only when combined with atypical hyperplasia
### B. Proliferative Disease WITHOUT Atypia — *small ↑ risk (1.5–2×)*
- **Epithelial hyperplasia** — filled ducts/lobules, both luminal + myoepithelial cells, irregular lumens
- **Sclerosing adenosis** — compressed acini in fibrotic stroma; can mimic invasive carcinoma
- **Complex sclerosing lesion / Radial scar** — central hyalinized nidus + radiating projections; mimics carcinoma radiologically/grossly/histologically (NOT from trauma, despite name)
- **Papilloma** — branching fibrovascular cores in dilated duct; large duct type (solitary, nipple discharge) vs small duct type (multiple, deeper)
### C. Proliferative Disease WITH Atypia — *moderate ↑ risk (4–5×)*
- **Atypical Ductal Hyperplasia (ADH)** — resembles DCIS but only partially fills duct
- **Atypical Lobular Hyperplasia (ALH)** — identical to LCIS cells, but fills <50% of acini in a lobule
- Both: ER-positive, low proliferation; ALH shows **loss of E-cadherin** (shared with LCIS)
### D. Gynecomastia
- Only common benign male breast lesion; subareolar button-like enlargement
- **Cause:** estrogen/androgen imbalance — cirrhosis (↓ estrogen metabolism), aging (↓ androgens), drugs (alcohol, marijuana, anabolic steroids), Klinefelter syndrome, Leydig/Sertoli cell tumors
- Histology: ↑ collagenous stroma + ductal epithelial hyperplasia; **no lobule formation**
### Clinical Significance
- Risk reduction: prophylactic mastectomy, tamoxifen (ER antagonist)
- <20% of atypical hyperplasia patients ever develop cancer → many opt for surveillance over intervention
---
## 2. INFLAMMATORY DISORDERS OF THE BREAST
| Condition | Key Features |
|---|---|
| **Acute Mastitis** | 1st month of breastfeeding; *S. aureus* (abscess) or strep (cellulitis); via nipple cracks; treat with antibiotics |
| **Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts** (Periductal mastitis / Zuska disease / recurrent subareolar abscess) | **>90% smokers**; keratin plug → duct dilation/rupture → granulomatous inflammation; nipple inversion; treat = duct excision |
| **Duct Ectasia** | 5th–6th decade, multiparous women; thick nipple discharge; **not** smoking-related; dilated ducts + periductal chronic inflammation + lipid-laden macrophages → fibrosis/retraction; mimics carcinoma |
| **Fat Necrosis** | History of trauma/surgery (~50%); mimics cancer; liquefactive necrosis → giant cells/calcification → scarring |
| **Lymphocytic Mastopathy** (Sclerosing Lymphocytic Lobulitis) | Type 1 DM or autoimmune thyroid disease; dense collagenized stroma + lymphocytic infiltrate around atrophic ducts |
| **Granulomatous Mastitis** | Systemic granulomatous disease (TB, sarcoid, GPA) or localized; granulomas around lobules with lipid vacuoles; cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis (Corynebacteria) |
---
## 3. STROMAL TUMORS
- Breast stroma = **intralobular** (gives biphasic tumors) vs **interlobular** (gives connective-tissue tumors as elsewhere in the body)
- Fibroadenoma & phyllodes tumor are both driven by **MED12 mutations**
### A. Fibroadenoma
- **Most common benign tumor of the female breast**; women in 20s–30s; hormonally responsive (grows in pregnancy, regresses post-menopause)
- Well-circumscribed, rubbery; pericanalicular or intracanalicular epithelial pattern
- Cyclosporin A (post-transplant) → multiple bilateral fibroadenomas (reversible)
### B. Phyllodes Tumor
- Less common; **6th decade** (later than fibroadenoma); leaf-like ("phyllodes") protrusions
- Distinguished from fibroadenoma by: ↑ cellularity, ↑ mitoses, stromal overgrowth, infiltrative border
- Malignant variants have additional **TERT** mutations; only stromal component metastasizes; axillary node dissection NOT indicated
### C. Interlobular Stroma Lesions
- **Myofibroblastoma** — equally common in males
- **Lipoma**
- **Fibromatosis** — locally aggressive, no metastasis; associated with FAP/Gardner syndrome
- **Angiosarcoma** (malignant) — rare; sporadic (young women) or post-radiation (older women, 5–10 yrs latency)
---
## 4. CARCINOMA OF THE BREAST
*(High-yield — most heavily tested topic)*
### Epidemiology & Risk Factors
- Most common cancer-related cause of death in women globally
- **Risk ↑:** age, female sex (99%), lifetime estrogen exposure, genetic mutations, obesity, alcohol, delayed childbearing/fewer pregnancies/reduced breastfeeding
- **Risk ↓:** early pregnancy (<20 yrs), prolonged breastfeeding, prophylactic mastectomy (~90% ↓), ER-antagonist chemoprevention
### Molecular Classification (by ER/HER2)
| Group | ER | HER2 |
|---|---|---|
| Luminal | + | − |
| HER2 | +/− | + |
| Triple-negative (TNBC) | − | − (also PR−) |
- 3 main pathogenic pathways: Luminal (precursor = flat epithelial atypia/atypical hyperplasia) → TNBC (precursor = p53-overexpressing normal cells) → HER2 (no defined precursor)
- **Hereditary genes** (germline): **BRCA1, BRCA2** (most important), TP53, PTEN, CDH1, STK11, ATM, CHEK2, PALB2
### Carcinoma In Situ (confined by basement membrane — cannot metastasize)
**DCIS:**
- Patterns: comedo, cribriform, micropapillary, papillary
- Untreated low-grade DCIS → invasive cancer ~1%/year; mastectomy curative >95%
**LCIS:**
- Dyscohesive cells, **loss of E-cadherin (CDH1)**; signet-ring cells; **pagetoid spread** within ducts (≠ Paget disease of nipple)
- Bilateral in 20–40% (vs DCIS 10–20%); always ER/PR+, HER2−
**Paget Disease of the Nipple:**
- Malignant (Paget) cells from DCIS spread via lactiferous sinuses into nipple skin (without crossing BM) → eczema-like eruption
- Palpable mass present → usually invasive (ER−, HER2+ overexpressing); no mass → usually just DCIS
### Invasive Carcinoma
- **Invasive Carcinoma of No Special Type (NST)** = majority; hard, gritty, desmoplastic mass → skin/nipple retraction
- **Grading (Nottingham):** tubule formation + nuclear pleomorphism + mitotic rate → Grade 1–3
- **Special types:**
  - **Lobular carcinoma** — biallelic CDH1 loss; single-file infiltration; metastasizes to peritoneum, leptomeninges, GI tract, ovary/uterus; germline CDH1 → also ↑ gastric signet-ring risk
  - **Medullary pattern** — associated with BRCA1 (germline or promoter hypermethylation); paradoxically better prognosis; heavy lymphocytic infiltrate
### Prognostic & Predictive Factors
- **Most important:** axillary lymph node status
- Others: distant metastases, tumor size, locally advanced disease (skin/muscle invasion), lymphovascular invasion, **inflammatory carcinoma** (dermal lymphatic invasion, 3-yr survival only 3–10%), gene expression profiling, response to neoadjuvant chemo
### Male Breast Cancer
- Rare (1% of female incidence); strongest hereditary factor = **germline BRCA2** (~6% of carriers affected)
- >90% luminal type; presents as subareolar mass/nipple discharge; similar prognosis to women when matched for stage
