Pulse is 72 beats per minute (b.p.m.), regular rhythm, normal equal volume, and normal character with a normal vessel wall

Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP)

#### 8.1 Introduction

•    The jugular vein is nearest to the “input” side of the heart.
•    Giving assessment of the pressure in the right atrium, which is the “filling pressure” of the right heart (central venous pressure).
•    The internal jugular vein is more reliable for examination as the external is sometimes kinked or partially obstructed when it traverses the deep fascia in the neck.
•    Internal jugular venous lies deep to the sternal and clavicular heads of the sternocleaidomatoid muscle.
•    The jugular venous pulsation reflects the sequence of pressure changes within the right atrium.
•    The centre of the right atrium lies 5 cm vertically below the manubriosternal angle.
•    The right Atrial pressure is measured (in cm of blood) by adding 5 cm to the vertical height above the jugular veins as distended.
•    The normal right Atrial pressure (JVP) is > 3 cm of water which is equivalent to a right Atrial pressure of 8 cm water.

## Topic 4- Inspection and Palpation of the Preacordium
Objectives

At the end of the lesson the learner will be able to: -

1) Examine the heart by inspection and palpation
2) Interpret the findings on physical examination

### 1.0 INTRODUCTION

•   Examination of the heart should follow the usual routine of:- inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation
•   Inspection enables the examiner to see the position, extent and rhythm of the cardiac impulse.
•   Palpation confirms the position of apex beat, gives more information on the force, duration and character of the cardiac impulse, helps in detection of thrills and expansible pulsations
•   Percussion has some value when the patient is too ill to move by showing the increased area of dullness due to pericardial effusion and absence of dullness due to emphysema of the lungs but has been a discredited examination method in favor of the accurate radiological information.
•   Auscultation is useful for detection of abnormalities of valves which produce both changes in heart sounds and added sounds and determining the rhythm of heart rate.

### 3.0 BASIC SURFACE ANATOMY

CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 45

The knowledge of the position of the heart, its chambers and its valves within the chest is the key to understanding the physical examination of the heart, the electrocardiogram, the chest X-ray and the echocardiogram. From the front, the heart is roughly triangular in shape. The heart lies mainly beneath the sternum with the base just protruding to the right of the sternum and apex in the left side of the chest in the mid clavicular line 5th costal space.

The Right Ventricle
• Occupies most of the front of the heart and lies beneath and just to the left of the sternum.
• Enlargement brings the heart more into contact with the sternum.

Right Atrium
• Forms the right boarder of the heart as seen from the front.

Left Ventricle
• Lies to the left of and behind the right ventricle.
• Left ventricular enlargement shifts the cardiac apex outwards and downwards.

Left Atrium
• Lies at the back of the heart
• Not part of cardiac silhouette seen from the front
• In side view it forms the upper part of the posterior heart boarder and it is adjacent to the oesophagus.

### 4.0 INSPECTION

•   Patient should be in good adequate light
•   Pulsations are examined both in erect and recumbent positions
•   Learnt by inspecting the precordium (anterior chest wall overlying the heart)
•   Helps in studying the position, character and rhythm of the cardiac impulse
•   Inspect for:
    1) Symmetry of the chest
    2) Any abnormalities such as scolosis, kyphoscoliosis and pectus excavatum
    3) Look for and identify any pulsation

### 4.1 Activity of the preacordium

•   The activity could be - normal, increased or reduced

Causes of increased activity of the preacordium

1) Fever
2) Anxiety
3) Exercise
4) Cardiac diseases (cardiomopathy ventricular dilatation)

Decreased activity

1) Obesity
2) A very muscular chest wall
3) Pleural effusion
4) Pericardial effusion
5) Obstructive airway disease

### 4.2 Abnormal pulsations

•   Observe for abnormal pulsations at the praecordium, great vessels in the neck and epigastrium and pulsations in the epigastrium
•   Causes of pulsations in the epigastrium
    1) Normal in the twin individuals
    2) Right ventricular enlargement
    3) Pulsation of the liver in tricuspid regurgitation
    4) Aneurysm of abdominal aorta
CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 47

### 5.0 PALPATION

•   Is an important examination method

### 5.1 Approach

•   Lay the whole hand flat on the chest wall to get a general impression of cardiac activity.
•   Now localize the apex beat and assess the character
•   Ask patient to roll onto the left side if necessary
•   Identify any other pulsations particularly in the parasternal area

### 5.2 Procedure

•   Should be carried out with the patient first in recumbent position and then the erect posture systematically.
•   The fingers are placed systematically over the apex area and over the base of the heart.
•   The palm of the hand should be placed on all areas of the preacordium in order to detect any abnormal pulsations or vibrations.
•   The cardiac impulse is usually circumscribed at the apex beat.
•   The palm is too large for accurate palpation; hence information obtained by it should be supplemented by use of fingers.
•   Palpation is a more reliable method of estimating the size of the heart.
•   In palpation, examine for:- the apex beat, heaves and thrills

### 6.0 APEX BEAT

•   Is the lower most, outer most point of maximum cardiac impulse (pulsation/activity) or the further point outward and downward at which the cardiac impulse can be palpated.
•   It is circumscribed and almost invariably within the nipple except in children and adolescents.
•   The cardiac impulse that is usually felt over the left side of the chest is the result of the heart rotating, moving forward and striking against the chestwall during systole.
•   With changes of posture (lying on one side) the apex beat may move as much as
### 1.5 to 2 cm.
•   About the apex beat examine for:- position and the character of the cardiac impulse
•   The position can be normal or displaced from the normal position (upwards, downwards, medially laterally)

CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 48

Position of apex beat

•    It is normally placed in the 5th intercostal space on the mid clavicular line (9 cm from the midline) lying within 7.5 cm to 10 cm (3-4”) in the 5th intercostal space (left).
•    An abnormal position is generally associated with cardiac enlargement.
•    Right ventricular hypertrophy causes strong pulsation in the left parasternal region and often movement of the sternum and ribs.
•    Left ventricular hypertrophy initially causes an increased duration of apex beat and later results in minimally displaced and forceful impulse.

Causes of Displacement

1) Upward Displacement
   a. Short and broad chest
   b. Pregnancy
   c. A high diaphragm
   d. Chest deformities
   e. Mediastinal shift

2) Downward Displacement
   a. Long narrow chest
   b. Chest deformities
   c. Cardiomegaly

3)

CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 49

Lateral Displacement
• Can be due to conditions of:- the heart, lungs, pleura, thoracic cage, mediastinum and abdomen

    a. The heart
• Hypertrophy and dilatation as a result of cardiomegaly whose causes include:-congestive cardiac failure, left ventricular failure, right ventricular failure and cardiomyopathies
b. The    lungs    e.g.   right    sided    hydrothorax,     pneumothorax        and hydropneumothorax; left sided lung collapse and lung fibrosis
    c. The Pleura – right-sided pleural effusion (fluid/blood).
    d. The Thoracic Cage - scoliosis, kyphosis, kyphoscoliosis and pectus excavatum
    e. Abdomen - pregnancy and ascites - are associated with a raised diaphragm.
    f. Mediastinum - masses like Lymph nodes and tumours.

4) Medial Displacement
   a. Cardiac - rarely dextrocardia
b. Lungs - lung fibrosis, left sided hydrothorax, left sided pneumothorax and left sided hydropneumothorax
   c. Pleura - left sided pleura effusion
   d. Thoracic Cage - Scoliosis

Character

•   Apex beat gently raises the palpating fingers.
•   Strength of its thrust is best judged by experience.
•   Is reduced in health by a thick chest wall (fat and muscles) and by emphysema.
•   Is noticeable in thin persons
•   Can be diffuse or discrete
•   Diffuse apex beat character is seen in:-
    1) Nervousness
    2) After exercise
    3) Hyperthyroidism
    4) Cardiac enlargement
•   A forcible thrust suggests cardiac hypertrophy
•   Position and character of the cardiac impulse gives valuable information about the presence of cardiac enlargement and whether this is due to hypertrophy or dilatation.

Abnormal forms of apex beat character

1) Tapping - a sudden but brief cardiac impulse in Mitral stenosis
2) Thrusting - vigorous but non-sustained pulsation typical of volume overload in
   Mitral    regurgitation/aortic regurgitation.
3) Heaving – a vigorous and sustained pulsation due to pressure overload aortic stenosis/systemic hypertension.
4) Impalpable due to conditions e.g. emphysema, pleural effusion, obesity and pericardial effusion

### 7.0 THRILLS

•   Are palpable vibrations kin the time with the cardiac cycle which are
CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 50

communicated to the palpating hand from the heart or its great vessels
•   Are palpable murmurs
•   Conditions causing thrills are more exaggerated than in cases of murmurs.
•   They are best detected when the breath is held in cases of murmurs.
•   Can be made more prominent by altering position of the patient.
•   Felt as purring or vibratory sensations.
•   Thrills may be systolic or diastolic.
•   They indicate an organic disease and give localization of the disease in the heart

Systolic Thrills

•   Are palpable during the systolic phase of the cardiac cycle
•   Causes
1) Aortic stenosis (2nd intercostal space on the spreading upwards towards the neck).
    2) Aneurysm of great vessels
    3) Pulmonary stenosis(2nd intercostal space on the left of the sternum)
4) VSD (2nd intercostal space best felt by asking the patient to sit up, lean forward and exhale)
    5) Mitral regurgitation

Diastolic Thrills
• Mitral stenosis (felt at the apex
• Tricuspid stenosis - best felt with patient rolled onto the left side, feels like placing ones hand on a purring cat

### 8.0 HEAVES

•   Are forceful sustained lifting or tapping feeling over the reference the praecordium due to ventricular enlargement (Hypertrophy)
•   There are 2 types of heaves - apical heave (elicited at the apex region and indicate left ventricular hypertrophy) and parasternal heaves (felt at the parasternal region by pressing the outstretched hand flat against the sternum or against coastal cartilage’s just to the left of the sternum and indicates right ventricular hypertrophy).

           Pressure
Grade 2     The palpating hand is lifted without application of pressure
Grade 3     The palpating hand is lifted even with application of pressure

## Topic 5: Percussion and Auscultation
Objectives

At the end of the lesson the learner will be able to: -
1) Percuss and palpate the preacordium in examination of the heart
2) Interpret the findings on physical examination

PERCUSSION

•   Is not routinely done because of the great accuracy of radiological examination.
•   Has some valve if patient is too ill to move by showing the increased area of dullness due to pericardial effusion.
•   It may demonstrate the basal dullness of right sternum in cases of aortic aneurysm.
•   Is done when there is a possibility of cardiomegally and cardiac tamponade.

AUSCULTATION

### 1.0 Introduction

•   Is an important examination method.
•   Use a suitable stethoscope with:-
1) A flat diaphragm - filters out low pitched sounds and helps identifying high pitched sounds e.g. murmur of aortic regurgitation.
    2) A bell - that is used for auscultation of low-pitched sounds e.g. murmur of

### 4.0 The Heart Sounds

•   Auscultate for the heart sounds (1st and 2nd ) and note the following:
    1) The rhythm
    2) Character
    3) Intensity
    4) Splitting of the heart sounds

The Rhythm

•   In a normal rhythm the 1st and 2nd heart sounds are quite close together with
CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 56

internal following 2nd heart sound being relatively longer.
•   The sequence is lub-dup-pause, lub-dub-pause.

Intensity

•   The intensity can be normal, exaggerated or diminished
•   Exaggeration – the heart sounds become louder in conditions that increase the activity of the heart.

    1) Nervousness
    2) Exercise
    3) Hyperthyroidism
    4) Most obvious in the 1st heart sound

•   Diminution is more due to extracardiac than to cardiac causes like:- emphysema and fluid/air in pleural/pericardial cavities

Splitting of sounds

• In a normal heart the 1st and 2nd sounds are quite close but, the interval following the 2nd sounds is relatively long.
THE FIRST HEART SOUND (1ST HS)

•   Is due to the closure of mitral and tricuspid valves (mainly from the mitral element that is louder hence most easily heard)
•   Best heard at the apex region
•   Splitting ‘I-Lub’ -’Dup’ is due to asynchronous closure of Mitral and tricuspid valves (not pathological).
•   Abnormalities of intensity of the 1st heart sounds include:- quiet heart sounds, loud heart sounds or variable heart sounds

Quiet 1st HS

1) Low cardiac output e.g. pericardial effusion, air in pericardial cavity and mitral regurgitation
2) Poor left ventricular function
3) Low filling pressure
4) Emphysema
5) Pleural effusion
6) Air in the pleural cavity

Loud 1st HS

1) Increased cardiac output
2) Large stroke volume
3) Mitral stenosis
4) Atrial fibrillation

Variable 1st HS

1) Atrial fibrillation
2) Extra systoles
CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 57

3) Complete heart block

THE SECOND HEART SOUNDS (2ND HS)

•   Due to the closure of pulmonary and aortic valves.
•   Best heard using the diaphragm of the stethoscope at the upper sternum at the level of 2nd intercostal space.
•   The aortic component is the loudest and is best heard at the aortic area and transmitted to the apex.
•   The pulmonary component is best heard at the pulmonary area.
•   Both may be heard (normal splitting) with the aortic component proceeding the pulmonary - ‘lub-d-dub’.
•   Intensity of the components varies with age in that the aortic component dominates in the older age group as does the pulmonary in the young individuals.
•   Splitting of the 2nd Hs persisting throughout the respiratory cycle is due to right bundle branch block.
•   Wide fixed splitting of the 2nd Hs is a feature of septal defects.

Abnormalities of the second heart sound.

Quiet
1) Low cardiac output
2) Calcific aortic stenosis
3) Extreme vasodilatation
4) Aortic stenosis
Loud
1) Systemic hypertension (aortic component)
2) Pulmonary hypertension
3) Mitral stenosis
4) Congenital Heart Disease (CHD)
5) Pulmonary disease
6) Corrected transposition of the great vessels

Splitting
1) Fixed splitting (unaffected by respiration)
        a. Aortic septal defect (ASD)
        b. Widens in inspiration (enhanced physiological splitting)
        c. Right bundle branch block
        d. Pulmonary stenosis
        e. Pulmonary hypertension
        f. Ventricular septal defects (VSD)
2) Widens in expiration (reverse splitting)
        a. Left ventricular outflow obstruction
        b. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
        c. Left bundle branch block

THE THIRD HEART SOUND (3RD HS)

•   Is a low-pitched sound (lub-dup-dum, lub-dup-dum) not heard in all subjects and comes after the 2nd Hs.
•   Best heard with the bell at the apex and left sternal boarder with patient in a
CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 58

recumbent position.
•   It is associated with a large stroke volume
•   Physiologically heard in:- children, health young adults, athletes and during pregnancy
•   Heard pathologically in-patients with a large poorly contracting ventricle (e.g.
dilated Cardiomyopathy) or when ventricular stroke volume is increased due to a leaking heart valve.

Causes of a third Hs

Physiological
1) Health young adults
2) Athletes
3) Pregnancy
4) Fever

Pathological
1) Large poorly contraction heart (Cardiomyopathy)
2) Mitral and aortic reflux - Large stroke volume
3) Constrictive pericarditis
4) Rheumatic Mitral stenosis
5) Mitral regurgitation
6) Aortic regurgitation
7) Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy

•   3rd Hs is associated with a fast heart beat and quiet 1st and 2nd Hs giving a triple rhythm - called a gallop rhythm (S3 gallop).
•   It is a sign of serious myocardial disease.
•   It is best-heard parasternally or in the epigastrium.

FOURTH HEART SOUND (4TH HS)

•   Is a soft low-pitched sound that occurs just before the 1st sound (da-lub-dup, da-lub-dup)
•   Caused by increased atrial activity.
•   Also called S4 gallop/presystolic gallop/triple rhythm
•   Heard at the apex

Causes

1) Left ventricular disease
2) Left ventricular hypertrophy
3) Dilated cavity/hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
4) Acute myocardial infarction/Ischaemic heart disease
5) Pulmonary stenosis
6) Pulmonary hypertension

MURMURS

Introduction

•   Are musical sounds made by the turbulent blood flow in the heart.
•   Murmurs can be innocent (insignificant) or organic (significant).
•   Are produced by normal volume of blood passing through an abnormal valve or increased volume of blood passing through a normal valve (flow murmurs).
•   Originate at the valves or great vessels.
•   Tend to be propagated in the same direction of flow of blood.
•   When examining murmurs consider the following features.
       1. Site
       2. Timing
       3. Character
       4. Intensity/Pitch
       5. Radiation
       6. Relationship to respiration, posture and exercise

CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 60

Causes of Murmurs

•   Murmurs result from turbulence/velocity of blood flow and Eddy currents resulting from modification in size of valve opening, irregularities and deformities of the valve and/or its surrounding.
•   Murmurs can be innocent (insignificant) or organic (significant)

    1) Systolic murmurs

       a. Ejection (mid) systolic
              i. Aortic stenosis
             ii. Pulmonary stenosis
            iii. Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)
            iv. Left outflow obstruction e.g. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HOLM)
v. Right outflow obstruction e.g. Fallot’s tetrology vi. Anaemia vii. Thyrotoxicosis viii. Pregnancy ix. Skeletal abnormalities e.g. Kyphoscoliosis and Funnel chest

       b. Pan-systolic
             i. Mitral regurgitation (blowing murmurs)
            ii. Tricuspid regurgitation (low pitched)
           iii. Ventricular septal defect (loud and rough)

       c. Late systolic
             i. Dynamic out flow obstruction (HOCM)
            ii. Mitral valve prolapse
           iii. Coarctication of the aorta

    2) Diastolic
       a. Mid diastolic
             i. Mitral stenosis (low frequency rumbling)
            ii. Tricuspid stenosis
           iii. Austin Flint Murmur
       b. Early diastolic
             i. Aortic regurgitation (Blowing with a variable pitch)
            ii. Graham Steel in pulmonary hypertension (due to Mitral stenosis)

    3) Combined systolic and diastolic
       a. PDA - Patent Ductus Arterious
       b. Aortic stenosis and regurgitation
       c. Mitral stenosis and regurgitation

Timing

•   A murmur can be:-
1) Systolic - occurs during ventricular systole and accompany the pulse, .follows the 1st Hs immediately
2) Diastolic - occurs during diastolic and follow the pulse, appears immediately after the 2nd heart sound.
•   Use the cardiac impulse or carotid pulse to time the murmur.
CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 61

Systolic Murmurs

•   Can be ejection, pansystolic or late systolic murmur

Ejection Murmur
• Commences after 1st Hs
• They increase in amplitude to a peak about mid-systole becoming quiet towards the end of systole (crescendo-decrescendo cadence).
• Appear as a diamond shape on phonocardiogram.
• Are due to:-
1.Ejection of a normal quantity of blood through a stenosed (normal) aortic or pulmonary valve. These are harsh and high-pitched murmurs.
2.       Ejection of an increased volume of blood through a normal valve (flow murmurs)
• Characteristics of flow murmurs.
       o Are of an ejection pattern.
o May have either a grunting or a musical component o Their timing is generally earlier in systole than murmurs due an organic obstruction of flow.
       o Arise from either left or right ventricular outflow tracts.
o Are never associated with any abnormality of the thoracic wall e.g. a depressed sternum.
o The intensity may be increased by physiological maneuvers that increase the cardiac output
• Flow murmurs are commonly seen in children, young adults and the elderly.
   They also occur when the stroke volume is increased as in:-
       - Anaemia
       - Thyrotoxicosis
       - Pregnancy
       - Hypertension
       - Chronic anxiety

Pansystolic Murmurs

•   Extend throughout systole right up to and beyond 2nd Hs
•   Have a “blowing” or tearing sound.
•   Show a constant amplitude on phonocardiogram (with a slight accentuation in mid systole)
•   Causes
    1) Leakage (regurgitation) - mitral and tricuspid valve
    2) Congenital/Acquired Ventricular Septal Defect
•   Late systolic murmurs are variants of Pansystolic murmurs (e.g. Mitral valve prolapse).

Diastolic Murmurs

•   Divided into:- early and mid-diastolic murmurs

Early Diastolic Murmurs

•   Usually due to aortic or pulmonary valve regurgitation.
CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 62

•   Start immediately after the second heart sound and become quieter as diastole proceeds (‘decrescendo murmur’).
•   Sounds like a whispered letter ‘r’.
•   Aortic regurgitation murmur is:
o Best heard along the left sternal boarder o High pitched hence best heard with the diaphragm o The patient sits up leaning forward and breathes out fully o Radiates in the direction of the regurgitant blood
•   Pulmonary regurgitation murmur.
       o Rare
       o Sometimes heard in-patients with pulmonary hypertension (“Graham
           Steell” murmur -Pulmonary regurgitation secondary to Mitral stenosis).

Mid Diastolic Murmurs

•   Best exemplified by the murmur of Mitral stenosis
•   Begins with the 2nd heart sound and are blowing (High pitched).
•   Mitral stenosis murmur
       o Starts just after the second heart sound.
       o Is proceeded by an opening snap.
       o Is a low-pitched rumbling murmur.
o Best heard with bell of the stethoscope and with the patient rolled onto the left-hand side.

Continuous Murmur

•   Bridges systole and diastole.
•   Most important cause is PDA (Persistent Ductus Arterious duct).

•   Six grades are used to describe systolic while 4 grades for diastolic murmurs.

CHARACTER/QUALITY

•   Vary from soft blowing to harsh rasping murmurs.
•   Loud and rough murmurs suggest organic valvular or congenital lesions.
•   Soft murmurs are usually innocent (although an aortic regurgitation murmur is soft).
•   There is no correlation between the loudness of a murmur and the haemodynamic severity of the lesions causing it.

DISTRIBUTION/SITE

• Murmurs are heard over the session causing them.
• Describe the position/site where the murmur is best-heard (area of greatest intensity of the murmur) and its place of origin (production).
RADIATION/SPREAD OF MURMURS

•   Murmurs radiate in the direction of the turbulent blood flow.
•   When the maximum intensity of a murmur has been noted, move the stethoscope radically from this point in different directions and determine whether the murmur is circumscribed/localized or widely transmitted/radiating.

 2.    ELECTROCARDIOGRAM (EGG)

     • Is a recording of the electrical activity of the heart
     • Is the only way of diagnosing rhythm and conduction problems
• Is the vector sum of the depolarization and repolarization potential of the myocardial cells (Summation of action potentials of all myocardial cells)
• The shape of the wave form of the EGG depends on the speed and direction of the depolarization process through the heart
• Depolarization initiating each heart beat begins at Sino-Atrial node and spreads as an advancing wave through the atria which are depolarized simultaneously to the A-V Node
• Depolarization spreads from the atria to ventricles via the Bundle of HIS that begins at A-V Node passing into the interventricular septum where it divides into right and left branches
• Left branch divides into 2 smaller branches (fascicles) which supply anterior and posterior parts of left ventricle respectively
• Bundle branches subdivide into the Purkinje fibres that form a network of cells to carry the depolarization wave to the myocardial cells
• Return of ventricular muscle cells to their resting electrical state is called repolarization

 EGG Waveform

 CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 69

Terminology

•   P wave - 1st deflection corresponds to depolarization and the atria
•   QRS Complex - 3 deflections - 1st downwards (Q wave), 2nd upwards (R wave)
    and 3rd downwards (S wave) corresponds to depolarization of the ventricle.
•   T Wave        - repolarization of ventricular muscles.
•   Upward deflection is a depolarization wave is moving towards recording electrodes
•   Downward deflection repolarization wave is moving away from the recording electrodes.

Time intervals

•   All EGG recorders run a standard paper speed of 25 mm/s.
•   EGG paper is standardized so that 5 large squares pass under the recorder stylus each second.
•   One large square is equivalent to 0.2 sec.
•   Each large square is subdivided into five small squares each equivalent to 0.04s.
•   Heart rate can be calculated from the number of squares between QRS
    complexes.
•   Time taken by each part of the depolarization sequence in each cardiac cycle is
•   Calculated by the number of small squares it occupies.

PR interval
• Is the time taken for depolarisation to spread from SAN to Atria to AVN through the Bundle of HIS bundle to the ventricle
• Shown by number of small squares between beginning of P wave and the beginning of the ORS complex.
• Normal upper limit 0.20 seconds.
• Width of QRS complex indicates the time taken by the depolarisation wave to spread throughout the ventricles.

QT intervals
• Time taken for the whole depolarization sequence in ventricles.
• Obtained from the number of squares between beginning of QRS complex and of
CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 70

T wave.

CVS Examination by Okinda, C. F. Page 71

Abnormalities of Conduction

(a) AV Node/Bundle of HIS
• Prolonged PR interval
    1) 1st degree heart block - P Wave is followed by QRS complex.
2) 2nd degree heart block - some P waves are followed by QRS complexes but others are not. There are 3 varieties of 2nd degree heart block
3) 3rd degree (complex) – no P waves are conducted, ventricular escape rhythm controls the heart with a slow rate, QRS complexes are wide and abnormal.

(b) His bundle branches

•   Right bundle - Branch block, broadening of QRS complex
•   Left bundle branch block - wide QRS complex, inverted T wave

*(Cell Biology / Physiology)*

**Q1. Which of the following statements about carrier-mediated transport systems is NOT true?**
A. Each carrier protein has a specific affinity for binding one or a small number of solutes
B. They are members of the solute carrier (SLC) superfamily
C. The simplest passive carrier-mediated transport is one that mediates facilitated diffusion
D. They hydrolyze ATP or couple to an electron transport chain
E. They transfer a broad range of ions and organic solutes across the cell membrane

**Answer: d**
**Explanation: Carrier-mediated transport includes facilitated diffusion (passive, no ATP) and active transport. Statement (d) wrongly generalizes that *all* carriers hydrolyze ATP or couple to electron transport — this only applies to active transporters, not facilitated diffusion carriers.

---

**Q2. The events that take place at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ), where acetylcholine (ACh) is released as a neurotransmitter, is an excellent example of:**
A. Autocrine signaling
B. Hormonal signaling
C. Paracrine signaling
D. Self-induced signaling
E. Endocrine signaling

**Answer: c**
**Explanation: Paracrine signaling affects target cells in close proximity to the signaling cell — exactly what happens at the NMJ, where ACh diffuses a very short distance across the synaptic cleft.

---

**Q3. Which of these statements is TRUE regarding the Na⁺–K⁺ pumps?**
A. They are energized by GTP hydrolysis and hence are GTPases
B. They are responsible in cells throughout the body for maintaining a high [K⁺]ᵢ and low [Na⁺]ᵢ, and are ATPases
C. In each cycle, the pump couples the extrusion of two K⁺ ions and the uptake of three Na⁺ ions
D. In most epithelial cells they are restricted to the basolateral side of the cell
E. They are the least important primary active transporter in human body cells

**Answer: d** (with b also broadly true in principle, but the pump extrudes 3 Na⁺ and takes up 2 K⁺ — opposite of option c)
**Explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is an ATPase (not GTPase), extrudes **3 Na⁺ out** and brings **2 K⁺ in** per cycle (so option c is reversed/wrong), and in most epithelial cells is localized to the **basolateral membrane**, making (d) the correct statement.

---

**Q4. Intracellular signaling effector molecules include the following, EXCEPT:**
A. Ligands
B. Contractile elements
C. Transport proteins and channels
D. Transcription factors
E. Enzymes

**Answer: a**
**Explanation: Ligands are *extracellular* signaling molecules that bind receptors; effectors act downstream inside the cell (enzymes, channels, transcription factors, contractile elements).

---

**Q5. In the parietal cells of the gastric gland, an ______ across the apical membrane into the gland lumen extrudes H⁺, regulated by histamine, acetylcholine, and gastrin:**
A. H⁺-K⁺ pump
B. Ca²⁺ pump
C. Na/K/Cl cotransporter
D. K/Cl cotransporter
E. Na-K pump

**Answer: a**
**Explanation: The gastric H⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps H⁺ into the gland lumen in exchange for K⁺; it is stimulated by histamine, acetylcholine, and gastrin.

---

**Q6. All the following are categories of receptors based on their associated mechanisms of signal transduction, EXCEPT:**
A. G protein-coupled receptors
B. Catalytic receptors (e.g. tyrosine kinase, activated by binding of ligand)
C. Nuclear receptors
D. Heterotrimeric guanosine triphosphate (GTP) receptors
E. Ligand-gated ion channels

**Answer: d**
**Explanation: "Heterotrimeric GTP receptors" is not a recognized receptor category — heterotrimeric G-proteins are downstream *effectors* of GPCRs, not a separate receptor class.

---

**Q7. With regard to control systems, what is NOT correct?**
A. The controlled variable is usually a measurable entity
B. The controlled system is any process or group of processes whose output is the controlled variable
C. The presence of sensors is mandatory for any control system
D. The controller may be in the central nervous system
E. External influences could be harmful or helpful to the system

**Answer: c**
**Explanation: Not all control (e.g., simple open-loop/feedforward) strictly requires sensors monitoring the controlled variable — sensors are mandatory for *closed-loop* feedback control specifically, not for control systems in general.

---

**Q8. Body fluid compartments:**
A. This refers to the physical distribution of water within the cells
B. Are completely physically and chemically distinct from one another
C. Intracellular compartment comprises 14 litres
D. Extracellular compartment is 1/3 of the total body water
E. Total blood volume is 3.5 litres

**Answer: d**
**Explanation: ECF is roughly ⅓ of total body water (ICF ≈ ⅔). Intracellular volume is ~28 L (not 14 L), and blood volume is ~5 L (not 3.5 L) in an average adult.

---

**Q9. The following single-cell forms are able to carry out de novo synthesis of nutrients from raw materials:**
A. Bacteria
B. DNA viruses
C. Ovum
D. Spermatozoa
E. Mature red blood cell

**Answer: a**
**Explanation: Bacteria are free-living cells capable of independent metabolism/synthesis. Viruses are obligate parasites with no synthetic machinery of their own; mature RBCs lack a nucleus and most organelles.

---

**Q10. What is NOT true about nucleoli?**
A. They stain lighter than the surrounding nucleoplasm
B. Site of ribosome synthesis
C. Store nucleic bases rather than complete nucleic acids
D. More abundant in rapidly dividing cells
E. Do not have a unit membrane

**Answer: c**
**Explanation: Nucleoli are the site of ribosomal RNA synthesis and ribosome assembly (containing complete rRNA and proteins, not "nucleic bases"), and they actually stain **darker** than surrounding nucleoplasm.

---

**Q11. Peroxisomes are rich in:**
A. Hydrolases and proteases compared to lysosomes
B. Hydrogen peroxide and catalase only
C. Decarboxylases and rases
D. Oxidases and catalytic enzymes
E. Hyaluronidase and other dehydrogenases

**Answer: d**
**Explanation: Peroxisomes contain oxidases (which generate H₂O₂) and catalase, which breaks it down — collectively "oxidases and catalytic enzymes."

---

**Q12. Mitochondria perform all the following functions EXCEPT:**
A. ATP synthesis from the common pool of intermediaries
B. Hydrolysing ATP through action of ATP synthetase
C. Hydrolyzing fatty acids to free fatty acids
D. Catecholamine and tryptophan oxidation
E. Hydrolyzing alcohol in the liver

**Answer: e**
**Explanation: Alcohol (ethanol) metabolism occurs mainly via alcohol dehydrogenase in the cytosol/smooth ER, not mitochondria (though acetaldehyde is later oxidized there — the *hydrolysis* step is not a mitochondrial function).

---

**Q13. During post-translational modification, proteins enter the Golgi apparatus through the:**
A. Cis-phase
B. Trans-plane
C. 3′-prime end
D. Translocons situated along the sides of the plate arrangement
E. Surface closely related to the nuclear membrane

**Answer: a**
**Explanation: Proteins from the rough ER enter the Golgi at the **cis face**, are processed through the stack, and exit at the trans face.

---

**Q14. With regard to control systems, what is NOT correct?** *(duplicate topic, different numbering — 13 in another copy)*
Same as Q7 above.

---

**Q15. In processes contributing to body homeostasis:**
A. Cellular processes have little relevance to the overall whole-body homeostasis
B. Organ systems usually control one or more variables that contribute to the whole body homeostasis
C. Body temperature control is under feedback control only
D. Body pH control is an example of intracellular control only
E. Height is under adaptive control

**Answer: b**
**Explanation: Organ systems (renal, respiratory, cardiovascular etc.) each regulate specific variables that collectively maintain whole-body homeostasis.

---

**Q16. In Open loop control mechanisms:**
A. The controlled variable level is constantly monitored
B. Sensors are necessary
C. Controllers are not necessary
D. The controlled variable is not measurable
E. Salivary secretion is an example

**Answer: e**
**Explanation: Open-loop (feedforward) control acts without feedback monitoring of the controlled variable — e.g. salivation on seeing/smelling food occurs before any change in oral conditions is sensed.

---

**Q17. Homeostasis:**
A. Refers to the static and absolutely constant state of life processes
B. Refers to the maintenance of physiological parameters within physiological limits
C. Homeokinesis and Homeodynamism are unrelated terms
D. Occurs at cellular level only
E. Implies that control mechanisms are not necessary

**Answer: b**
**Explanation: Homeostasis is dynamic maintenance of internal parameters within a physiological range, not an absolutely static state.

---

**Q18. In the theoretical control model, what is NOT true?**
A. The controller must have a 'set-point'
B. Forcing functions have an effect on the controller
C. The controlled system may be affected by external inputs
D. The controlled variable level should remain relatively constant
E. Sensors may not be anatomically distinct from the controller

**Answer: b**
**Explanation: Forcing functions (external disturbances) act on the **controlled system/variable**, not directly on the controller.

---

**Q19. In Negative feedback control:**
A. Changes in the controlled variable level are prevented
B. The response of the system is in the opposite direction to the change in the controlled variable
C. Sensors feed back information to the controlled system
D. Fluctuation is an advantage
E. Simplicity of design is a disadvantage

**Answer: b**
**Explanation: Negative feedback by definition opposes ("negates") the direction of change in the controlled variable to restore it toward the set point.

---

**Q20. In Positive feedback control:**
A. Vicious cycles may develop if the system is working normally
B. A progressive rise in controlled variable level occurs
C. A cut-off point is only sometimes required
D. It is not used for transient events
E. The act of salivation on seeing food is an example

**Answer: b**
**Explanation: Positive feedback amplifies the initial change, producing a progressive, escalating rise in the controlled variable (e.g., labour contractions, clotting cascade) until a cut-off event ends the loop.

---

**Q21. In Adaptive control, what is NOT true?**
A. The controller may cause the system to adapt to external influences
B. The controlled system may proliferate
C. The stimulus for the adaptation may be a feedback from the controlled variable
D. If the demand for the controlled variable falls, the controlled system may undergo effects of disuse
E. It is usually reversible

**Answer:** *(marked with an X on the question — likely testing which option is false)* **b**
**Explanation: Adaptive control mechanisms involve reversible structural/functional change (hypertrophy, disuse atrophy) in response to demand — "proliferate" as a blanket description is not the defining feature; disuse effects (d) and reversibility (e) are hallmark features.

---

**Q22. As regards the importance of water, what is NOT correct?**
A. It comprises 65% of body weight
B. It is a universal solvent
C. It is a poor conductor of ions
D. Acts as a medium of transport
E. Contributes to the presence of osmotic pressure

**Answer: c**
**Explanation: Water is actually a **good** conductor of ions/electrolytes because dissolved ions dissociate freely in it — it is not a poor conductor.

---

**Q23. Which of the following is not a characteristic of life?**
A. Respiration
B. Irritability
C. Growth
D. Immunity
E. Reproduction

**Answer: d**
**Explanation: Immunity is a specific defence property of some organisms, not one of the universal characteristics of life (which are: nutrition, respiration, excretion, irritability, movement, growth, reproduction).

---

**Q24. The maintenance of internal environment within physiological limits is termed:**
A. Hemostasis
B. Homeostasis
C. Homeodynamism
D. a & b
E. b & c

**Answer: e**
**Explanation: Homeostasis and homeodynamism both describe the dynamic maintenance of the internal environment within set limits; hemostasis refers specifically to blood clotting, unrelated here.

---

**Q25. Which statement best describes 'internal environment'?**
A. The conditions within the cells
B. The conditions in the interstitium
C. The conditions within the body
D. The conditions within the abdomen
E. The conditions within the intravascular compartment

**Answer: b**
**Explanation: "Internal environment" (Claude Bernard's *milieu intérieur*) refers to the extracellular fluid bathing the cells — i.e., the interstitial fluid.

---

**Q26. The interstitial body fluid compartment size in an adult male is:**
A. 42 litres
B. 28 litres
C. 14 litres
D. 10 litres
E. 4 litres

**Answer: d**
**Explanation: Of ~42 L total body water: ICF ≈ 28 L, ECF ≈ 14 L, of which plasma ≈ 3.5–4 L and interstitial fluid ≈ 10 L.

---

**Q27. What is NOT true regarding why water is important to life?**
A. Acts as a universal solvent
B. Is a medium of transport
C. Freezes at 0°C
D. Is a universal medium
E. Is a conductor of ions

**Answer: c**
**Explanation: Freezing point is a physical property, not a reason water is *important to life* in a physiological sense — the other options describe water's biological roles.

---

**Q28. What is NOT true with regard to fluid in the body?**
A. Amounts to about 42 L in a normal adult man
B. May be 50% reduced without any ill-effects
C. Osmosis is an important means of fluid movement
D. Amounts to 3.5 L in the intra-vascular compartment
E. Amounts to 28 L in the intracellular compartment

**Answer: b**
**Explanation: A 50% reduction in total body water is incompatible with life — severe, even 10–15% loss can be life-threatening.

---

**Q29. In Feedforward control:**
A. Simplicity of design is an advantage
B. The sensors accurately detect the level of controlled variable
C. Errors are quickly corrected
D. Errors should not occur
E. Sweating after exercise is an example

**Answer: d**
**Explanation: Feedforward (open-loop) control anticipates change and acts before an error occurs, aiming to prevent errors altogether (rather than correcting them after detection, as in negative feedback).

---

**Q30. The DNA site at which transcription commences is exposed by the action of:**
A. Second messenger
B. DNA helicase
C. Reverse transcriptase
D. DNA polymerase
E. Integrase

**Answer: b**
**Explanation: DNA helicase unwinds the double helix, exposing the template strand for RNA polymerase to begin transcription.

---

**Q31. During transcription:**
A. All nucleic bases on the DNA molecule are copied as they are
B. Purines are interchanged with pyrimidines
C. Guanosine is substituted for Uracil
D. Uracil is substituted for Thymine
E. Cytosine replaces adenine in the new RNA molecule

**Answer: d**
**Explanation: RNA polymerase transcribes using uracil in place of thymine wherever the DNA template calls for adenine's complement.

---

**Q32. The process of self-splicing during post-transcriptional modification of pre-mRNA:**
A. Involves standard spliceosomes found at the regulatory segment of every mammalian gene
B. Removes exons only, leaving introns to be eliminated by external spliceosomes
C. Eliminates both introns and exons equally
D. Is carried out by a complex of small RNAs and proteins contained in the same pre-mRNA
E. Results in only one RNA being formed from one gene

**Answer: d**
**Explanation: Self-splicing (as in some pre-mRNAs, and generally spliceosomal splicing) is catalyzed by ribonucleoprotein complexes (snRNPs/proteins) intrinsic to the RNA-processing machinery; introns are removed and exons ligated.

---

**Q33. The nucleotide sequence that codes for the start of protein synthesis is:**
A. ATAATA or TATA box
B. AUGG or UAAG
C. The poly-A sequence
D. Basal promoter region or CAAT
E. Totally different for each protein

**Answer: a**
**Explanation: The TATA box (consensus ATAAAT/TATAAA) is the core promoter element marking the transcription start site region.

---

**Q34. Endoplasmic Reticulum-related ribosomes mainly synthesize:**
A. Neurotransmitters destined for packaging into secretory granules
B. Cholesterol and steroids
C. Structural proteins for unit membranes and lysosomal enzymes
D. Free proteins of the cytoplasm, such as haemoglobin and immunoglobulins
E. Signal Recognition Peptides to direct protein entry into the correct site on the ER

**Answer: c**
**Explanation: Rough ER-bound ribosomes synthesize proteins destined for membranes, lysosomes, secretion, and the ER/Golgi system (e.g. membrane and lysosomal enzyme proteins) — haemoglobin/immunoglobulins as noted are actually made on free/bound ribosomes for secretion but "structural proteins for membranes and lysosomal enzymes" is the classic RER product description.

---

**Q35. The one disease that is NOT a lysosomal storage disorder is:**
A. Fabry's disease
B. Pompe's disease
C. McArdle's disease
D. Von Gierke's disease
E. Tay-Sachs disease

**Answer: c**
**Explanation: McArdle's disease is a **glycogen storage disease (Type V)** caused by myophosphorylase deficiency, causing exercise-induced muscle cramping — it is not a lysosomal disorder. (Pompe's = lysosomal α-glucosidase deficiency; Fabry's and Tay-Sachs are lysosomal storage diseases; Von Gierke's, though a glycogen storage disease, was marked differently in this set — McArdle's is the standard "odd one out" as it is purely a metabolic enzyme defect unrelated to lysosomes.)

---

**Q36. The one disorder that is NOT a single-gene defect is:**
A. Sickle cell disease
B. Diabetes
C. Fabry's disease
D. Phenylketonuria
E. Down's syndrome

**Answer: e** (both b and e were marked; the canonical answer is Down's syndrome)
**Explanation: Down's syndrome results from **chromosomal trisomy 21**, not a single-gene mutation. (Type 2 diabetes is polygenic/multifactorial too, but the classic single best answer here is Down's syndrome as a chromosomal, not gene-level, defect.)

A. Body water
B. Ionic composition of extracellular fluid

**Q2. Select the statement that is NOT correct regarding the sensory system:**
A. Provides information about the environment
B. Changes raw energy into action potentials

A. Pain
B. Mechanical
C. Thermal

**Explanation: Pain is a *perceptual category/modality*, not a physical energy form (unlike mechanical, thermal, light/electromagnetic, and chemical energy).

B. Refers to the conditions within the cell

E. Refers to the conditions created by pathological processes within the body

**Explanation: As above — the internal environment is the extracellular fluid bathing the cells.

A. It amounts to about 60–66% of total body mass

**Answer: e**
**Explanation: Most body water is **intracellular** (~⅔ of TBW), not extracellular.

**Explanation: The basement membrane is an extracellular matrix structure supporting epithelium, not a specialized intercellular junction between cells.

E. Motor system

**Answer: d**
**Explanation: The autonomic nervous system provides motor control to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands of the viscera.

**Q8. What percentage of the cells of the brain are nerve cells?**
A. 10
B. 30
C. 50
D. 70
E. 90

**Answer: a**
**Explanation: Neurons make up only about 10% of brain cells; the remainder are glial cells (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells).

**Q9. Which of the following is NOT a hormone?**
A. Prolactin
B. Prolactin-inhibiting hormone
C. Thyroxine-binding globulin
D. Atrial natriuretic peptide
E. Cortisol

**Answer: c**
**Explanation: Thyroxine-binding globulin is a plasma **transport/carrier protein** for thyroid hormone, not a hormone itself.

**Q10. Where are the receptors for insulin located?**
A. In the pancreatic beta cells
B. In the blood plasma
C. On the target-cell membrane
D. In the target-cell cytoplasm
E. In the target-cell nucleus

**Answer: c**
**Explanation: Insulin is a peptide hormone that binds its receptor tyrosine kinase on the **plasma membrane** of target cells.

**Q11. The blood contained in a ventricle during isovolumetric relaxation is:**
A. The end-systolic volume
B. The end-diastolic volume
C. The stroke volume
D. The ejection fraction
E. None of these; the ventricle is empty then

**Answer: a**
**Explanation: Isovolumetric relaxation occurs immediately after systole, when the ventricle contains the residual (end-systolic) volume, before the mitral/tricuspid valves open for filling.

**Q12. Drugs that increase the heart rate have a ______ effect.**
A. Myogenic
B. Negative inotropic
C. Positive inotropic
D. Negative chronotropic
E. Positive chronotropic

**Answer: e**
**Explanation: Chronotropic effects relate to heart *rate*; a positive chronotropic drug increases heart rate (inotropic effects relate to contractile force).

**Q13. Deficiency of cobalamin (vitamin B₁₂) can arise from the following EXCEPT:**

**Answer: a**
**Explanation: Simple peptic ulcer disease does not typically impair B₁₂ absorption; atrophic gastritis (loss of intrinsic factor), ileal resection, and fish tapeworm (*Diphyllobothrium latum*, which consumes B₁₂) all cause deficiency.

**Q14. Which of the following haemoglobin forms has oxygen-carrying capacity?**
A. Carboxyhaemoglobin

**Explanation: Deoxyhaemoglobin (unbound Hb, iron still in Fe²⁺ state) retains the ability to bind and carry oxygen. Carboxy-, met-, and sulph-haemoglobin are all dysfunctional forms unable to carry O₂.

**Q15. One molecule of transferrin normally binds how many iron atoms?**
A. 4
B. 2
C. 6

E. 4500

**Answer: b**
**Explanation: Transferrin has two iron-binding sites and normally carries two Fe³⁺ ions per molecule.

**Q13. The following statements hold true about the "fluid mosaic" structure of the plasma membrane EXCEPT:**

**Explanation: Voltage-gated (voltage-dependent) ion channel permeability is the defining feature of excitable membranes, enabling action potential generation — a property non-excitable membranes lack (though they may still have RMPs and selective permeability).

**Q1.** A 62-year-old man has had dull, constant back pain for 3 months. He recently developed a cough productive of yellowish sputum. On physical examination there are crackles at the right lung base. A plain film radiograph of the spine reveals several 1 to 2 cm lytic lesions of the vertebral bodies. Labs: glucose 78, urea nitrogen 49, creatinine 5, total protein 8.3, albumin 3.7, alkaline phosphatase 176, AST 45, ALT 22, total bilirubin 1.2. Sputum culture grows Streptococcus pneumoniae. Which pathologic finding is most likely on bone marrow biopsy?
A) Scattered small granulomas
B) Nodules of small mature lymphocytes
C) Occasional Reed-Sternberg cells
D) Numerous plasma cells
E) Hypercellularity with many blasts
**Answer: D** — Multiple myeloma (protein/albumin gap, lytic bone lesions, renal failure from light chains, susceptibility to encapsulated organisms).

**Q2.** A 33-year-old woman has experienced low grade fevers, night sweats, and generalized malaise for the past 2 months. On physical examination she has non-tender cervical and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Cervical lymph node biopsy at high magnification shows occasional CD15+ and CD30+ Reed-Sternberg cells along with large and small lymphocytes and bands of fibrosis. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Burkitt lymphoma
B) Hodgkin lymphoma
C) Cat scratch disease
D) Mycosis fungoides
E) Multiple myeloma
**Answer: B** — Reed-Sternberg cells with CD15+/CD30+ markers are diagnostic of Hodgkin lymphoma.

**Q3.** A 17-year-old adolescent has had malaise for the past 3 weeks. He has mild pharyngitis on exam, plus tender axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. The spleen is palpable. CBC: Hgb 14.0, Hct 42.2%, MCV 90, platelets 301,300, WBC 8120 with 'atypical lymphocytes' on smear. His illness is most likely acquired via which mechanism?
A) Congenital genetic abnormality
B) From close contact on a date
C) As a result of an insect bite
D) Through an environmental exposure at work
E) Without any known etiology
**Answer: B** — Infectious mononucleosis (EBV), transmitted via saliva/close contact.

**Q4.** A 30-year-old woman has had mild fatigue for many years. Exam reveals a palpable spleen tip. Labs: Hgb 11.1, Hct 28.8%, MCV 77, platelets 229,000, WBC 7340, reticulocyte count 3.9%. Peripheral smear shows small RBCs lacking central pallor. Which inheritance pattern is most likely?
A) Autosomal dominant, European ancestry
B) Autosomal recessive, Asian ancestry
C) X-linked recessive, Middle Eastern ancestry
D) Autosomal recessive, West African ancestry
E) Sporadic occurrence
**Answer: A** — Hereditary spherocytosis, autosomal dominant, most common in Northern European descent.

**Q5.** A 3-year-old child has small pinpoint hemorrhages on the skin for the past 3 days. Vital signs normal. Petechiae over extremities and trunk. CBC: Hgb 14.3, Hct 43%, MCV 90, platelet count 19,300, WBC 9370. Resolves over the next month without treatment. Most likely antecedent event?
A) Acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) ingestion
B) Congenital HIV infection
C) Dietary cobalamin deficiency
D) Repetitive trauma
E) Respiratory syncytial virus infection
F) Sulfonamide ingestion
**Answer: E** — Acute (viral-triggered) immune thrombocytopenia, self-limited in children.

**Q6.** A 30-year-old man has had sore throat with fever for 5 days. Exam: mildly tender generalized cervical lymphadenopathy, enlarged erythematous tonsils with overlying exudate. Labs: Hgb 13, platelets 277,000, WBC 12,670 with differential 75 segs, 10 bands, 15 lymphs. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Lymphocytic lymphoma
B) Hodgkin lymphoma
C) Group A Streptococcus infection
D) Human immunodeficiency virus infection
E) Brucellosis
**Answer: C** — Exudative pharyngitis with neutrophilic leukocytosis and left shift = bacterial (strep) infection.

**Q7.** A 30-year-old man has had a progressively worsening productive cough for one month. Exam: small non-tender axillary lymph nodes, spleen tip palpable. Labs: Hgb 10.2, Hct 31.1%, MCV 90, WBC 67,000, platelets 36,000. Peripheral smear shows many blasts with Auer rods. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Leukemoid reaction
B) Acute myelogenous leukemia
C) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
D) Lymphoblastic leukemia
E) Leukoerythroblastosis
**Answer: B** — Auer rods are pathognomonic for AML.

**Q8.** A 68-year-old man has had malaise for the past year. No abnormal exam findings. Labs: Hgb 10.5, Hct 31.5%, MCV 88, platelets 211,000, WBC 6980. **Q9.** A 69-year-old man has noted several lumps on the right side of his neck for 5 months. Exam: firm, non-tender, movable lymph nodes in right posterior cervical region, no spleno/hepatomegaly. **Q10.** A 45-year-old man has had increasing abdominal discomfort with abdominal enlargement for two years. Exam: spleen felt below left costal margin, no fluid wave. Abdominal CT: massive splenomegaly (~3000g). Labs: Hgb 9, WBC 5,000, platelets 50,000. Most likely underlying condition?
A) Myelofibrosis
B) Sickle cell anemia

**Answer: A** — Massive splenomegaly from extramedullary hematopoiesis = myelofibrosis.

**Q11.** A 72-year-old man has had increasing fatigue for the past year. No abnormal exam findings. Labs: Hgb 9.1, Hct 27.9%, MCV 96, WBC 3700, platelets 125,000. A) Metastatic carcinoma
B) Chronic alcoholism
C) Malabsorption
D) Hemoglobinopathy
E) Chronic blood loss
F) Systemic lupus erythematosus
**Answer: A** — Leukoerythroblastic (myelophthisic) picture with immature myeloid/nucleated RBCs = marrow infiltration by metastatic tumor.

**Q12.** A 40-year-old woman has had a week-long course of fever and mental confusion. T 38.2°C, P 100, RR 22, BP 100/60. Widespread petechiae of skin/mucosa. Urea nitrogen 52, creatinine 5.3. A) Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy
B) Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
C) Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
D) Trousseau syndrome
E) Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia
**Answer: C** — Classic TTP pentad: fever, mental changes, renal failure, thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolysis; normal coagulation studies distinguish from DIC.

**Q13.** For the past 4 months, a 62-year-old previously healthy man has had increasing fatigue and shortness of breath with minimal exercise, abdominal discomfort. Exam: non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy, liver span 15 cm, palpable spleen 3 cm below costal margin. A) Leukemoid reaction
B) Chronic myelogenous leukemia
C) Acute myelogenous leukemia
D) Acute lymphocytic leukemia
E) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
F) Systemic lupus erythematosus
**Answer: E** — Marked mature lymphocytosis in an older adult, with organ infiltration (SLL component) and associated warm AIHA (positive Coombs) = CLL.

**Q14.** A 16-year-old boy has had low energy for as long as he can remember. Exam: palpable spleen tip. CBC: Hgb 8.8, Hct 24.1%, MCV 65, platelets 187,000, WBC 7400. Serum ferritin 3740. Bone marrow biopsy: myeloid:erythroid ratio 1:4, 4+ stainable iron. Most likely diagnosis?
A) G6PD deficiency
B) Beta-thalassemia
C) Sickle cell anemia
D) Hereditary spherocytosis
E) Malaria
**Answer: B** — Severe microcytosis with erythroid hyperplasia and iron overload from ineffective erythropoiesis = beta-thalassemia.

**Q15.** An 83-year-old woman fell and broke her left wrist; underwent ORIF. Postoperatively received heparin prophylaxis and diuretics. On admission: Hgb 13.2, platelets 209,000, PT 13s, PTT 28s. **Answer: D** — Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (platelet drop >50% within days of heparin exposure) with thrombotic complication (stroke).

**Q16.** A 48-year-old man has had increasing malaise and difficulty concentrating for 6 months. Exam: splenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, afebrile. **Q18.** A 55-year-old man has had fatigue, fever, and episodes of epistaxis for 3 months. T 37.4°C. Labs: Hgb 12.5, Hct 37.6%, MCV 89, platelets 170,000, WBC 52,000. Peripheral smear: large blasts with Auer rods. Which risk factor most likely preceded this illness?
