D) Iron deficiency
E) Von Willebrand factor deficiency
**Answer: D** — Severe microcytic anemia in a reproductive-age woman = iron deficiency (most common cause).

**Q21.** A 25-year-old man is given antimalarial prophylaxis before travel to West Africa. Over the next week he develops fatigue. No abnormal exam findings. Hct 30%. Smear: RBCs with numerous Heinz bodies. Family history shows males, not females, affected. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Beta-thalassemia
B) Sickle cell anemia
C) Alpha-thalassemia
D) Hereditary spherocytosis
E) G6PD deficiency
**Answer: E** — Heinz bodies + oxidative drug trigger (antimalarial) + X-linked male-only pattern = G6PD deficiency.

**Q22.** A study estimates spleen size by CT for adults with complications of hematologic disease. For which disease is the spleen most likely to remain normal in size?
A) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
B) Chronic ethanol abuse
C) Myeloproliferative disorder
D) Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
E) Sickle cell anemia
**Answer: D** — ITP causes platelet destruction without splenomegaly (unlike hemolytic/myeloproliferative causes).

**Q23.** A 51-year-old man has become increasingly fatigued for 10 months. No abnormal exam findings. Hgb 9.2, Hct 27.9%, MCV 132, platelets 242,000, WBC 7590. Most likely peripheral smear finding?
A) Hypersegmented neutrophils
B) Nucleated red blood cells
C) Blasts with Auer rods
D) Hypochromic, microcytic RBCs
E) Schistocytes
**Answer: A** — MCV 132 = severe macrocytosis, megaloblastic anemia causes hypersegmented neutrophils from delayed nuclear maturation.

**Q24.** A 72-year-old man has felt tired for 8 months. No abnormal exam findings. Hgb 10.4, Hct 30.3%, MCV 72, platelets 239,000, WBC 7500 (70.1% grans, 18.8% lymphs, 11.1% monos). Total bilirubin 1.0. Most likely smear finding?
A) Fragmentation
B) Many nucleated forms
C) Hypochromasia
D) Spherocytosis
E) Howell-Jolly bodies
**Answer: C** — Microcytic anemia in an older man is most probably iron deficiency, giving hypochromic RBCs.

**Q25.** A 19-year-old primigravida of Southeast Asian ancestry delivers at 35 weeks a male infant who is markedly hydropic. Hematocrit 17%. Smear shows numerous nucleated RBCs and erythroblasts, marked anisocytosis/poikilocytosis. Most likely disease in this infant?
A) Sickle cell anemia
B) Alpha-thalassemia
C) Hemoglobin E disease
D) G6PD deficiency
E) Hereditary elliptocytosis
**Answer: B** — Hydrops fetalis in a Southeast Asian infant = alpha-thalassemia major (Hb Barts), from complete loss of alpha-globin genes.

**Q26.** A 46-year-old man has had worsening arthritis and foot swelling for a year. Rales in all lung fields, chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema. Hgb 13.0, Hct 39.1%, MCV 86, platelets 255,500, WBC 5920. Serum iron 406, TIBC 440, ferritin 830. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Beta-thalassemia
B) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
C) Anemia of chronic disease
D) Polycythemia vera
E) Pernicious anemia
F) Hereditary hemochromatosis
**Answer: F** — Arthritis, cardiomyopathy, high iron/ferritin/saturation = systemic iron overload (hemochromatosis).

**Q27.** A 52-year-old man has had fever with cough for a month. Crackles in upper lung fields, chest X-ray shows reticulonodular pattern with upper lobe cavitary lesions. Sputum positive for acid-fast bacilli. CBC: Hgb 14.2, Hct 42.5%, MCV 92, platelets 225,000, WBC 44,500 (59 segs, 20 bands, 8 metas, 4 myelos, 2 promyelos, 5 lymphs, 2 monos). Which lab finding is most likely present?
A) High leukocyte alkaline phosphatase
B) Karyotype with 46, XY, t(9;22)
C) Monoclonal gammopathy
D) Elevated D-dimer
E) Positive TdT assay
**Answer: A** — Marked neutrophilia with a left-shifted but orderly maturation spectrum in the setting of active TB = leukemoid reaction, which shows high LAP (unlike CML, which is low).

**Q28.** A 5-year-old boy has become increasingly lethargic for 2 months. T 37.3°C, ecchymoses on lower legs. Hgb 9.2, Hct 27.8%, MCV 91, platelets 101,000, WBC 12,128. Bone marrow: ~100% cellularity, replacement by primitive cells with large nuclei, delicate chromatin, indistinct nucleoli, scant cytoplasm; cells mark for CD10 (CALLA). Most likely diagnosis?
A) Acute myeloid leukemia
B) Hodgkin lymphoma
C) Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
D) Epstein-Barr virus infection
E) Chronic myelogenous leukemia
F) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
**Answer: C** — CD10 (CALLA)-positive lymphoblasts replacing marrow in a child = ALL (common/CALLA subtype).

**Q29.** A 78-year-old woman has had increasing dyspnea for 2 weeks. Diffuse rales, scleral icterus. CBC: Hgb 7.1, Hct 22.2%, MCV 93, platelets 205,000, WBC 6500 (60 segs, 4 bands, 25 lymphs, 9 monos, 2 eos) with 10 nucleated RBCs/100 WBCs. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Iron deficiency anemia
B) Pernicious anemia
C) Anemia of chronic disease
D) Sickle cell anemia
E) Hemolytic anemia
**Answer: E** — Icterus, marked anemia with nucleated RBCs (high marrow erythroid output responding to destruction) = hemolytic anemia, here with high-output cardiac failure.

**Q30.** A 53-year-old man has had constant dull right lower back pain for 4 months. Tenderness on percussion of right costovertebral angle. CT: 6 cm mass in upper pole of right kidney. CBC: Hgb 21.3, Hct 64.0%, MCV 96, platelets 199,000, WBC 8230. Glucose 77, urea nitrogen 17, creatinine 1.1. Most likely cause?
A) Polycythemia rubra vera
B) Erythroleukemia
C) Hemophilia A
D) Diabetes insipidus
E) Increased erythropoietin
**Answer: E** — Renal mass + markedly elevated Hgb/Hct = paraneoplastic erythropoietin secretion from renal cell carcinoma (secondary polycythemia).

**Q31.** A 38-year-old woman has become increasingly fatigued for 3 months, purple blotches on skin for the past week. Purpuric areas on trunk/extremities, no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Hgb 6.8, Hct 20.7%, MCV 91, platelets 28,760, WBC 1940. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Aplastic anemia
B) Myeloproliferative disorder
C) Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
D) Large B cell lymphoma
E) Hereditary spherocytosis
**Answer: A** — Pancytopenia (anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia) without organomegaly = aplastic anemia (marrow failure of all three lines).

**Q32.** A 44-year-old man has noted a change in his facial appearance over 7 months. Facial skin thickened and reddened. Punch biopsy: infiltration by neoplastic CD4+ T lymphocytes. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Hodgkin lymphoma
B) Mycosis fungoides
C) Burkitt lymphoma
D) Acute lymphocytic leukemia
E) Hairy cell leukemia
**Answer: B** — Cutaneous CD4+ T-cell infiltration causing facial thickening/erythroderma = mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma).

**Q33.** A 49-year-old man has had increasing fatigue for 4 months. Massive splenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy. Hgb 10.1, Hct 30.3%, MCV 90, WBC 1600, platelets 48,000. Smear: increased lymphocytes containing tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP). Most likely diagnosis?
A) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
B) HTLV-1 infection with leukemia
C) Hairy cell leukemia
D) Gaucher disease
E) Myelodysplasia
**Answer: C** — TRAP-positive lymphocytes with massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia, no lymphadenopathy = hairy cell leukemia.

**Q34.** A 10-year-old girl has had increasing sluggishness with poorer school performance for a year, no increased infections, now headaches. No hepatosplenomegaly/lymphadenopathy. CBC: Hgb 11.8, Hct 33.9%, MCV 71, platelets 293,000, WBC 8160. Smear shows basophilic stippling. Serum haptoglobin 5. Which lab finding is most likely present?
A) Hemoglobin S on electrophoresis
B) Increased osmotic fragility
C) Positive direct antiglobulin test
D) Decreased serum iron
E) Elevated free erythrocyte protoporphyrin
**Answer: E** — Basophilic stippling + microcytic anemia + low haptoglobin (mild hemolysis) in a child with behavioral/school changes = lead poisoning; elevated free erythrocyte protoporphyrin reflects impaired heme synthesis.

**Q35.** A 2-year-old boy has had a seborrheic eruption over scalp/trunk for a month, then a right earache with erythematous bulging tympanic membrane. Hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy. Hgb 9.5, Hct 28.7%, MCV 90, platelets 58,000, WBC 3540. Bone marrow biopsy: 100% cellularity, extensive infiltration by CD1a+ macrophage-like cells with Birbeck granules on EM. Most likely underlying condition?
A) Myeloproliferative disorder
B) Plasmodium vivax infection
C) Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte depletion type
D) Langerhans cell histiocytosis
E) AIDS
**Answer: D** — CD1a+ cells with Birbeck granules = Langerhans cell histiocytosis (disseminated/Letterer-Siwe pattern in this infant).

**Q36.** A 73-year-old woman has had increasing fatigue with 3 kg weight loss over 7 months. Hands become purple/painful with cold exposure. Palpable spleen tip. Hgb 10.5, Hct 31.7%, MCV 99, platelets 193,600, WBC 5390. Direct Coombs positive at 4°C, negative at 37°C. Most likely underlying disease?
A) Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
B) Systemic lupus erythematosus
C) Pernicious anemia
D) Scleroderma
E) Thalassemia minor
**Answer: A** — Cold agglutinin disease (Coombs+ at 4°C only) with weight loss and splenomegaly points to an underlying B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder.

**Q37.** A 12-year-old girl has sudden onset severe abdominal and back pain. Diffusely tender abdomen, no masses, afebrile. CBC: Hgb 6.5, Hct 19.0%, MCV 99, platelets 149,000, WBC 11,200. Smear: nucleated RBCs and sickled RBCs. Which gene mutation type is most likely present?
A) Deletion
B) Duplication
C) Insertion
D) Missense
E) Nonsense
F) Splice site
G) Tandem repeat
**Answer: D** — Sickle cell disease results from a missense mutation (single amino acid substitution, valine for glutamic acid) in beta-globin.

**Q38.** A 32-year-old man has had worsening headaches for 2 months. Afebrile, no lymphadenopathy/hepatosplenomegaly. Hgb 12, platelets 250,000, WBC 6000. Head CT: 3 cm mass near lateral ventricle. Stereotactic biopsy shows diffuse large B cell lymphoma. Which lab finding is most likely present in this patient?
A) Elevated terminal deoxyribonucleotidyl transferase
B) Bence-Jones proteinuria
C) Elevated serum IgM
D) HIV-1 RNA of 80,000 copies/mL
E) Lymphoma positive for tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase
**Answer: D** — Primary CNS lymphoma (diffuse large B-cell) is classically associated with underlying HIV/AIDS.

**Q39.** A 28-year-old woman has had worsening fatigue for 2 months. Erythematous macular rash on chest, forearms, face. Hgb 9.2, Hct 27.9%, MCV 101, platelets 179,000, WBC 5850. RDW markedly increased, smear shows polychromasia, reticulocyte count 4.2%, haptoglobin 3. Total protein 7.9, albumin 3.8, alkaline phosphatase 49, AST 81, ALT 27, total bilirubin 3.3, direct bilirubin 0.8. Hemoglobinuria on urinalysis. Most likely underlying condition?
A) Multiple myeloma
B) Systemic lupus erythematosus
C) Hepatitis C infection
D) Hereditary spherocytosis
E) Vitamin B12 deficiency
**Answer: B** — Malar-type rash + hemolytic anemia with reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, hemoglobinuria (intravascular hemolysis) = SLE-associated warm AIHA.

**Q40.** A 37-year-old man with HIV for 10 years has had abdominal pain for 3 days. Abdominal distension, diffuse tenderness, absent bowel sounds. CT: mass lesion involving small intestine. Surgery removes an ileal obstruction; gross exam shows a near-encircling firm white mass 10 cm long, 3 cm deep, infiltrating the bowel wall. Most likely neoplasm?
A) Plasmacytoma
B) Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte predominant type
C) High-grade B cell lymphoma
D) Metastatic adenocarcinoma
E) Myeloproliferative disorder
F) Adenocarcinoma
**Answer: C** — Extranodal high-grade B-cell lymphoma of bowel is classic in longstanding HIV/AIDS.

**Q41.** A 20-year-old healthy man incurs blunt abdominal trauma in an MVA. Upper abdominal tenderness. CT shows splenic hematoma; splenectomy performed. Which peripheral blood finding is most likely present afterward?
A) Tear drop cells
B) Elliptocytes
C) Target cells
D) Macro-ovalocytes
E) RBC inclusions
**Answer: E** — Post-splenectomy, Howell-Jolly bodies and Pappenheimer bodies (RBC inclusions normally removed by the spleen) appear.

**Q42.** A 10-year-old girl has had increasing facial distortion for 8 months from a jaw lesion. Right mandibular mass. Biopsy shows a monotonous pattern of small non-cleaved lymphocytes; cytogenetics show t(8;14). Infection with which organism is most likely associated?
A) Adenovirus
B) Cytomegalovirus
C) Epstein-Barr virus
D) Hepatitis C virus
E) Herpes simplex virus
F) HIV
G) HTLV-1
**Answer: C** — t(8;14) MYC translocation with jaw mass in a child = Burkitt lymphoma (endemic African form), strongly EBV-associated.

**Q43.** Two teenage siblings have frequent nosebleeds and easy bruising from minor trauma, with menorrhagia since menarche, no prior family history. One girl's CBC: Hgb 14, Hct 42.3%, MCV 90, platelets 242,000, WBC 7720. PT 12s, PTT 25s. Platelet function studies show decreased aggregation in response to ADP, collagen, epinephrine, and thrombin. Most likely disorder?
A) Hemophilia A
B) Antithrombin III deficiency
C) Glanzmann thrombasthenia
D) Systemic lupus erythematosus
E) Von Willebrand disease
**Answer: C** — Normal platelet count with globally impaired aggregation to multiple agonists = Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GpIIb/IIIa defect).

**Q44.** A 47-year-old man has been chronically fatigued for a year. No abnormal exam findings. CBC: Hgb 10.8, Hct 33.1%, MCV 105, platelets 239,000, WBC 7720. Smear shows normal WBC morphology, mild poikilocytosis, a few target cells. Serum B12 and methylmalonic acid normal. Haptoglobin 151. Direct/indirect Coombs negative. Most likely underlying condition?
A) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
B) Peptic ulcer disease
C) Lead poisoning
D) Chronic alcohol abuse
E) Hereditary spherocytosis
**Answer: D** — Mild macrocytosis with normal B12/methylmalonic acid, target cells, no hemolysis = alcohol-related marrow/liver effect on RBC maturation, not megaloblastic anemia.

**Q45.** A 42-year-old man has had multiple painful red nodules from dermal venous thrombosis, plus abdominal pain from mesenteric vein thrombosis over the past year. He notes darker urine. Hgb 9.4, Hct 29.2%, MCV 100, platelets 215,000, WBC 8800. RBCs show increased sensitivity to complement lysis. Flow cytometry shows reduced CD55 on RBCs. Most likely diagnosis?
A) HIV infection
B) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
C) Acute myelogenous leukemia
D) Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
E) Langerhans cell histiocytosis
**Answer: D** — Unusual-site venous thrombosis + hemoglobinuria + reduced CD55/CD59 (complement regulatory proteins) = PNH (PIGA gene mutation).

Q.

**Q1.** A 62-year-old man has had dull, constant back pain for 3 months. He recently developed a cough productive of yellowish sputum. On physical examination there are crackles at the right lung base. A plain film radiograph of the spine reveals several 1 to 2 cm lytic lesions of the vertebral bodies. Labs: glucose 78, urea nitrogen 49, creatinine 5, total protein 8.3, albumin 3.7, alkaline phosphatase 176, AST 45, ALT 22, total bilirubin 1.2. Sputum culture grows Streptococcus pneumoniae. Which pathologic finding is most likely on bone marrow biopsy?
A) Scattered small granulomas
B) Nodules of small mature lymphocytes
C) Occasional Reed-Sternberg cells
D) Numerous plasma cells
E) Hypercellularity with many blasts
**Answer: D** — Multiple myeloma (protein/albumin gap, lytic bone lesions, renal failure from light chains, susceptibility to encapsulated organisms).

**Q2.** A 33-year-old woman has experienced low grade fevers, night sweats, and generalized malaise for the past 2 months. On physical examination she has non-tender cervical and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Cervical lymph node biopsy at high magnification shows occasional CD15+ and CD30+ Reed-Sternberg cells along with large and small lymphocytes and bands of fibrosis. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Burkitt lymphoma
B) Hodgkin lymphoma
C) Cat scratch disease
D) Mycosis fungoides
E) Multiple myeloma
**Answer: B** — Reed-Sternberg cells with CD15+/CD30+ markers are diagnostic of Hodgkin lymphoma.

**Q3.** A 17-year-old adolescent has had malaise for the past 3 weeks. He has mild pharyngitis on exam, plus tender axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. The spleen is palpable. CBC: Hgb 14.0, Hct 42.2%, MCV 90, platelets 301,300, WBC 8120 with 'atypical lymphocytes' on smear. His illness is most likely acquired via which mechanism?
A) Congenital genetic abnormality
B) From close contact on a date
C) As a result of an insect bite
D) Through an environmental exposure at work
E) Without any known etiology
**Answer: B** — Infectious mononucleosis (EBV), transmitted via saliva/close contact.

**Q4.** A 30-year-old woman has had mild fatigue for many years. Exam reveals a palpable spleen tip. Labs: Hgb 11.1, Hct 28.8%, MCV 77, platelets 229,000, WBC 7340, reticulocyte count 3.9%. Peripheral smear shows small RBCs lacking central pallor. Which inheritance pattern is most likely?
A) Autosomal dominant, European ancestry
B) Autosomal recessive, Asian ancestry
C) X-linked recessive, Middle Eastern ancestry
D) Autosomal recessive, West African ancestry
E) Sporadic occurrence
**Answer: A** — Hereditary spherocytosis, autosomal dominant, most common in Northern European descent.

**Q5.** A 3-year-old child has small pinpoint hemorrhages on the skin for the past 3 days. Vital signs normal. Petechiae over extremities and trunk. CBC: Hgb 14.3, Hct 43%, MCV 90, platelet count 19,300, WBC 9370. Resolves over the next month without treatment. Most likely antecedent event?
A) Acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) ingestion
B) Congenital HIV infection
C) Dietary cobalamin deficiency
D) Repetitive trauma
E) Respiratory syncytial virus infection
F) Sulfonamide ingestion
**Answer: E** — Acute (viral-triggered) immune thrombocytopenia, self-limited in children.

**Q6.** A 30-year-old man has had sore throat with fever for 5 days. Exam: mildly tender generalized cervical lymphadenopathy, enlarged erythematous tonsils with overlying exudate. Labs: Hgb 13, platelets 277,000, WBC 12,670 with differential 75 segs, 10 bands, 15 lymphs. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Lymphocytic lymphoma
B) Hodgkin lymphoma
C) Group A Streptococcus infection
D) Human immunodeficiency virus infection
E) Brucellosis
**Answer: C** — Exudative pharyngitis with neutrophilic leukocytosis and left shift = bacterial (strep) infection.

**Q7.** A 30-year-old man has had a progressively worsening productive cough for one month. Exam: small non-tender axillary lymph nodes, spleen tip palpable. Labs: Hgb 10.2, Hct 31.1%, MCV 90, WBC 67,000, platelets 36,000. Peripheral smear shows many blasts with Auer rods. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Leukemoid reaction
B) Acute myelogenous leukemia
C) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
D) Lymphoblastic leukemia
E) Leukoerythroblastosis
**Answer: B** — Auer rods are pathognomonic for AML.

**Q8.** A 68-year-old man has had malaise for the past year. No abnormal exam findings. Labs: Hgb 10.5, Hct 31.5%, MCV 88, platelets 211,000, WBC 6980. Total serum iron 130, TIBC 230, soluble serum transferrin receptor normal. Bone marrow biopsy: normal maturation in all cell lines, no abnormal cells, increased stainable iron. Most likely underlying disease?
A) Diverticulosis
B) Hepatitis C infection
C) Systemic lupus erythematosus
D) Atrophic gastritis
E) Fanconi anemia
**Answer: B** — Increased marrow iron stores with normal/high saturation = anemia of chronic disease from chronic infection.

**Q9.** A 69-year-old man has noted several lumps on the right side of his neck for 5 months. Exam: firm, non-tender, movable lymph nodes in right posterior cervical region, no spleno/hepatomegaly. Labs: Hgb 11.3, Hct 40%, MCV 87, platelets 256,000, WBC 7230. Cervical lymph node biopsy shows numerous crowded nodules of small, monomorphic lymphocytes. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
B) Follicular lymphoma
C) Infectious mononucleosis
D) Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte predominance type
E) Reactive hyperplasia
**Answer: B** — Nodular pattern of small monomorphic lymphocytes = follicular lymphoma.

**Q10.** A 45-year-old man has had increasing abdominal discomfort with abdominal enlargement for two years. Exam: spleen felt below left costal margin, no fluid wave. Abdominal CT: massive splenomegaly (~3000g). Labs: Hgb 9, WBC 5,000, platelets 50,000. Most likely underlying condition?
A) Myelofibrosis
B) Sickle cell anemia
C) Portal hypertension
D) Infectious mononucleosis
E) Hemochromatosis
**Answer: A** — Massive splenomegaly from extramedullary hematopoiesis = myelofibrosis.

**Q11.** A 72-year-old man has had increasing fatigue for the past year. No abnormal exam findings. Labs: Hgb 9.1, Hct 27.9%, MCV 96, WBC 3700, platelets 125,000. Differential: 53 segs, 5 bands, 2 metamyelocytes, 1 myelocyte, 32 lymphs, 7 monos, 5 nucleated RBCs/100 WBCs. Negative direct/indirect Coombs. Most likely disease?
A) Metastatic carcinoma
B) Chronic alcoholism
C) Malabsorption
D) Hemoglobinopathy
E) Chronic blood loss
F) Systemic lupus erythematosus
**Answer: A** — Leukoerythroblastic (myelophthisic) picture with immature myeloid/nucleated RBCs = marrow infiltration by metastatic tumor.

**Q12.** A 40-year-old woman has had a week-long course of fever and mental confusion. T 38.2°C, P 100, RR 22, BP 100/60. Widespread petechiae of skin/mucosa. Urea nitrogen 52, creatinine 5.3. Hgb 12.2, Hct 36.8%, MCV 93, platelets 19,000, WBC 8180. Schistocytes on smear. PT, PTT, D-dimer not elevated. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy
B) Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
C) Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
D) Trousseau syndrome
E) Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia
**Answer: C** — Classic TTP pentad: fever, mental changes, renal failure, thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolysis; normal coagulation studies distinguish from DI
C.

**Q13.** For the past 4 months, a 62-year-old previously healthy man has had increasing fatigue and shortness of breath with minimal exercise, abdominal discomfort. Exam: non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy, liver span 15 cm, palpable spleen 3 cm below costal margin. CBC: WBC 23,100 (16 segs, 2 bands, 78 lymphs, 4 monos), Hgb 11.9, Hct 36%, MCV 90, platelets 277,300. Direct Coombs positive. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Leukemoid reaction
B) Chronic myelogenous leukemia
C) Acute myelogenous leukemia
D) Acute lymphocytic leukemia
E) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
F) Systemic lupus erythematosus
**Answer: E** — Marked mature lymphocytosis in an older adult, with organ infiltration (SLL component) and associated warm AIHA (positive Coombs) = CLL.

**Q14.** A 16-year-old boy has had low energy for as long as he can remember. Exam: palpable spleen tip. CBC: Hgb 8.8, Hct 24.1%, MCV 65, platelets 187,000, WBC 7400. Serum ferritin 3740. Bone marrow biopsy: myeloid:erythroid ratio 1:4, 4+ stainable iron. Most likely diagnosis?
A) G6PD deficiency
B) Beta-thalassemia
C) Sickle cell anemia
D) Hereditary spherocytosis
E) Malaria
**Answer: B** — Severe microcytosis with erythroid hyperplasia and iron overload from ineffective erythropoiesis = beta-thalassemia.

**Q15.** An 83-year-old woman fell and broke her left wrist; underwent ORIF. Postoperatively received heparin prophylaxis and diuretics. On admission: Hgb 13.2, platelets 209,000, PT 13s, PTT 28s. One week later: Hgb 13, platelets 101,000, PT 12s, PTT 27s. She suddenly developed difficulty moving her right arm. Most likely cause?
A) Hypersplenism
B) Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
C) Disseminated intravascular coagulation
D) Drug-induced thrombocytopenia
E) Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
**Answer: D** — Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (platelet drop >50% within days of heparin exposure) with thrombotic complication (stroke).

**Q16.** A 48-year-old man has had increasing malaise and difficulty concentrating for 6 months. Exam: splenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, afebrile. Labs: Hgb 12.0, Hct 35.8%, MCV 92, platelets 390,000, WBC 190,000 (73 segs, 12 bands, 6 metamyelocytes, 2 myelocytes, 2 myeloblasts, 5 lymphs). LAP score very low. Bone marrow biopsy — most likely finding?
A) Sheets of plasma cells
B) Atypical cytokeratin positive glands
C) Numerous mature and immature myeloid cells
D) Predominance of adipocytes
E) Granulomas with acid-fast bacilli
**Answer: C** — Full myeloid maturation spectrum with low LAP score = chronic myelogenous leukemia.

**Q17.** A 29-year-old woman has sudden onset fever, abdominal pain, tachycardia, nausea. Conjunctivae icteric. Spleen tip palpable. Labs: Hgb 9.0, Hct 27.3%, MCV 99, platelets 209,500, WBC 6840. Reticulocyte count 0.1%. Smear: RBCs small, lacking central pallor. Most likely trigger for this acute illness?
A) Quinacrine use
B) Parvovirus infection
C) Decreased oxygen tension
D) Exposure to cold
E) Transfusion therapy
**Answer: B** — Aplastic crisis (sudden reticulocytopenia) in a patient with underlying hereditary spherocytosis, triggered by Parvovirus B19.

**Q18.** A 55-year-old man has had fatigue, fever, and episodes of epistaxis for 3 months. T 37.4°
C. Labs: Hgb 12.5, Hct 37.6%, MCV 89, platelets 170,000, WBC 52,000. Peripheral smear: large blasts with Auer rods. Which risk factor most likely preceded this illness?
A) Malaria
B) Infectious mononucleosis
C) Diabetes mellitus
D) Beta-thalassemia
E) Myelodysplasia
**Answer: E** — AML frequently arises from antecedent myelodysplastic syndrome.

**Q19.** A 42-year-old woman has noticed minor bumps produce major bruises for the past month. Purpura on arms/legs, afebrile. PT 12.9s (control 13), PTT 26.2s (control 25). CBC: Hgb 11.1, Hct 33.1%, MCV 84, platelets 790,000, WBC 45,400. Bone marrow: hypercellularity with myeloid and megakaryocytic hyperplasia. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Epstein-Barr virus infection
B) Myeloproliferative disorder
C) Drug reaction to recent antibiotic therapy
D) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
E) Megaloblastic anemia
**Answer: B** — High platelet count with bruising (functionally abnormal platelets) plus myeloid/megakaryocytic marrow hyperplasia = myeloproliferative disorder.

**Q20.** A 20-year-old woman has had worsening fatigue for the past year. Pale mucous membranes, no hepatosplenomegaly. CBC: Hgb 7.1, Hct 19.9%, MCV 67, platelets 190,000, WBC 5,400. No drug history. Most likely etiology?
A) Cobalamin deficiency
B) G6PD deficiency
C) Folate deficiency
D) Iron deficiency
E) Von Willebrand factor deficiency
**Answer: D** — Severe microcytic anemia in a reproductive-age woman = iron deficiency (most common cause).

**Q21.** A 25-year-old man is given antimalarial prophylaxis before travel to West Africa. Over the next week he develops fatigue. No abnormal exam findings. Hct 30%. Smear: RBCs with numerous Heinz bodies. Family history shows males, not females, affected. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Beta-thalassemia
B) Sickle cell anemia
C) Alpha-thalassemia
D) Hereditary spherocytosis
E) G6PD deficiency
**Answer: E** — Heinz bodies + oxidative drug trigger (antimalarial) + X-linked male-only pattern = G6PD deficiency.

**Q22.** A study estimates spleen size by CT for adults with complications of hematologic disease. For which disease is the spleen most likely to remain normal in size?
A) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
B) Chronic ethanol abuse
C) Myeloproliferative disorder
D) Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
E) Sickle cell anemia
**Answer: D** — ITP causes platelet destruction without splenomegaly (unlike hemolytic/myeloproliferative causes).

**Q23.** A 51-year-old man has become increasingly fatigued for 10 months. No abnormal exam findings. Hgb 9.2, Hct 27.9%, MCV 132, platelets 242,000, WBC 7590. Most likely peripheral smear finding?
A) Hypersegmented neutrophils
B) Nucleated red blood cells
C) Blasts with Auer rods
D) Hypochromic, microcytic RBCs
E) Schistocytes
**Answer: A** — MCV 132 = severe macrocytosis, megaloblastic anemia causes hypersegmented neutrophils from delayed nuclear maturation.

**Q24.** A 72-year-old man has felt tired for 8 months. No abnormal exam findings. Hgb 10.4, Hct 30.3%, MCV 72, platelets 239,000, WBC 7500 (70.1% grans, 18.8% lymphs, 11.1% monos). Total bilirubin 1.0. Most likely smear finding?
A) Fragmentation
B) Many nucleated forms
C) Hypochromasia
D) Spherocytosis
E) Howell-Jolly bodies
**Answer: C** — Microcytic anemia in an older man is most probably iron deficiency, giving hypochromic RBCs.

**Q25.** A 19-year-old primigravida of Southeast Asian ancestry delivers at 35 weeks a male infant who is markedly hydropic. Hematocrit 17%. Smear shows numerous nucleated RBCs and erythroblasts, marked anisocytosis/poikilocytosis. Most likely disease in this infant?
A) Sickle cell anemia
B) Alpha-thalassemia
C) Hemoglobin E disease
D) G6PD deficiency
E) Hereditary elliptocytosis
**Answer: B** — Hydrops fetalis in a Southeast Asian infant = alpha-thalassemia major (Hb Barts), from complete loss of alpha-globin genes.

**Q26.** A 46-year-old man has had worsening arthritis and foot swelling for a year. Rales in all lung fields, chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema. Hgb 13.0, Hct 39.1%, MCV 86, platelets 255,500, WBC 5920. Serum iron 406, TIBC 440, ferritin 830. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Beta-thalassemia
B) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
C) Anemia of chronic disease
D) Polycythemia vera
E) Pernicious anemia
F) Hereditary hemochromatosis
**Answer: F** — Arthritis, cardiomyopathy, high iron/ferritin/saturation = systemic iron overload (hemochromatosis).

**Q27.** A 52-year-old man has had fever with cough for a month. Crackles in upper lung fields, chest X-ray shows reticulonodular pattern with upper lobe cavitary lesions. Sputum positive for acid-fast bacilli. CBC: Hgb 14.2, Hct 42.5%, MCV 92, platelets 225,000, WBC 44,500 (59 segs, 20 bands, 8 metas, 4 myelos, 2 promyelos, 5 lymphs, 2 monos). Which lab finding is most likely present?
A) High leukocyte alkaline phosphatase
B) Karyotype with 46, XY, t(9;22)
C) Monoclonal gammopathy
D) Elevated D-dimer
E) Positive TdT assay
**Answer: A** — Marked neutrophilia with a left-shifted but orderly maturation spectrum in the setting of active TB = leukemoid reaction, which shows high LAP (unlike CML, which is low).

**Q28.** A 5-year-old boy has become increasingly lethargic for 2 months. T 37.3°C, ecchymoses on lower legs. Hgb 9.2, Hct 27.8%, MCV 91, platelets 101,000, WBC 12,128. Bone marrow: ~100% cellularity, replacement by primitive cells with large nuclei, delicate chromatin, indistinct nucleoli, scant cytoplasm; cells mark for CD10 (CALLA). Most likely diagnosis?
A) Acute myeloid leukemia
B) Hodgkin lymphoma
C) Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
D) Epstein-Barr virus infection
E) Chronic myelogenous leukemia
F) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
**Answer: C** — CD10 (CALLA)-positive lymphoblasts replacing marrow in a child = ALL (common/CALLA subtype).

**Q29.** A 78-year-old woman has had increasing dyspnea for 2 weeks. Diffuse rales, scleral icterus. CBC: Hgb 7.1, Hct 22.2%, MCV 93, platelets 205,000, WBC 6500 (60 segs, 4 bands, 25 lymphs, 9 monos, 2 eos) with 10 nucleated RBCs/100 WBCs. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Iron deficiency anemia
B) Pernicious anemia
C) Anemia of chronic disease
D) Sickle cell anemia
E) Hemolytic anemia
**Answer: E** — Icterus, marked anemia with nucleated RBCs (high marrow erythroid output responding to destruction) = hemolytic anemia, here with high-output cardiac failure.

**Q30.** A 53-year-old man has had constant dull right lower back pain for 4 months. Tenderness on percussion of right costovertebral angle. CT: 6 cm mass in upper pole of right kidney. CBC: Hgb 21.3, Hct 64.0%, MCV 96, platelets 199,000, WBC 8230. Glucose 77, urea nitrogen 17, creatinine 1.1. Most likely cause?
A) Polycythemia rubra vera
B) Erythroleukemia
C) Hemophilia A
D) Diabetes insipidus
E) Increased erythropoietin
**Answer: E** — Renal mass + markedly elevated Hgb/Hct = paraneoplastic erythropoietin secretion from renal cell carcinoma (secondary polycythemia).

**Q31.** A 38-year-old woman has become increasingly fatigued for 3 months, purple blotches on skin for the past week. Purpuric areas on trunk/extremities, no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Hgb 6.8, Hct 20.7%, MCV 91, platelets 28,760, WBC 1940. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Aplastic anemia
B) Myeloproliferative disorder
C) Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
D) Large B cell lymphoma
E) Hereditary spherocytosis
**Answer: A** — Pancytopenia (anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia) without organomegaly = aplastic anemia (marrow failure of all three lines).

**Q32.** A 44-year-old man has noted a change in his facial appearance over 7 months. Facial skin thickened and reddened. Punch biopsy: infiltration by neoplastic CD4+ T lymphocytes. Most likely diagnosis?
A) Hodgkin lymphoma
B) Mycosis fungoides
C) Burkitt lymphoma
D) Acute lymphocytic leukemia
E) Hairy cell leukemia
**Answer: B** — Cutaneous CD4+ T-cell infiltration causing facial thickening/erythroderma = mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma).

**Q33.** A 49-year-old man has had increasing fatigue for 4 months. Massive splenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy. Hgb 10.1, Hct 30.3%, MCV 90, WBC 1600, platelets 48,000. Smear: increased lymphocytes containing tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP). Most likely diagnosis?
A) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
B) HTLV-1 infection with leukemia
C) Hairy cell leukemia
D) Gaucher disease
E) Myelodysplasia
**Answer: C** — TRAP-positive lymphocytes with massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia, no lymphadenopathy = hairy cell leukemia.

**Q34.** A 10-year-old girl has had increasing sluggishness with poorer school performance for a year, no increased infections, now headaches. No hepatosplenomegaly/lymphadenopathy. CBC: Hgb 11.8, Hct 33.9%, MCV 71, platelets 293,000, WBC 8160. Smear shows basophilic stippling. Serum haptoglobin 5. Which lab finding is most likely present?
A) Hemoglobin S on electrophoresis
B) Increased osmotic fragility
C) Positive direct antiglobulin test
D) Decreased serum iron
E) Elevated free erythrocyte protoporphyrin
**Answer: E** — Basophilic stippling + microcytic anemia + low haptoglobin (mild hemolysis) in a child with behavioral/school changes = lead poisoning; elevated free erythrocyte protoporphyrin reflects impaired heme synthesis.

**Q35.** A 2-year-old boy has had a seborrheic eruption over scalp/trunk for a month, then a right earache with erythematous bulging tympanic membrane. Hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy. Hgb 9.5, Hct 28.7%, MCV 90, platelets 58,000, WBC 3540. Bone marrow biopsy: 100% cellularity, extensive infiltration by CD1a+ macrophage-like cells with Birbeck granules on EM. Most likely underlying condition?
A) Myeloproliferative disorder
B) Plasmodium vivax infection
C) Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte depletion type
D) Langerhans cell histiocytosis
E) AIDS
**Answer: D** — CD1a+ cells with Birbeck granules = Langerhans cell histiocytosis (disseminated/Letterer-Siwe pattern in this infant).

**Q36.** A 73-year-old woman has had increasing fatigue with 3 kg weight loss over 7 months. Hands become purple/painful with cold exposure. Palpable spleen tip. Hgb 10.5, Hct 31.7%, MCV 99, platelets 193,600, WBC 5390. Direct Coombs positive at 4°C, negative at 37°
C. Most likely underlying disease?
A) Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
B) Systemic lupus erythematosus
C) Pernicious anemia
D) Scleroderma
E) Thalassemia minor
**Answer: A** — Cold agglutinin disease (Coombs+ at 4°C only) with weight loss and splenomegaly points to an underlying B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder.

**Q37.** A 12-year-old girl has sudden onset severe abdominal and back pain. Diffusely tender abdomen, no masses, afebrile. CBC: Hgb 6.5, Hct 19.0%, MCV 99, platelets 149,000, WBC 11,200. Smear: nucleated RBCs and sickled RBCs. Which gene mutation type is most likely present?
A) Deletion
B) Duplication
C) Insertion
D) Missense
E) Nonsense
F) Splice site
G) Tandem repeat
**Answer: D** — Sickle cell disease results from a missense mutation (single amino acid substitution, valine for glutamic acid) in beta-globin.

**Q38.** A 32-year-old man has had worsening headaches for 2 months. Afebrile, no lymphadenopathy/hepatosplenomegaly. Hgb 12, platelets 250,000, WBC 6000. Head CT: 3 cm mass near lateral ventricle. Stereotactic biopsy shows diffuse large B cell lymphoma. Which lab finding is most likely present in this patient?
A) Elevated terminal deoxyribonucleotidyl transferase
B) Bence-Jones proteinuria
C) Elevated serum IgM
D) HIV-1 RNA of 80,000 copies/mL
E) Lymphoma positive for tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase
**Answer: D** — Primary CNS lymphoma (diffuse large B-cell) is classically associated with underlying HIV/AIDS.

**Q39.** A 28-year-old woman has had worsening fatigue for 2 months. Erythematous macular rash on chest, forearms, face. Hgb 9.2, Hct 27.9%, MCV 101, platelets 179,000, WBC 5850. RDW markedly increased, smear shows polychromasia, reticulocyte count 4.2%, haptoglobin 3. Total protein 7.9, albumin 3.8, alkaline phosphatase 49, AST 81, ALT 27, total bilirubin 3.3, direct bilirubin 0.8. Hemoglobinuria on urinalysis. Most likely underlying condition?
A) Multiple myeloma
B) Systemic lupus erythematosus
C) Hepatitis C infection
D) Hereditary spherocytosis
E) Vitamin B12 deficiency
**Answer: B** — Malar-type rash + hemolytic anemia with reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, hemoglobinuria (intravascular hemolysis) = SLE-associated warm AIH
A.

**Q40.** A 37-year-old man with HIV for 10 years has had abdominal pain for 3 days. Abdominal distension, diffuse tenderness, absent bowel sounds. CT: mass lesion involving small intestine. Surgery removes an ileal obstruction; gross exam shows a near-encircling firm white mass 10 cm long, 3 cm deep, infiltrating the bowel wall. Most likely neoplasm?
A) Plasmacytoma
B) Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte predominant type
C) High-grade B cell lymphoma
D) Metastatic adenocarcinoma
E) Myeloproliferative disorder
F) Adenocarcinoma
**Answer: C** — Extranodal high-grade B-cell lymphoma of bowel is classic in longstanding HIV/AIDS.

**Q41.** A 20-year-old healthy man incurs blunt abdominal trauma in an MV
A. Upper abdominal tenderness. CT shows splenic hematoma; splenectomy performed. Which peripheral blood finding is most likely present afterward?
A) Tear drop cells
B) Elliptocytes
C) Target cells
D) Macro-ovalocytes
E) RBC inclusions
**Answer: E** — Post-splenectomy, Howell-Jolly bodies and Pappenheimer bodies (RBC inclusions normally removed by the spleen) appear.

**Q42.** A 10-year-old girl has had increasing facial distortion for 8 months from a jaw lesion. Right mandibular mass. Biopsy shows a monotonous pattern of small non-cleaved lymphocytes; cytogenetics show t(8;14). Infection with which organism is most likely associated?
A) Adenovirus
B) Cytomegalovirus
C) Epstein-Barr virus
D) Hepatitis C virus
E) Herpes simplex virus
F) HIV
G) HTLV-1
**Answer: C** — t(8;14) MYC translocation with jaw mass in a child = Burkitt lymphoma (endemic African form), strongly EBV-associated.

**Q43.** Two teenage siblings have frequent nosebleeds and easy bruising from minor trauma, with menorrhagia since menarche, no prior family history. One girl's CBC: Hgb 14, Hct 42.3%, MCV 90, platelets 242,000, WBC 7720. PT 12s, PTT 25s. Platelet function studies show decreased aggregation in response to ADP, collagen, epinephrine, and thrombin. Most likely disorder?
A) Hemophilia A
B) Antithrombin III deficiency
C) Glanzmann thrombasthenia
D) Systemic lupus erythematosus
E) Von Willebrand disease

**Q44.** A 47-year-old man has been chronically fatigued for a year. No abnormal exam findings. CBC: Hgb 10.8, Hct 33.1%, MCV 105, platelets 239,000, WBC 7720. Smear shows normal WBC morphology, mild poikilocytosis, a few target cells. Serum B12 and methylmalonic acid normal. Haptoglobin 151. Direct/indirect Coombs negative. Most likely underlying condition?
A) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
B) Peptic ulcer disease
C) Lead poisoning
D) Chronic alcohol abuse
E) Hereditary spherocytosis
**Answer: D** — Mild macrocytosis with normal B12/methylmalonic acid, target cells, no hemolysis = alcohol-related marrow/liver effect on RBC maturation, not megaloblastic anemia.

**Q45.** A 42-year-old man has had multiple painful red nodules from dermal venous thrombosis, plus abdominal pain from mesenteric vein thrombosis over the past year. He notes darker urine. Hgb 9.4, Hct 29.2%, MCV 100, platelets 215,000, WBC 8800. RBCs show increased sensitivity to complement lysis. Flow cytometry shows reduced CD55 on RBCs. Most likely diagnosis?
A) HIV infection
B) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
C) Acute myelogenous leukemia
D) Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
E) Langerhans cell histiocytosis
**Answer: D** — Unusual-site venous thrombosis + hemoglobinuria + reduced CD55/CD59 (complement regulatory proteins) = PNH (PIGA gene mutation).

## VECTOR CONTROL METHODS
1. Physical/Mechanical
- Screened windows/doors, mosquito nets, draining pools, clearing long grass, emptying containers
2. Biological
- Toxorhynchites larvae — prey on Anopheles/Culex/Aedes larvae
- Gambusia affinis (fish) — eats larvae
- Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), Bacillus sphaericus — bacterial larvicides
- Other natural predators
3. Genetic Engineering
- Sterile male technique
- Refractory vectors — gene modification blocks pathogen development → change in target site

**4. Chemical — LD50 classification:** 1–50 = extremely toxic, 50–500 = moderately toxic

| Class | Mechanism | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chlorinated hydrocarbons | Nerve poison, disrupts Na⁺ channels, lipid-soluble | DDT, Dieldrin, Endrin | Mostly banned — persistent, bioaccumulates |
| Organophosphates (OP) | Blocks cholinesterase | Malathion, Chlorpyrifos, Parathion, Diazinon, Dimethoate | Less persistent than organochlorines |
| Carbamates | Bind acetylcholinesterase (reversible) | Carbaryl, Propoxur, Bendiocarb | Lower toxicity, better than OPs on chronic exposure |
| Pyrethroids | Bind voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, delay inactivation | Permethrin (ITNs/LLINs), Deltamethrin | Rapid "knockdown" effect, safe outdoors |
| Insect Growth Regulators (IGRs) | Block chitin/sugar biosynthesis | Pyriproxyfen, Diflubenzuron | |
| Formamidines | Mimic octopamine, disordered neuronal excitation | Amitraz, Chlordimeform | Effective on resistant insects, mites/ticks |
| Avermectins | Inhibit nerve impulse transmission | Abamectin | Narrow spectrum; also anti-nematode |
| Neonicotinoids | Mimic nicotine, systemic + contact | Imidacloprid | Targets sucking insects |
| Miticides | Anti-mite | Bromopropylate, Cyhexatin, Tetradifon | |

**Application types:** contact poison, fumigant, systemic, stomach poison, respiratory poison

## KEY TERMINOLOGY
- **Anthropophilic** (human blood) vs **Zoophilic** (animal blood)
- **Endophagic** (feeds indoors) vs **Exophagic** (feeds outdoors)
- **Endophilic** (rests indoors) vs **Exophilic** (rests outdoors)
- **Autogenous** (eggs w/o blood meal) vs **Anautogenous** (needs blood meal)
- **Parthenogenesis** — asexual, no fertilization needed

---

## MOSQUITOES (Culicidae)

**Anopheles**
- Species: gambiae complex (supervector), funestus, arabiensis (zoophilic), melas, **stephensi** (supervector, Asia-origin, recently in Africa — heat/arid-tolerant, unlike native African species)
- Anthropophilic, endophagic, endophilic
- Life cycle: holometabolous (complete); optimal 25°C, 78% humidity
- Eggs: laid singly, float on surface
- Larvae: 4 instars (L1–L4), lie **parallel** to surface, breathe via body-side spiracles, feeding stage
- Pupa: comma-shaped, resting stage, emerges 2–3 days
- Adults rest at **45° angle**; males bushy/plumose antennae, females smooth/pilose
- Only females bite (anautogenous); males feed on sugar only; parthenogenesis possible
- **Vector:** Malaria (Plasmodium)
- **Control:** larvicides, Toxorhynchites (biological), refractory index/endosymbionts (genetic), draining, nets, IRS, trans-ovarian light traps, screening, cutting grass

**Culex**
- Species:
C. quinquefasciatus
- Exophagic, exophilic; feeds 3pm–6pm (nocturnal), diurnal feeding ~10am
- Breeds: contaminated water (sewage, drains)
- Eggs: laid simultaneously as a **raft**, float
- Larvae: siphon breathing, hang at **45° angle** (unlike Anopheles' parallel posture)
- Host detection: eyes + olfactory cues
- **Vector:** Wuchereria bancrofti (filariasis), Rift Valley fever, West Nile virus — transovarial transmission (adults emerge already infected)
- **Control:** sanitation/sewage systems, insecticide on larval habitats (7–10 days spray), light traps, wire mesh

**Aedes**
- Species: aegypti, albopictus
- Black with white spots, painful biters
- "Container breeders" — clean containers, tires, flower vases
- Bimodal biting: early morning + late evening; both sexes bite during oviposition
- **Vector:** Dengue, Chikungunya, Zika, Yellow fever, O'nyong-nyong, Japanese encephalitis; Rift Valley fever (mechanical); transovarial transmission of arboviruses
- **Control:** remove vegetation/containers, straighten rivers to increase flow, Bt insecticide, light traps, larvivorous fish

---

## SANDFLIES (Psychodidae: Phlebotominae)
- Old World: **Phlebotomus** (4 subgenera) | New World: **Lutzomyia** (e.g. L. umbratilis, Brazil) | **Sergentomyia** — zoophilic
- Distribution: worldwide — Mediterranean, Indian subcontinent, Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, Central/South America
- Breed: cracks, holes in ground, termite mound bases, chicken coops, animal burrows, rubbish heaps; need high humidity, can't survive desiccation
- Weak fliers, short mouthparts, bite exposed skin; anthropophilic; some autogenous
- Bimodal biting: early morning + early evening
- **Vector:**
 - L. donovani → visceral leishmaniasis
 - L. tropica → cutaneous leishmaniasis (Old World)
 - L. braziliensis complex → mucocutaneous leishmaniasis
 - Bartonella bacilliformis → Carrion's disease
 - Sandfly fever virus (Phlebovirus)
- **Control:** remove termite mounds, DEET/Picaridin, protective clothing, time outdoor activity, spray cracks/burrows, destroy rodent reservoirs

---

## BITING MIDGES (Ceratopogonidae) — "no-see-ums"
- Genera: Leptoconops (tropics), Culicoides (worldwide)
- Breed in wet mud/sand (fresh + salt water)
- Both diurnal + nocturnal, active in wind, exophagic/exophilic; some autogenous
- **Vector:** Mansonella ozzardi (filarial nematode); monkey = reservoir in Africa
- **Control:** hard to control with insecticide; avoid peak times, repellents, screens

---

## BLACK FLIES (Simuliidae)
- Genera: Simulium, Prosimulium, Cnephia
- Breed: riverbanks, fast-flowing, well-oxygenated water
- Both sexes feed on plant juices; females need blood for eggs; few autogenous
- Bimodal: early morning + early evening; exophilic/exophagic; bite head/arms more than legs
- **Vector:** Onchocerca volvulus → **river blindness (onchocerciasis)**; S. metallicum → Mansonella ozzardi (non-pathogenic)
- Bites cause bleeding → predispose to secondary bacterial infection
- **Control:** protective clothing, repellents, timing outdoor activity, insecticide on breeding/resting sites, larvicides (15–30 min), Bti, straighten rivers/remove obstructions

---

## HORSE FLIES / DEER FLIES (Tabanidae)
- Tabanus (horse fly — green head, breeds in swamps) | Chrysops (deer fly — yellow/brown) | Haematopota (clegs)
- Females feed by day in bright sunlight; locate host by sight + smell
- Purely exophagic **except** Chrysops silacea (attracted by darkness, hangs from objects)
- Painful bites (large mouthparts)
- **Vector:** Tabanus → Bacillus anthracis (anthrax), also implicated in Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme — primarily tick-borne); Chrysops silacea/dimidiata → **Loa loa** (West/Central Africa)
- **Control:** barriers, canopy traps, aerial sprays (dry season), drainage of larval habitat (costly), repellents, protective clothing

---

## TSETSE FLIES (Glossinidae)
- Sub-Saharan Africa, 15°N–20°S
- **Forest/Fusca group:** G. palpalis, G. tachinoides, G. fuscipes
- **Savanna/Morsitans group:** G. morsitans (most widespread), G. swynnertoni, G. pallidipes, G. longipalpis (smallest, causes dermatitis in Angola)
- **Riverine/Palpalis group:** G. palpalis, G. tachinoides, G. fuscipes
- **Reproduction:** adenotrophic viviparity (larviparous, unique) — larva nourished via milk gland, deposited in shaded soil/cracks (2.5cm deep), pupates immediately, adult emerges 4–5 weeks
- Both sexes feed on blood every 2–3 days; diurnal, sight-based host detection, attracted to dark moving objects; rest 23 hrs/day on vegetation
- **Vector:**
 - G. palpalis, G. tachinoides → T. b. gambiense (**West African/Gambian** sleeping sickness)
 - G. morsitans, G. swynnertoni, G. pallidipes → T. b. rhodesiense (**East African/Rhodesian** sleeping sickness)
- **Control:** barriers, aerial sprays, **Ngu traps**, bush/vegetation clearing along rivers, insecticides, sterile insect technique
- **Trap colours: black and blue**

---

## HOUSEFLIES & RELATIVES (Muscidae/Fanniidae)
- 5 genera: Musca domestica (housefly), Muscina stabulans (greater housefly), Stomoxys calcitrans (stable fly — biting), Fannia canicularis (lesser housefly), Fannia scalaris (latrine fly)
- Mechanical vectors — 3 transmission routes: body hairs/mouthparts, regurgitation on food, **defecation (most important)**
- Stomoxys bites → dermatitis, secondary bacterial infection
- Muscidae/Fanniidae → biologically transmit **Thelazia spp. (eyeworms)**; **Tabanus is the vector for Thelazia**
- **Control:** light-bulb traps, air curtains, source reduction (sealed garbage)

**Aedes trap colours: black and white**

## MYIASIS
Invasion of tissues/organs by fly larvae. Larvae feed on living tissue, dead tissue, or ingested food.

- **Accidental** — food contaminated with fly eggs/larvae (e.g. housefly); larvae may survive briefly in gut → diarrhoea, dysentery, abdominal pain, vomiting; no species truly adapted to this
- **Obligatory** — larvae must live in a live host for part of life cycle
- **Facultative** — normally free-living, attack carcasses but can infect living tissue

**Types by site:**
- **Urogenital** — flies attracted to dirty distal areas, eggs hatch, larvae enter urethra
- **Cutaneous/Dermal (furuncular)** — "creeping eruption," boil-like inflammation in wounds; remove larvae aseptically
- **Ophthalmic/Ocular** — eggs near dirty eyes; lacrimation, redness, pain; may need enucleation if damage severe; prevent with hygiene/eyewear
- **Nasopharyngeal** — via nose, larvae crawl to nasopharynx → tonsillitis
- **Intestinal** — via mouth, contaminated food swallowed

**Maggot therapy:** sterile Lucilia sericata larvae used to clean wounds (feed on dead tissue only)

## FLEAS
- Key genera: Xenopsylla cheopis, Ctenocephalides (felis/canis), Tunga penetrans, Pulex irritans
- **X. cheopis** → Yersinia pestis (plague), Rickettsia typhi (murine typhus)
- **Ctenocephalides** → intermediate host for Dipylidium caninum, Hymenolepis diminuta; also Bartonella henselae (cat scratch disease)
- **Tunga penetrans** ("jigger") → gravid female burrows into feet, deposits eggs in dermis
- **Pulex irritans** — human flea, causes allergic dermatitis
- Both sexes blood-feed
- **Life cycle:** eggs laid in host's dwelling/debris (sticky, fall off host) → larvae feed on organic matter + **partially digested blood meal** (regurgitated/faeces) essential for development → spin silken cocoon (covered in debris) → pupa (4–12 days, avg 7–8) → adult
- Movement: crawling on host; **resilin protein** in legs → powerful jumping
- Nuisance: bites on ankles/legs; dermatitis in hypersensitive people; inhaled faeces → allergy
- **Plague:** hunters handling infected wild mammals at risk
- **Murine typhus:** via rodent fleas, esp. X. cheopis
- **Tularemia** (Francisella tularensis) — transmissible via fleas
- **Control:** DEET on clothing, insecticidal dusts (carbaryl, pyrethroids, OPs) on rodent burrows/pets

---

## LICE
- 3 blood-sucking human types: **Body louse** (Pediculus humanus corporis), **Head louse** (P. humanus capitis), **Pubic/crab louse** (Pthirus pubis)
- Worldwide, linked to poor hygiene/dense slums
- **Pediculosis** — repeated saliva injection on biting → itchiness, dermatitis, possible asthma/bronchitis, secondary impetigo (contagious), fever from scratching
- **Body louse vectors:** Epidemic typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii), Relapsing fever (Borrelia recurrentis), Trench fever (Bartonella quintana) — all **transcutaneous**
- **Body louse control:** wash/iron/dry-clean clothing, permethrin-impregnated clothing, oral ivermectin
- **Head louse** → pediculosis capitis, can cause alopecia; control: combing, shaving, insecticidal shampoo
- **Nits (eggs):** body lice on clothing seams; head lice on hair shaft; **crab lice may lay on a single hair strand** — found on beard, armpits, occasionally chest hair
- **Crab lice** → pediculosis pubis, faecal deposits → small blue maculae; control: shave pubic hair, dusts/lotions, malathion (irritant), petroleum jelly on eyelashes (8–10 days)

---

## BEDBUGS (Cimicidae)
- Species: Cimex lectularius (tropical + non-tropical), Cimex hemipterus (Old/New World tropics), Leptocimex (mainly Africa)
- Rising infestations due to insecticide resistance + warmer climates
- Both sexes feed at night; hide by day under wallpaper, mattresses, wall cracks; rest in groups
- **Medical importance:** sleepless nights, iron deficiency in infants/children/elderly from repeated feeding, **associated with Hepatitis B** — but **no confirmed disease transmission** to humans
- **Control:** hot water wash, ironing/sun-drying, freezing (48hrs), insecticide dusting

---

## COCKROACHES (Blattidae)
- Genera: Blattella germanica (German), Blatta orientalis (Oriental), Periplaneta americana (American), Supella longipalpa
- **Mechanical vectors:** Shigella,
E. coli, Salmonella
- Ecdysis (molting) → allergic reactions/asthma; ~10% of non-asthmatics show cockroach allergy (sneezing, rash, sore eyes, respiratory distress, severe cases → shortness of breath)
- **Control:** IGRs, contact poisons (boric acid), spraying walls/floors, sanitation

## TRIATOMINE (KISSING) BUGS (Reduviidae)
- Genera: Triatoma (infestans, dimidiata), Rhodnius prolixus, Panstrongylus megistus
- **Vector:** Trypanosoma cruzi → **Chagas disease** (American trypanosomiasis)
- Mechanism: bug feeds then defecates near bite → faeces contain parasite (contamination, not bite itself)
- Heavy biting → anaemia; hypersensitivity → oedema, pruritus, erythema
- Prefer warm areas (chicken sheds, goat pens), dark hiding places
- **Control:** spraying interior wall/floor surfaces, reduce hiding places, fumigation

---

## TICKS

**General:** Arachnids — no antennae, chelicerate mouthparts, body = cephalothorax + abdomen, hemimetabolous (incomplete metamorphosis)

**ARGASIDAE (Soft ticks)**
- Genera: Ornithodoros (O. moubata), Argas
- Found in warm areas; **nidicolous** (stay in host's nest/dwelling)
- Multi-host tick; multiple nymphal stages (N1–N4, usually 4–5 instars)
- Feed briefly (hours) compared to hard ticks
- **Vector:** Borrelia duttoni → tick-borne relapsing fever; also other spirochetes, viruses; tick paralysis (saliva toxin)
- **Control:** DEET, permethrin-impregnated nets, acaricides on furniture/walls

**IXODIDAE (Hard ticks)**
- Genera: Dermacentor, Amblyomma, Haemaphysalis, Rhipicephalus, Hyalomma, Boophilus
- Worldwide, mostly temperate regions
- Non-nidicolous, **1 nymphal stage only**, stays on host longer than soft ticks
- **3-host tick:** each stage (larva/nymph/adult) feeds on a different host — Dermacentor, Amblyomma, Rhipicephalus, Hyalomma
- **2-host tick:** larvae molt to nymph on 1st host, nymph seeks 2nd host — Rhipicephalus, Hyalomma
- **1-host tick:** all stages on same host — Boophilus
- Larvae quest by climbing vegetation, waiting for host contact
- **Vector:** tick paralysis (breathing/swallowing/speech difficulty), Q fever, tick-borne encephalitis, poliomyelitis-like illness in allergic people, **Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi)**
- **Control:** DEET, regular acaricide dipping of livestock, garden spraying, proper tick removal, permethrin clothing
- **Why hard to control:** survive long periods without feeding, adapt to multiple host types

## MITES

**Sarcoptes scabiei (Sarcoptidae)** — causes **scabies** (humans) / **mange** (animals)
- Arachnid, no teeth on hypostome, has sensory setae
- Female burrows into skin, deposits eggs → narrow twisting tunnels (dark pepper-like tracks)
- Detection: ink test (smear + wipe reveals tunnels) or liquid tetracycline under UV (fluoresces yellow-green)
- **Classic scabies:** papular, non-painful rash — interdigital webs, wrists, elbows, armpits, genitals; never above the head; severe nocturnal pruritus, worse after hot bath; scratching → secondary infection
- **Crusted/Norwegian scabies:** highly contagious, huge mite burden, scaly/hyperkeratotic skin, diagnosed via skin scraping
- **Treatment:**
 - Permethrin 5% cream — 2 applications, wash off 8–12 hrs
 - Benzyl benzoate — wash after 24 hrs, reapply day 2–3
 - Crotamiton — 5 daily applications, safe in children/pregnancy
 - Ivermectin — single topical dose
- **Control:** treat whole household, disinfect bedding/clothes (hot wash, dry-clean, freeze 48hrs), antihistamines for itch

**Trombiculid (Harvest) mites**
- Species: Leptotrombidium deliense, L. akamushi, L. fletcheri, Eutrombicula alfreddugesi (red bug), Trombicula autumnalis (harvest mite)
- **Only larvae are parasitic** — attach to small mammals (rodents = key hosts); nymphs/adults free-living
- Humans = accidental hosts, aid larval dispersal
- **Vector:** Rickettsia tsutsugamushi/Orientia tsutsugamushi → **scrub typhus**
- Also cause intense itching/welts (nuisance)
- **Control:** DEET, benzyl benzoate, permethrin-impregnated clothing, burning scrub vegetation, aerial insecticide

## TRANSMISSION TYPES (high-yield distinction)
- **Cyclopropagative** — cyclic development **+** multiplication (e.g. malaria)
- **Cyclodevelopmental** — cyclic development only, **no** multiplication (e.g. filarial worms)
- **Propagative** — multiplication only, **no** development (e.g. plague in fleas)
- **Mechanical/Passive** — no biological development, fomite-like (e.g. houseflies)

## Section B — Essay (10 marks)

**Q1. Discuss yellow fever.**

**Model answer:**

**(a) Transmission and symptoms (4 marks)**

- Caused by yellow fever virus, a single-stranded RNA flavivirus
- Transmitted by the bite of an infected female Aedes aegypti mosquito (urban cycle); a sylvatic cycle also circulates between monkeys and Aedes or Haemagogus species
- Incubation period 3–6 days
- Phase 1 (acute infection): fever, chills, headache, myalgia and back pain, nausea, vomiting, dizziness
- Phase 2 (remission): symptoms subside for 24–48 hours
- Phase 3 (toxic phase, about 15% of cases): high fever returns with jaundice, abdominal pain, vomiting that may be bloody, bleeding from gums, mucous membranes and eyes, and renal failure; mortality in this phase reaches 50%

**(b) Diagnosis, with sources of confusion with other infections (3 marks)**

- Clinically confused with other causes of febrile jaundice: malaria, viral hepatitis A, B and E, leptospirosis, and other viral haemorrhagic fevers such as dengue, Lassa and Ebola
- RT-PCR detects viral RNA early in illness
- ELISA for IgM antibodies is useful later in illness
- Liver function tests show raised transaminases and bilirubin
- Viral isolation early in illness in specialised laboratories
- Co-infection or misdiagnosis with malaria and dengue is common in endemic tropical settings and delays correct management

**(c) Treatment and prevention (3 marks)**

- No specific antiviral; management is supportive
- Fluid and electrolyte replacement
- Antipyretics, avoiding aspirin and NSAIDs because of bleeding risk
- Blood transfusion for haemorrhage and dialysis for renal failure
- Intensive care support during the toxic phase
- Live attenuated 17D vaccine gives long-lasting, essentially lifelong immunity after a single dose
- Vector control: eliminate Aedes breeding sites and apply insecticides
- Personal protection with mosquito nets and repellents
- Mandatory vaccination certificate for travel to and from endemic zones

## Section B — Short Answer Questions (25 marks)

**Q1. Give reasons why Coccidioides immitis is not similar to any bacterium (5 marks)**

**Model answer:**

- It is a dimorphic fungus, existing as a mould with arthroconidia in soil and as spherules containing endospores in host tissue; bacteria show no such morphological switching
- It is eukaryotic, with a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, unlike prokaryotic bacteria
- Its cell wall is made of chitin and glucans, not peptidoglycan
- It reproduces by spores (arthroconidia and endospores) rather than binary fission
- It is susceptible to antifungals such as azoles and amphotericin B, not to antibiotics, because it lacks bacterial drug targets
- It is much larger and structurally more complex, with mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum

**Q2. Medical importance of ergot toxins from Claviceps purpurea (5 marks)**

**Model answer:**

- Ergot alkaloids cause ergotism after ingestion of contaminated grain, classically rye
- Gangrenous ergotism: severe vasoconstriction causing ischaemia of the extremities and gangrene
- Convulsive ergotism: CNS toxicity with seizures, hallucinations and muscle spasm
- Therapeutic uses: ergometrine and ergotamine control postpartum haemorrhage as uterotonics
- Ergotamine is used in migraine because of vasoconstriction of cranial vessels
- Historically the pharmacological precursor to LSD research
- Toxicity reflects vasoconstriction plus serotonin and dopamine receptor activity

**Q3. Targets in fungi for antifungal drug development (5 marks)**

**Model answer:**

- Membrane ergosterol: polyenes such as amphotericin B bind ergosterol and form pores; azoles inhibit lanosterol demethylase and block ergosterol synthesis
- Cell wall (1,3)-beta-D-glucan synthase: the echinocandin target, selective because human cells have no cell wall
- Nucleic acid synthesis: flucytosine is converted to 5-fluorouracil inside fungal cells and inhibits DNA and RNA synthesis
- Microtubule function: griseofulvin disrupts the fungal mitotic spindle
- Rationale: each target exploits structural or biochemical differences between fungal and human cells, such as ergosterol versus cholesterol

**Q4. General characteristics of herpesviruses (2 marks) and pathogenesis of HSV I and II (3 marks)**

**Model answer:**

- Enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses with an icosahedral capsid
- Establish latency after primary infection with potential for reactivation
- The family includes HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, CMV, EBV and HHV-6, 7 and 8
- HSV enters through mucosal surfaces or breaks in the skin
- Replicates locally in epithelial cells, producing vesicular lesions such as cold sores or genital ulcers
- Travels retrograde along sensory axons to the trigeminal or dorsal root ganglia
- Establishes lifelong latency in sensory ganglia: HSV-1 typically trigeminal, HSV-2 typically sacral
- Reactivation from stress, UV light, fever or immunosuppression sends virus back down the nerve to produce recurrent lesions near the original site
- HSV-1 is classically oral or facial and HSV-2 genital, although overlap occurs

**Q5. How viral receptors relate to epidemic and pandemic potential (5 marks)**

**Model answer:**

- Receptors determine tissue tropism, which cells and organs a virus can infect, and therefore the clinical picture
- Receptor conservation across species allows zoonotic spillover and raises pandemic potential
- Abundant receptors in the respiratory tract, such as ACE2 for SARS-CoV-2 and sialic acid for influenza, favour efficient airborne transmission
- Mutations in surface proteins such as influenza haemagglutinin alter receptor-binding affinity, enabling antigenic shift and drift with immune escape
- Ubiquitous receptor expression in the population enlarges the susceptible pool and speeds community spread
- Receptor binding also determines whether pre-existing immunity from prior exposure or vaccination protects against a new strain

## Section C — Long Answer Questions (choose 2, 20 marks each)

**Q1. Role of antifungal agents in the management of human fungal infections (20 marks)**

**Model answer:**

- Polyenes (amphotericin B, nystatin) bind ergosterol, form membrane pores and cause leakage and cell death; amphotericin B treats severe systemic mycoses such as cryptococcal meningitis and invasive candidiasis or aspergillosis, while nystatin is used topically or orally for thrush
- Azoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, ketoconazole) inhibit lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase and block ergosterol synthesis; used in candidiasis, cryptococcosis, dermatophytoses and histoplasmosis, with fluconazole widely used for maintenance therapy in HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis
- Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin) inhibit (1,3)-beta-D-glucan synthase and weaken the cell wall; active against Candida and Aspergillus and well tolerated because the target is absent in humans
- Flucytosine is converted intracellularly to 5-fluorouracil and inhibits fungal DNA and RNA synthesis; combined with amphotericin B in cryptococcal meningitis to limit resistance and toxicity
- Griseofulvin disrupts the fungal mitotic spindle and treats dermatophyte infection of skin, hair and nails
- Topical agents such as clotrimazole and terbinafine treat superficial mycoses
- Clinical role: they make life-threatening systemic mycoses treatable in immunocompromised patients, provide prophylaxis in high-risk groups, and combination therapy limits toxicity and resistance
- Choice of agent depends on the site of infection, the organism, the patient's immune status and the toxicity profile, for example amphotericin B nephrotoxicity

**Q2. Aetiology, transmission, pathogenesis and diagnosis of subcutaneous mycoses (20 marks)**

**Model answer:**

**Aetiology**

- Sporothrix schenckii causes sporotrichosis
- Madurella species and related fungi cause eumycetoma
- Fonsecaea and Cladophialophora species cause chromoblastomycosis

**Transmission**

- Traumatic inoculation of spores or hyphae into the skin from soil, plant material or thorns, classically a rose thorn injury in sporotrichosis
- Occupational exposure among gardeners, farmers and forestry workers
- No person-to-person transmission

**Pathogenesis**

- The fungus is introduced subcutaneously through a break in the skin
- Local proliferation forms a nodule or pustule that progresses to ulceration
- In sporotrichosis, spread along lymphatic channels produces a chain of subcutaneous nodules
- In mycetoma, grains form within tissue with chronic swelling, sinus tracts and discharging pus containing grains
- The infection is chronic and slowly progressive, usually remaining localised in immunocompetent hosts

**Diagnosis**

- Clinical examination of the characteristic lesion pattern and lymphatic spread
- Direct microscopy of exudate or tissue in KOH mount for grains or fungal elements
- Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar for definitive identification
- Histopathology of biopsy specimens with PAS or GMS stains
- Serology, used less often and mainly relevant to systemic mycoses

**Q3. Discuss yellow fever: transmission (8), symptoms (4), treatment (4), prevention (4)**

**Model answer:**

**Transmission**

- Yellow fever virus is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus
- Urban cycle: human to human via infected Aedes aegypti
- Sylvatic cycle: monkey to monkey via Aedes and Haemagogus species, with humans infected on entering forest habitat
- Intermediate savannah cycle occurs in African moist savannah
- Incubation period 3–6 days
- Endemic in tropical Africa and South America
- Not spread by direct person-to-person contact
- Risk rises with unvaccinated populations, urban mosquito breeding sites and travel

**Symptoms**

- Acute phase: fever, chills, headache, myalgia and back pain, nausea, vomiting
- Brief remission over 24–48 hours
- Toxic phase in about 15%: recurrent high fever, jaundice, abdominal pain, haematemesis, mucosal bleeding, renal failure
- Mortality up to 50% in the toxic phase

**Treatment**

- No specific antiviral; supportive care only
- Fluid and electrolyte replacement, antipyretics avoiding aspirin and NSAIDs
- Transfusion for haemorrhage and dialysis for renal failure
- Intensive care support in severe disease

**Prevention**

- Live attenuated 17D vaccine, single dose, long-lasting immunity
- Vector control by removing breeding sites and using insecticides
- Personal protection with nets and repellents
- International certificate of vaccination for travel to endemic zones

## Section B: Short Answer (Answer all — 25 Marks)- Highlight the use of Bti in control of vector-borne diseases. (5 Marks)
- Bti = Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis, a spore-forming bacterium
- Produces crystal (Cry) toxin proteins that are toxic specifically to mosquito, blackfly, and fungus gnat larvae
- Toxin must be ingested by the larva; activated by the alkaline larval gut environment
- Forms pores in the larval gut epithelium, causing cell lysis, gut paralysis, and larval death
- Highly target-specific (safe for humans, fish, and most non-target insects), making it an environmentally preferred larvicide for malaria/dengue vector control programs
-
---

- Describe IRS and its significance in control of vector-borne diseases. (5 Marks)
- IRS = Indoor Residual Spraying
- Involves applying long-lasting insecticide to the interior walls and ceilings of houses
- Targets endophilic (indoor-resting) vectors that land on treated surfaces after feeding
- Kills mosquitoes before they can survive long enough to transmit pathogens (extrinsic incubation period)
- A core pillar of malaria vector control programs globally, alongside insecticide-treated bed nets
- Significance: reduces vector density and longevity, interrupting disease transmission cycles at the community level
-
---

- Compare treponemal chancre and Haemophilus ducreyi chancroid. (5 Marks)
- Treponemal chancre (syphilis, Treponema pallidum): typically single, painless, indurated (firm) ulcer with a clean base
- Chancroid (H. ducreyi): typically multiple, painful, soft, ragged-edged ulcers ("soft chancre") with a purulent base
- Lymphadenopathy: syphilitic chancre has non-tender regional nodes; chancroid causes tender, sometimes suppurative (fluctuant) inguinal nodes ("bubo")
- Diagnosis: syphilis via darkfield microscopy/serology; chancroid via culture on special media (Gram stain shows "school of fish" pattern)
- Both are genital ulcer diseases but differ sharply in pain, number, and node characteristics — this comparison is a classic exam pairing
-

## Section B continued (Page 9)- Describe the pathogenesis of Clostridium botulinum. (5 Marks)
- Spores or preformed toxin ingested (foodborne), or spores germinate in wound (wound botulism) or infant gut (infant botulism)
- Toxin is a zinc metalloprotease
- Acts at the peripheral neuromuscular junction
- Cleaves SNARE proteins, blocking acetylcholine release
- Result: flaccid (descending) paralysis, starting with cranial nerves, progressing to respiratory muscles if untreated
-
---

- Classify Streptococcus based on hemolytic properties. (5 Marks)
- Alpha (α) hemolysis: partial/incomplete hemolysis, greenish discoloration on blood agar (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, viridans streptococci)
- Beta (β) hemolysis: complete hemolysis, clear zone around colonies (e.g., Streptococcus pyogenes/Group A, Streptococcus agalactiae/Group
B)

- Gamma (γ) hemolysis: no hemolysis, no change to blood agar (e.g., most Enterococcus species)
- This hemolysis classification is the first screening step in strep identification, followed by Lancefield grouping for definitive species-level classification

## Section C: Essay Questions (Answer only TWO — 40 Marks)- Using relevant examples, discuss biological control of vector-borne diseases. (20 Marks)
-
Suggested point structure:

- Definition: use of living organisms or their products to suppress vector populations, reducing disease transmission
- Larvivorous fish (e.g., Gambusia affinis) — predate on mosquito larvae in stagnant water
- Bacterial larvicides — Bti and Bacillus sphaericus, producing larvicidal crystal toxins
- Endosymbiont-based control — Wolbachia pipientis, inducing cytoplasmic incompatibility and reducing pathogen transmission capacity
- Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) — mass-release of sterilized males to reduce reproductive success
- Predatory insects/copepods — e.g., Mesocyclops species preying on mosquito larvae
- Fungal biopesticides — e.g., Beauveria bassiana, Metarhizium species, infecting and killing adult mosquitoes
- Advantages: environmentally sustainable, reduced insecticide resistance pressure, target specificity
- Limitations: slower acting than chemical control, environmental/ecological considerations, cost of production and distribution

- HIV/TB Case Essay — 33-year-old male, weight loss, cough with rust-colored sputum, HIV-positive (20 Marks)
a) Why a chest X-ray was ordered:

- To evaluate for pulmonary infiltrates, cavitation, or other findings suggestive of active pulmonary tuberculosis, given the chronic cough, weight loss, and fever
b) Why a sputum sample was taken:

- To perform acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear microscopy and culture, confirming active Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and assessing infectiousness

c) What a positive tuberculin skin test looks like:
- A firm, raised induration (not just redness) at the injection site
- Measured in millimeters of induration 48-72 hours after placement
- Positivity threshold varies by risk category (e.g., ≥5mm in immunocompromised/HIV patients, ≥10-15mm in lower-risk groups)
d) What such a result indicates:

- Prior exposure/sensitization to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens (latent or active infection)
- Does NOT distinguish between latent infection and active disease — requires clinical/radiographic/microbiological correlation

E. Use of separate towels
Answer: B
Explanation: Self-treating with over-the-counter medication is not a recognized preventive strategy — UTIs require proper diagnosis and prescribed antibiotics; OTC "cures" are not clinically validated prevention methods.

34. Clostridium botulinum-associated foodborne illness may occur within 18-24 hours of ingestion. Which of the following are NOT common symptoms of the illness?
A. Poor vision

Answer: B, E

## Section B: Short Answer (Answer all — 25 Marks)
37. Using relevant examples, describe maggot therapy. (5 Marks)
- Maggot (larval) debridement therapy uses sterile fly larvae (typically Lucilia sericata, the green bottle fly) applied to chronic, non-healing wounds
- Larvae selectively consume necrotic/dead tissue while sparing healthy tissue
- Larval secretions contain proteolytic enzymes that liquefy dead tissue for ingestion
- Secretions also have antimicrobial properties, helping reduce bacterial load in the wound
- Used clinically for diabetic ulcers, pressure sores, and other wounds resistant to conventional debridement
---
38. Giving examples, write short notes on refractory vectors in control of vector-borne diseases. (5 Marks)
- Refractory vectors are insects genetically or biologically modified/manipulated so they cannot support pathogen development or transmission
- Achieved through endosymbiotic bacteria such as Wolbachia pipientis, which interferes with pathogen replication inside the mosquito
- Paratransgenesis — using engineered symbiotic bacteria (e.g., Sodalis glossinidius in tsetse flies) to express anti-pathogen molecules
- Genetic modification of vector genomes directly to block pathogen development (e.g., malaria-refractory Anopheles strains)
- Goal: break the transmission cycle without necessarily killing the vector population
---
39. Explain the differences between cellulitis and erysipelas caused by Staphylococcus aureus. (5 Marks)
- Cellulitis: infection of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous fat; borders are poorly demarcated/diffuse; skin appears less sharply red, may be warm and tender without a clear raised edge
- Erysipelas: infection confined to the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics; borders are sharply demarcated and raised, with intense, well-defined redness
- Erysipelas has a more acute onset, often with systemic symptoms (fever, chills) appearing early
- Note: classically, erysipelas is most associated with Streptococcus pyogenes rather than S. aureus — worth clarifying this distinction with your lecturer, since the question specifically attributes both to S. aureus
---
40. Describe the mode of action of exotoxin produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. (5 Marks)
- Toxin production requires lysogenic conversion by a bacteriophage carrying the tox gene
- A-B toxin structure: B subunit binds host cell receptor and mediates entry; A subunit has enzymatic activity
- A subunit ADP-ribosylates Elongation Factor-2 (EF-2)
- This inactivates EF-2, halting ribosomal protein synthesis
- Leads to host cell death, with particular clinical impact on cardiac and neural tissue (myocarditis, neuropathy)
---
41. Explain the pathogenesis of Neisseria gonorrhea. (5 Marks)
- Pili mediate initial attachment to mucosal epithelium (urethra, cervix, rectum, pharynx, conjunctiva)
- Opa proteins strengthen adhesion and promote invasion into epithelial cells
- IgA protease destroys protective mucosal secretory IgA
- Lipooligosaccharide (LOS) triggers local inflammation (TNF-alpha release), producing the characteristic purulent discharge
- Organism can survive intracellularly within neutrophils, aided by Por protein interfering with neutrophil killing mechanisms
- Antigenic/phase variation of pili and Opa proteins allows immune evasion and explains lack of lasting immunity after infection
---
## Section C: Essay Questions (Answer only TWO — 40 Marks)
42. Using relevant examples, discuss mating behavior and its application in control of vector-borne diseases. (20 Marks)
Suggested point structure:
- Understanding vector mating behavior is exploited in several vector control strategies
- Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) — mass-rearing and sterilizing male vectors (via radiation), releasing them to mate with wild females, producing no viable offspring, progressively reducing population size
- Requires knowledge of species-specific mating swarm behavior, timing, and location to ensure released sterile males successfully compete with wild males
- Mating swarms — many vector species (e.g., Anopheles) form swarms at specific times/locations for mating; disrupting these swarms (e.g., via pheromone traps or swarm-site targeting with insecticide) can reduce successful reproduction
- Genetic control extensions — combining sterile insect technique with genetic modification (e.g., self-limiting gene drives) to further suppress populations
- Pheromone-based trapping — synthetic sex pheromones used to lure and trap males, reducing mating success and monitoring population density
- Advantages: species-specific, environmentally friendly, does not rely on chemical insecticides
- Limitations: requires detailed knowledge of local vector mating ecology, costly mass-rearing infrastructure, needs sustained release programs over time
